query: Are there any constants of motion for non-spinning particles in Kerr spacetime?
golden_answer: Yes, there are four constants of motion for non-spinning particles in Kerr spacetime.
source_title: Flux-balance laws for spinning bodies under the gravitational self-force
source_text:
## A. Non-spinning particles

We first consider the non-spinning case. Here, the 8dimensional phase space is integrable: for the background motion, there exists a set of four constants of motion $P_{\alpha}$ which are linearly independent, so that

$$
\left(\mathrm{d} P_{1}\right) \wedge \cdots \wedge\left(\mathrm{d} P_{4}\right) \neq 0
$$

and are in involution, so that

$$
\left\{P_{\alpha}, P_{\beta}\right\}=0
$$

Two of these constants of motion, $E$ and $L_{z}$, are linear in $p_{a}$ and related to the isometries of the Kerr spacetime:

$$
E \equiv-t^{a} p_{a}, \quad L_{z} \equiv \varphi^{a} p_{a}
$$

where $t^{a}$ and $\varphi^{a}$ are the Killing vectors generating $t$ and $\varphi$ translations, respectively, in Boyer-Lindquist coordinates. The other two constants, $m^{2}$ and the Carter constant $K$, are quadratic, and are given by

$$
m^{2} \equiv-g^{a b} p_{a} p_{b}, \quad K \equiv K_{a b} p^{a} p^{b}
$$

where $K_{a b}$ is a second-rank Killing tensor satisfying

$$
\nabla_{(a} K_{b c)}=0
$$

(note that the metric $g_{a b}$ is also, trivially, a second-rank Killing tensor).

Since this system is integrable, there exist [83-85] action-angle variables $\left(\vartheta^{\alpha}, J_{\alpha}\right)$, which are canonical in the sense that the only nonzero Poisson bracket is determined by

$$
\left\{\vartheta^{\alpha}, J_{\beta}\right\}=\delta^{\alpha}{ }_{\beta}
$$

and $H$ is only a function of $J_{\alpha}$, so that Hamilton's equations become

$$
\dot{\vartheta}^{\alpha}=\frac{\partial H}{\partial J_{\alpha}}, \quad \dot{J}_{\alpha}=0
$$

where $\partial H / \partial J_{\alpha}$ are the frequencies associated with the action variables. Generically, one can instead use the variables $\left(\vartheta^{\alpha}, P_{\alpha}\right)$, which have similar properties, except they fail to be exactly canonical:

$$
\left\{\vartheta^{\alpha}, P_{\beta}\right\}=\frac{\partial P_{\beta}}{\partial J_{\alpha}} \equiv A^{\alpha}{ }_{\beta}
$$

This set of coordinates is sufficient for the discussion in this paper.

In the coordinates $\left(\vartheta^{\alpha}, P_{\alpha}\right)$, the fact that

$$
\dot{\vartheta}^{\alpha}=\nu^{\alpha}(P), \quad \dot{P}_{\alpha}=0
$$

for some frequencies $\nu^{\alpha}$, implies that

$$
\begin{aligned}
P_{\alpha}\left(\tau^{\prime}\right) & =P_{\alpha}(\tau) \\
\vartheta^{\alpha}\left(\tau^{\prime}\right) & =\vartheta^{\alpha}(\tau)+\left(\tau^{\prime}-\tau\right) \nu^{\alpha}(P)
\end{aligned}
$$

Using Eq. (2.15) for the Hamilton propagator in coordinates, it follows that

$$
\Upsilon^{\theta}{ }_{\mathcal{S}}\left(\tau^{\prime}, \tau\right)=\left(\begin{array}{cc}
\delta^{\alpha}{ }_{\beta} & \left(\tau^{\prime}-\tau\right) \frac{\partial \nu^{\alpha}}{\partial P_{\beta}} \\
0 & \delta^{\beta}{ }_{\alpha}
\end{array}\right)
$$

As such, by taking the $P_{\alpha}$ component of Eq. (1.1), one finds from Eqs. (5.12) and (5.15) that

$$
\begin{aligned}
\left\langle\delta \hat{P}_{\alpha}\left(\tau^{\prime}\right)\right\rangle_{\tau^{\prime}}=-A^{\beta}{ }_{\alpha}\{ & \left(\partial_{\vartheta^{\beta}}\right)^{A} \mathcal{F}_{A} \\
& \left.+\frac{\partial\left\langle\mathcal{H}\left[\Upsilon_{\tau^{\prime}-\tau}(X)\right]\right\rangle_{\tau^{\prime}}}{\partial \vartheta^{\beta}}\right\}
\end{aligned}
$$

In order to derive Eq. (1.2), we then need only show that the second term on the right-hand side of this equation vanishes. This follows from an argument analogous to that in Secs. 2.3 and 3.2 of [1], at least in the case of non-resonant background orbits. There is another, more straightforward way of understanding this argument which we present below.

First, note that we can Fourier expand $\delta H(X, \bar{X})$ in these coordinates as ${ }^{15}$

$$
\delta H(X, \bar{X})=\sum_{\boldsymbol{n}, \bar{n}} H_{\boldsymbol{n}, \bar{n}}(P, \bar{P}) e^{i\left[n_{\alpha} \vartheta^{\alpha}+\bar{n}_{\alpha} \hat{\vartheta}^{\alpha}\right)}
$$

However, note that the dependence of $\delta H$ on $\bar{X}$ is only through the full phase-space trajectory which passes through $\bar{X}$, and so

$$
\begin{aligned}
\delta H(X, \bar{X}) & =\delta H\left[X, \Upsilon_{\Delta}(\bar{X})\right] \\
& =\sum_{\boldsymbol{n}, \bar{n}} H_{\boldsymbol{n}, \bar{n}}(P, \bar{P}) e^{i\left\{n_{\alpha} \vartheta^{\alpha}+\bar{n}_{\alpha}\left[\hat{\vartheta}^{\alpha}+\Delta \bar{\nu}^{\alpha}(\bar{P})\right]\right\}}
\end{aligned}
$$

for any $\Delta$. Comparing this with Eq. (5.17), using the linear independence of the complex exponential, and using the non-resonance condition

$$
n_{\alpha} \neq 0 \quad \Longrightarrow \quad n_{\alpha} \nu^{\alpha}(P) \neq 0
$$

we therefore find that only $H_{\boldsymbol{n}, 0}$ can be non-zero. As such, we can write

$$
\mathcal{H}\left[\Upsilon_{\tau^{\prime}-\tau}(X)\right]=\sum_{\boldsymbol{n}} \mathcal{H}_{\boldsymbol{n}}(P) e^{i n_{\alpha}\left[\vartheta^{\alpha}+\left(\tau^{\prime}-\tau\right) \nu^{\alpha}(P)\right]}
$$

15 That this is a Fourier series (and not a Fourier transform) for the non-compact angle variable follows from the fact that the background orbit from which this quantity is constructed is (multi)periodic. In particular, we need to assume that the background orbit is bound.
in general, if the only nonzero terms in the Fourier expansion weren't those with $\bar{n}^{\alpha}=0$, there could be different quadruples of integers appearing in front of the $\vartheta^{\alpha}$ and $\nu^{\alpha}(P)$ terms. Upon averaging this equation over $\tau^{\prime}$, and once again using the non-resonance condition, we find that

$$
\left\langle\mathcal{H}\left[\Upsilon_{\tau^{\prime}-\tau}(X)\right]\right\rangle_{\tau^{\prime}}=\mathcal{H}_{0}(P)
$$

from which it follows that the second term in Eq. (5.16) vanishes, and so Eq. (1.2) holds.

We conclude this section by considering the angle components of Eq. (1.1). Applying this equation naïvely, and using Eqs. (5.12) and (5.15), we would find that

$$
\begin{aligned}
\left\langle\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{~d} \tau^{\prime}}\right. & {\left[\delta \vartheta^{\alpha}\left(\tau^{\prime}\right)-\left(\tau^{\prime}-\tau\right) \frac{\partial \nu^{\alpha}}{\partial P_{\beta}} \delta P_{\beta}\left(\tau^{\prime}\right)\right]\right\rangle_{\tau^{\prime}} } \\
& =A^{\alpha}{ }_{\beta}\left\{\left(\partial_{P_{\beta}}\right)^{A} \mathcal{F}_{A}+\frac{\partial}{\partial P_{\beta}}\left\langle\mathcal{H}\left[\Upsilon_{\tau^{\prime}-\tau}(X)\right]\right\rangle\right\}
\end{aligned}
$$

This equation, however, is not entirely correct. First, the left-hand side diverges: the quantity inside the average does not have a well-defined average, as one can show that it grows linearly with $\tau^{\prime}-\tau$. This is also reflected in the right-hand side as well: the flux term also diverges, as $\partial_{P^{\alpha}} h_{\alpha^{\prime} b^{\prime}}(X)$ grows linearly with $\tau^{\prime}-\tau$, and so the assumption that $\nabla_{A} h_{\alpha^{\prime} b^{\prime}}(X)$ stays finite no longer holds.

There are two possible ways around this issue. First, note that, in general, there can exist points in phase space where $A^{\alpha}{ }_{\gamma} \partial \nu^{\beta} / \partial P_{\gamma}$ is no longer invertible: this will occur where the mapping between action variables and frequencies is no longer injective; that is, along isofrequency curves. As such, there will exist at least one dual vector $V_{\alpha}$ such that

$$
V_{\alpha} A^{\alpha}{ }_{\beta} \frac{\partial \nu^{\gamma}}{\partial P_{\beta}}=0
$$

and so contracting $V_{\alpha}$ into both sides of Eq. (5.22) would give an expression which is well-defined, although it would not be a true flux-balance law, as it would still involve the local self-force through the conservative Hamiltonian. As another option, it may be possible to recover useful results by generally considering both sides of Eq. (5.22) in a power series in $\tau^{\prime}-\tau$, and equating terms of equal powers. As this begins to stretch the notion of what one can mean by a "flux-balance law", we leave a more careful exploration of this possibility to future work.

query: Does regularity imply subfitness in non-distributive lattices?
golden_answer: No, in non-distributive lattices, regularity no longer implies subfitness.
source_title:
Dedekind-MacNeille and related completions: subfitness, regularity, and
  Booleanness
source_text:
# 5. Regularity 

In this section we characterize when the four completions are regular. For distributive lattices, regularity is a natural strengthening of subfitness. As we saw above, subfitness of the canonical completion is equivalent to the lattice being Boolean. As we will see below, regularity yields the same result for the ideal completion. A more subtle result occurs for the Bruns-Lakser completion. The situation for the Dedekind-MacNeille completion is further complicated by the fact that the latter need not be distributive. Regular lattices behave very differently in the non-distributive setting; in particular, regularity no longer implies subfitness. This will be discussed in more detail in a forthcoming paper. Here we will restrict our attention to Dedekind-MacNeille completions that are distributive.

The next definition is well known for frames (see, e.g., [PP12, Sec. V.5]) and generalizes directly to bounded lattices.

Definition 5.1. Let $A$ be a bounded lattice.
(1) For $a, b \in A, a$ is rather below (well inside) $b$, written $a \prec b$, provided there is $\mathrm{c} \in \mathrm{A}$ such that $\mathrm{a} \wedge \mathrm{c}=0$ and $\mathrm{b} \vee \mathrm{c}=1$.
(2) $A$ is regular if $a \nless b$ implies the existence of $c \in A$ such that $c \prec a$ but $c \nless b$.

Remark 5.2.
(1) If $a$ has the pseudocomplement $a^{*}$, then $a \prec b$ iff $a^{*} \vee b=1$.
(2) A is regular iff every element is the join of elements rather below it. This is the usual definition of regularity in frames, but the above definition is more appealing for arbitrary bounded lattices. Observe that while arbitrary joins may not exist in $A \in$ DLat, if $A$ is regular then the join of $\{b \in A: b \prec a\}$ is $a$, so this join does exist for every $a \in A$.
(3) Every Boolean lattice is regular and in [BMPWW17, p. 360] it is shown that every regular distributive lattice is subfit. In a forthcoming paper we will show that this is no longer true for non-distributive lattices.

Our first goal is to characterize when distributive lattices are regular using Priestley duality. We do so by generalizing some existing results for frames, proved in [BGJ16, Lem. 3.3, 3.6]. Since pseudocomplements may not exist in an arbitrary distributive lattice, the proofs below are somewhat more involved. We start by characterizing the rather below relation.

Lemma 5.3. For $\mathrm{A} \in$ DLat with Priestley dual X ,

$$
a \prec b \text { iff } \downarrow \mathfrak{s}(\mathfrak{a}) \subseteq \mathfrak{s}(\mathfrak{b})
$$

Proof. First suppose $a \prec b$. Then there is $c \in A$ such that $a \wedge c=0$ and $b \vee c=1$. Therefore, $\mathfrak{s}(\mathfrak{a}) \cap \mathfrak{s}(\mathrm{c})=\varnothing$ and $\mathfrak{s}(\mathfrak{b}) \cup \mathfrak{s}(\mathrm{c})=\mathrm{X}$. Since $\mathfrak{s}(\mathrm{c})$ is an upset, $\downarrow \mathfrak{s}(\mathfrak{a}) \cap \mathfrak{s}(\mathrm{c})=\varnothing$. Thus, $\downarrow \mathfrak{s}(\mathfrak{a}) \subseteq \mathrm{X} \backslash \mathfrak{s}(\mathrm{c}) \subseteq \mathfrak{s}(\mathfrak{b})$.

Conversely, suppose $\downarrow \mathfrak{s}(\mathfrak{a}) \subseteq \mathfrak{s}(\mathfrak{b})$. Since $\downarrow \mathfrak{s}(\mathfrak{a})$ is a closed downset, it is the intersection of clopen downsets containing it (see Fact 2.6). But then by compactness, there is a clopen downset D such that $\downarrow \mathfrak{s}(\mathfrak{a}) \subseteq \mathrm{D} \subseteq \mathfrak{s}(\mathfrak{b})$. Let $\mathrm{c} \in \mathrm{A}$ be such that $\mathfrak{s}(\mathrm{c})=\mathrm{X} \backslash \mathrm{D}$. Then $\downarrow \mathfrak{s}(\mathfrak{a}) \cap \mathfrak{s}(\mathrm{c})=\varnothing$ and $\mathrm{X} \backslash \mathfrak{s}(\mathfrak{b}) \subseteq \mathfrak{s}(\mathrm{c})$. Therefore, $\mathfrak{s}(\mathfrak{a}) \cap \mathfrak{s}(\mathrm{c})=\varnothing$ and $\mathfrak{s}(\mathfrak{b}) \cup \mathfrak{s}(\mathrm{c})=\mathrm{X}$. Thus, $\mathfrak{a} \wedge \mathrm{c}=0$ and $\mathrm{b} \vee \mathrm{c}=1$, and hence $\mathfrak{a} \prec \mathfrak{b}$.

Following [BGJ16, Def. 3.4], for each $V \in L(X)$, define the regular part of $V$ to be

$$
\mathrm{R}(\mathrm{~V})=\bigcup\{\mathrm{U} \in \mathrm{~L}(\mathrm{X}): \downarrow \mathrm{U} \subseteq \mathrm{~V}\}
$$

For simplicity, we abbreviate the regular part of $\mathfrak{s}(\mathfrak{a})$ by $\mathrm{R}_{\mathfrak{a}}$.
Proposition 5.4. For $\mathrm{A} \in$ DLat with Priestley dual X , the following are equivalent:
(1) A is regular.
(2) $R_{a}$ is dense in $\mathfrak{s}(\mathfrak{a})$ for each $\mathfrak{a} \in A$.

Proof. (1) $\Rightarrow$ (2): Let $a \in A$. Take $x \in s(a)$ and let $U$ be a clopen neighborhood of $x$ in $\mathfrak{s}(\mathfrak{a})$. We must show that $U \cap R_{a} \neq \varnothing$. Since $U$ is an open neighborhood of $x$, there are $\mathrm{c}, \mathrm{d} \in \mathrm{A}$ such that $\mathrm{x} \in \mathfrak{s}(\mathrm{c}) \backslash \mathfrak{s}(\mathrm{d}) \subseteq \mathrm{U}$ (see Fact 2.6(1)). Without loss of generality we may assume that $\mathfrak{s}(\mathrm{c}) \subseteq \mathfrak{s}(\mathfrak{a})$ (by intersecting $\mathfrak{s}(\mathrm{c})$ with $\mathfrak{s}(\mathfrak{a})$ ). Because $\mathfrak{s}(\mathrm{c}) \backslash \mathfrak{s}(\mathrm{d}) \neq \varnothing$, $\mathfrak{s}(\mathrm{c}) \nsubseteq \mathfrak{s}(\mathrm{d})$, so $\mathrm{c} \nless \mathrm{d}$. Since A is regular, there is $\mathrm{e} \in \mathrm{A}$ such that $\mathrm{e} \prec \mathrm{c}$ and $\mathrm{e} \nless \mathrm{d}$. By Lemma 5.3, $\downarrow \mathfrak{s}(\mathrm{e}) \subseteq \mathfrak{s}(\mathrm{c})$, so $\mathfrak{s}(\mathrm{e}) \subseteq \mathrm{R}_{\mathrm{c}} \subseteq \mathrm{R}_{\mathfrak{a}}$ and $\mathfrak{s}(\mathrm{e}) \nsubseteq \mathfrak{s}(\mathrm{d})$. Thus, $\mathrm{R}_{\mathfrak{a}} \cap(\mathfrak{s}(\mathrm{c}) \backslash \mathfrak{s}(\mathrm{d})) \neq \varnothing$, so $R_{a} \cap U \neq \varnothing$, and hence $R_{a}$ is dense in $\mathfrak{s}(\mathfrak{a})$.

(2) $\Rightarrow$ (1): Let $a \nless b$. Then $s(a) \nsubseteq s(b)$, so $R_{a} \nsubseteq s(b)$ since $R_{a}$ is dense in $s(a)$. Therefore, there is $\mathrm{c} \in \mathrm{A}$ such that $\downarrow \mathrm{s}(\mathrm{c}) \subseteq \mathrm{s}(\mathrm{a})$ and $\mathrm{s}(\mathrm{c}) \nsubseteq \mathrm{s}(\mathrm{b})$. Thus, $\mathrm{c} \prec \mathrm{a}$ (by Lemma 5.3) and $\mathrm{c} \nless \mathrm{~b}$, yielding that A is regular.

We next give a general characterization, akin to Theorem 4.2, of when regularity is preserved and/or reflected when moving between $A$ and $B$, where $A$ is a bounded sublattice of B. We write $\prec_{A}$ or $\prec_{B}$ to emphasize which rather below relation is being used. Clearly $a \prec_{A} b$ implies $a \prec_{B} b$ for all $a, b \in A$, however the converse is not true in general. Because of this, the proposition below requires an extra assumption. As in Theorem 4.2, distributivity plays no rôle.

Proposition 5.5. Let A be a bounded sublattice of B. Suppose that $a \prec_{A} b$ iff $a \prec_{B} b$ for all $\mathrm{a}, \mathrm{b} \in \mathrm{A}$.
(1) If A is join-dense in B and B is regular then A is regular.
(2) If A is both join- and meet-dense in B and A is regular then B is regular.

Proof. (1) Let $a, b \in A$ with $a \nless b$. Since $B$ is regular, there is $x \in B$ with $x \prec_{B} a$ and $x \nless b$. Because $A$ is join-dense in $B$, there is $c \in A$ with $c \leqslant x$ and $c \nless b$. Therefore, $\mathrm{c} \leqslant \mathrm{x} \prec_{\mathrm{B}} \mathrm{a}$, so $\mathrm{c} \prec_{\mathrm{B}} \mathrm{a}$, and hence $\mathrm{c} \prec_{\mathrm{A}} \mathrm{a}$ (by assumption) and $\mathrm{c} \nless \mathrm{~b}$. Thus, A is regular.
(2) Let $x, y \in B$ with $x \nless y$. Since $A$ is both join- and meet-dense in $B$, there are $a, b \in A$ such that $a \leqslant x, y \leqslant b$, and $a \nless b$. Because $A$ is regular, there is $c \in A$ with $c \prec_{A} a$ and $\mathrm{c} \nless \mathrm{~b}$. Therefore, $\mathrm{c} \prec_{\mathrm{B}} \mathrm{a}$ (by assumption) and $\mathrm{c} \nless \mathrm{~b}$, so $\mathrm{c} \prec_{\mathrm{B}} \mathrm{x}$ and $\mathrm{c} \nless \mathrm{y}$. Thus, B is regular.

Since $A$ is both join- and meet-dense in $\mathcal{D M A}$, one could expect that regularity is both preserved and reflected by the Dedekind-MacNeille completion, but this is not the case since the additional assumption in Proposition 5.5 may not be satisfied. We again emphasize that $\mathcal{D M A}$ is not always distributive and hence regularity of $\mathcal{D M A}$ need not imply subfitness. Thus, we make the blanket assumption that $\mathcal{D M A}$ is distributive. While this does not necessarily imply that $\mathcal{D M A}$ is a frame, it is indeed the case provided $\mathcal{D M A}$ is regular.

Proposition 5.6. Let $\mathrm{A} \in$ DLat and $\mathcal{D M A}$ be distributive. Then regularity of $\mathcal{D M A}$ implies that $\mathcal{D M A}$ is a frame, and hence $\mathcal{D M A} \cong \mathcal{B} \mathcal{L} A$.

Proof. If $\mathcal{D M A}$ is distributive, by [BMPWW17, p. 360] regularity of $\mathcal{D M A}$ implies subfitness of $\mathcal{D M A}$, and consequently subfitness of $A$ by Corollary 4.3. But then $A$ is proHeyting by Lemma 4.6. Hence, $\mathcal{D M A}$ is a frame and $\mathcal{D M A} \cong \mathcal{B} \mathcal{L} A$ by Proposition 3.7.

The above proposition yields the following characterization of when a distributive Dede-kind-MacNeille completion is regular.

Proposition 5.7. Let $\mathrm{A} \in$ DLat and $\mathcal{D M A}$ be distributive. The following are equivalent:
(1) $\mathcal{D M A}$ is regular.
(2) A is subfit and $\mathcal{B} \mathcal{L} A$ is regular.
(3) A is proHeyting and $\mathcal{B} \mathcal{L} A$ is regular.

Proof. (1) $\Rightarrow$ (2): That $\mathcal{B} \mathcal{L} A$ is regular follows from Proposition 5.6. Regular implies subfit for distributive lattices, so $\mathcal{D} M A$ is subfit, but then so is $A$ by Corollary 4.3.
$(2) \Rightarrow(3):$ This follows from Lemma 4.6.
$(3) \Rightarrow(1):$ This follows from Proposition 3.7.
We next concentrate on characterizing when $\mathcal{B} \mathcal{L} A$ is regular. Since $\mathcal{B} \mathcal{L} A$ is a frame, the rather below relation is conveniently expressible in terms of the pseudocomplement (see Remark 5.2(1)). We use Priestley duality to describe this pseudocomplement. By Theorem 2.10(2), $\mathcal{B} \mathcal{L} A \cong B L(X)$ and by Remark 2.11, $\mathrm{BL}(\mathrm{X})$ is the sublocale of $\mathrm{OpUp}(\mathrm{X})$ given by the nucleus $\operatorname{int}_{1} \mathrm{cl}$. Since the pseudocomplement in $\mathrm{OpUp}(\mathrm{X})$ is given by

$$
\mathrm{U}^{*}=\mathrm{X} \backslash \downarrow \mathrm{cl}(\mathrm{U})
$$

the pseudocomplement in $\mathrm{BL}(\mathrm{X})$ is given by

$$
\neg \mathrm{U}=\operatorname{int}_{1} \mathrm{cl}\left(\mathrm{U}^{*}\right)=\operatorname{int}_{1} \mathrm{cl}(\mathrm{X} \backslash \downarrow \mathrm{cl}(\mathrm{U}))
$$

Lemma 5.8. Let $\mathrm{U}, \mathrm{V} \in \mathrm{BL}(\mathrm{X})$.
(1) int $\downarrow$ clint $\downarrow \mathrm{cl}(\mathrm{U})=\operatorname{int} \downarrow \mathrm{cl}(\mathrm{U})$.
(2) $\mathrm{U} \prec_{\mathrm{BL}} V$ iff $\operatorname{int} \downarrow \mathrm{cl}(\mathrm{U}) \subseteq \mathrm{cl}(\mathrm{V})$.
(3) If $\mathrm{U}, \mathrm{V} \in \mathrm{L}(\mathrm{X})$, then $\mathrm{U} \prec_{\mathrm{BL}} \mathrm{V}$ iff $\operatorname{int} \downarrow \mathrm{U} \subseteq \mathrm{V}$.

Proof. (1) The right-to-left inclusion is obvious. For the other inclusion, observe that

$$
\text { int } \downarrow \mathrm{cl} \text { int } \downarrow \mathrm{cl}(\mathrm{U}) \subseteq \operatorname{int} \downarrow \mathrm{cl} \downarrow \mathrm{cl}(\mathrm{U}) \subseteq \operatorname{int} \downarrow \mathrm{cl}(\mathrm{U})
$$

because $\downarrow \mathrm{cl}(\mathrm{U})$ is a closed downset (see Fact 2.6(4)).
(2) Recalling how joins are defined in $\mathrm{BL}(\mathrm{X})$ (see Remark 2.11) and that $\mathrm{cl}_{1}=\downarrow \mathrm{cl}$, by (1) we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{U} \prec_{\mathrm{BL}} \mathrm{~V} & \Leftrightarrow \neg \mathrm{U} \vee \mathrm{~V}=\mathrm{X} \\
& \Leftrightarrow \mathrm{cl}(\neg \mathrm{U}) \cup \mathrm{cl}(\mathrm{~V})=\mathrm{X} \\
& \Leftrightarrow \mathrm{clint}_{1} \mathrm{cl}(\mathrm{X} \backslash \downarrow \mathrm{cl}(\mathrm{U})) \cup \mathrm{cl}(\mathrm{~V})=\mathrm{X} \\
& \Leftrightarrow(\mathrm{X} \backslash \text { int } \mathrm{cl}_{1} \text { int } \downarrow \mathrm{cl}(\mathrm{U})) \cup \mathrm{cl}(\mathrm{~V})=\mathrm{X} \\
& \Leftrightarrow \text { int } \downarrow \mathrm{clint} \downarrow \mathrm{cl}(\mathrm{U}) \subseteq \mathrm{cl}(\mathrm{~V}) \\
& \Leftrightarrow \operatorname{int} \downarrow \mathrm{cl}(\mathrm{U}) \subseteq \mathrm{cl}(\mathrm{~V}) .
\end{aligned}
$$

(3) This follows from (2) since $\mathrm{U}, \mathrm{V} \in \mathrm{L}(\mathrm{X})$ imply $\mathrm{cl}(\mathrm{U})=\mathrm{U}$ and $\mathrm{cl}(\mathrm{V})=\mathrm{V}$.

This allows us to see that when restricted to $A$, the rather below relations on $\mathcal{B} \mathcal{L} A$ and $p \mathcal{H}(A$ coincide.
Proposition 5.9. For each $\mathfrak{a}, \mathfrak{b} \in \mathrm{A}, \mathfrak{a} \prec_{\mathcal{B} \mathcal{L} A} \mathfrak{b}$ iff $\mathfrak{a} \prec_{p \mathcal{H}(A} \mathfrak{b}$.
Proof. First suppose that $\mathfrak{a} \prec_{\mathcal{B} \mathcal{L} A} \mathfrak{b}$. Let $X$ be the Priestley space of $A$. Then int $\downarrow \mathfrak{s}(\mathfrak{a}) \subseteq \mathfrak{s}(\mathfrak{b})$ by Lemma 5.8(3). Let $\mathrm{U}=\mathrm{X} \backslash \downarrow \mathfrak{s}(\mathfrak{a})$. Then $\mathrm{U} \in \mathrm{pH}(\mathrm{X})$ by Lemma 3.14, and $\mathfrak{s}(\mathfrak{a}) \cap \mathrm{U}=\varnothing$. Moreover, since int $\downarrow \mathfrak{s}(\mathfrak{a}) \subseteq \mathfrak{s}(\mathfrak{b})$, we have

$$
\mathrm{cl}(\mathrm{U}) \cup \mathfrak{s}(\mathfrak{b})=\mathrm{cl}(\mathrm{X} \backslash \downarrow \mathfrak{s}(\mathfrak{a})) \cup \mathfrak{s}(\mathfrak{b})=\{\mathrm{X} \backslash \operatorname{int} \downarrow \mathfrak{s}(\mathfrak{a})\} \cup \mathfrak{s}(\mathfrak{b})=\mathrm{X}
$$

Therefore, $U \vee_{p H(X)} s(b)=X$, so $s(a)$ is rather below $s(b)$ in $p H(X)$, and hence $a \prec_{p \cap A} b$ by Proposition 3.15 .

For the converse, suppose that $a \prec_{p \cap A} b$. By Proposition 3.15, there is $U \in \mathrm{pH}(\mathrm{X})$ such that $s(a) \cap U=\varnothing$ and $U \vee_{p H(X)} s(b)=X$. The former gives $\downarrow s(a) \cap U=\varnothing$, so $U \subseteq X \backslash \downarrow s(a)$. The latter yields that $c l(U) \cup s(b)=X$. Therefore, $c l(X \backslash \downarrow s(a)) \cup s(b)=X$, so $(X \backslash \operatorname{int} \downarrow s(a)) \cup s(b)=X$, and hence int $\downarrow s(a) \subseteq s(b)$. Thus, $a \prec_{\mathcal{B} \mathcal{L} A} b$ by Lemma 5.8(3).

In order to show that regularity of $\mathcal{B} \mathcal{L} A$ is equivalent to that of $p \mathcal{O}(A$, we require the following general fact.

Proposition 5.10. Let A be a bounded sublattice of B . If A is join-dense in B , then the following are equivalent:
(1) B is regular.
(2) $b=\bigvee\left\{c \in A: c \prec_{B} b\right\}$ for each $b \in B$.
(3) $a=\bigvee\left\{c \in A: c \prec_{B} a\right\}$ for each $a \in A$.

Proof. (1) $\Rightarrow$ (2): Let $b \in B$. Since $B$ is regular, $b=\bigvee\left\{d \in B: d \prec_{B} b\right\}$ (see Remark 5.2(2)). Because A is join-dense in $B, d=\bigvee\{c \in A: c \leqslant d\}$. But $c \leqslant d \prec_{B} b$ implies $c \prec_{B} b$, so $b=\bigvee\left\{c \in A: c \prec_{B} b\right\}$
(2) $\Rightarrow$ (3): This is obvious.
(3) $\Rightarrow$ (1) Let $b \in B$. Since $A$ is join-dense in $B, b=\bigvee\left\{a \in A: a \leqslant b\right\}$. By assumption, $a=\bigvee\left\{c \in A: c \prec_{B} a\right\}$ for each $a \in A$. From $c \prec_{B} a \leqslant b$ it follows that $c \prec_{B} b$. Therefore, $b=\bigvee\left\{c \in A: c \prec_{B} b\right\}$, and hence $B$ is regular.

Theorem 5.11. For $A \in$ DLat, $\mathcal{B} \mathcal{L} A$ is regular iff $p \mathcal{O}(A$ is regular.
Proof. Let $a \in A$. Since $p \mathcal{O}(A$ is join-dense in $\mathcal{B} \mathcal{L} A$, it follows from Proposition 5.9 that $a=\bigvee_{\mathcal{B} \mathcal{L} A}\left\{c \in A: c \prec_{\mathcal{B} \mathcal{L} A} a\right\}$ iff $a=\bigvee_{p \mathcal{O}(A}\left\{c \in A: c \prec_{p \mathcal{O}(A} a\right\}$. But $A$ is join-dense in both $p \mathcal{O}(A$ and $\mathcal{B} \mathcal{L} A$, and thus, by Proposition 5.10, $\mathcal{B} \mathcal{L} A$ is regular iff $p \mathcal{O}(A$ is regular.

We next give a characterization of when $\mathcal{B} \mathcal{L} A$ is regular akin to Proposition 5.4.
Definition 5.12. Let $V \in \mathrm{BL}(\mathrm{X})$. We call

$$
R_{B L}(V):=\bigcup\left\{U \in L(X): U \prec_{B L} V\right\}
$$

the regular part of $V$ in $\mathrm{BL}(\mathrm{X})$.
Theorem 5.13. Let $A \in$ DLat. The following are equivalent:
(1) $\mathcal{B} \mathcal{L} A$ is regular.
(2) $\mathrm{R}_{\mathrm{BL}}(\mathrm{V})$ is dense in V for each $\mathrm{V} \in \mathrm{BL}(\mathrm{X})$.
(3) $\mathrm{R}_{\mathrm{BL}}(\mathrm{V})$ is dense in V for each $\mathrm{V} \in \mathrm{L}(\mathrm{X})$.

Proof. (1) $\Leftrightarrow$ (2): Since $\mathcal{B} \mathcal{L} A \cong B L(X)$, it is enough to show that $B L(X)$ is regular iff $R_{B L}(V)$ is dense in $V$ for each $V \in B L(X)$. Let $V \in B L(X)$. We have

$$
\bigvee\left\{U \in L(X): U \prec_{B L} V\right\}=\operatorname{int}_{1} c l \bigcup\left\{U \in L(X): U \prec_{B L} V\right\}=\operatorname{int}_{1} c l\left(R_{B L}(V)\right)
$$

Therefore, by Proposition 5.10, $\mathrm{BL}(\mathrm{X})$ is regular iff $\mathrm{V}=\operatorname{int}_{1} \mathrm{cl}\left(\mathrm{R}_{\mathrm{BL}}(\mathrm{V})\right)$ iff $\mathrm{R}_{\mathrm{BL}}(\mathrm{V})$ is dense in $V$ for each $V \in \operatorname{BL}(X)$.
$(1) \Leftrightarrow(3)$ : By Proposition 5.10, $\mathrm{BL}(\mathrm{X})$ is regular iff $\mathrm{V}=\bigvee\left\{\mathrm{U} \in \mathrm{L}(\mathrm{X}): \mathrm{U} \prec_{\mathrm{BL}} \mathrm{V}\right\}$ for each $V \in L(X)$. The same proof as in $(1) \Leftrightarrow(2)$ may be used to show that this is equivalent to $\mathrm{R}_{\mathrm{BL}}(\mathrm{V})$ being dense in V for each $\mathrm{V} \in \mathrm{L}(\mathrm{X})$.

We now compare regularity of $A$ to that of $\mathcal{B} \mathcal{L} A$.

query: Can macroscopic quantities like prices and entropy be measured even if microfoundations are unknown or complex?
golden_answer: Yes, macroscopic quantities such as prices, temperature, and entropy can be measured even when microfoundations are not known or too complex to model.
source_title:
Thermal Macroeconomics: An axiomatic theory of aggregate economic
  phenomena
source_text:
### 21.8 Externalities

A particularly important application of the framework will be to consider externalities, where (in our simple exchange economy) the goods held by an agent affect not only that agent's welfare, but indirectly affect the welfare of others (either positively or negatively). So, for example, we might imagine an economy of leisure activities around a small lake, where people can buy and sell fishing rods among other things. But buying (and, presumably using) a fishing rod will reduce the utility of fishing for others, by reducing the number of fish for them to catch. The trader can slowly and hence reversibly sell fishing rods to the lakeside economy until the price of a fishing rod is near zero ${ }^{65}$. At this point there are almost no fish and almost no utility to be gained from owning a fishing rod.

Thus, when fishing rods are few, a subset of people enjoy fishing (so that the summed utility for fishers may be large); but when the number of fishing rods is high, the summed utility for fishers may be much lower. So the existence of externalities breaks the relationship between entropy and "utility" in any sense relevant to the welfare of individual agents. This is analogous to the breakdown of the welfare theorems in conventional microeconomics. The connection between the equililbrium outcomes of a competitive market and Pareto optimality requires that there are no externalities, and does not hold otherwise.

Following conventional economic analysis, we can address the problem of externalities in our lakeside economy by, for example, having a market for a fixed number of fishing permits (a "cap and trade" scheme), or simply fixing the number of fishing rods, so that voluntary exchanges involving fishing rods no longer harms other agents. Notice that the present approach still provides a potential route to analyse whether one set of rules in an economy is "better" than another, without having to measure and sum the utilities of individual agents. Specifically, we can make clones of our lakeside economy, each governed by different rules; and then put these in contact and ask about the direction of the flow of money when the clones are put in financial contact ${ }^{66}$. A natural assumption is that money will flow to the clone with the "best" set of rules-which imply that an economy with such a set of rules would have a lower temperature (and thus that the marginal utility of money will be greater). We leave this and related cases (e.g., dealing with positive externalities) for future work.

[^0]
[^0]:    ${ }^{65}$ Reversibility assumes, perhaps implausibly, that fish stocks would fully recover as the number of fishing rods reduces-though the assumption is perhaps less implausible if we recall that reversible trades are required to be arbitrarily slow
    ${ }^{66}$ or indeed migration of people, if we include this in our analysis.

We see the fact that the thermal macroeconomic framework applies straightforwardly in the context of externalities as a significant strength: economies will be governed by the second law whether there are externalities or not. All that changes is the interpretation of entropy as corresponding to aggregate welfare. Indeed, by operating at the macro-level, the TM approach, and the second law in particular, applies irrespective of the micro-foundations concerning agents and their interactions, so long as the macro-level axioms hold. So, for example, there are no requirements that agents make decisions based on consulting a utility function of any form, that their preferences are transitive or complete, and so on. Moreover, an agent's utility (if it has one) and behaviour may depend in complex ways on the utilities and behaviours of other agents $[\mathrm{FF}]^{67}$ or on comparisons with the agent's own prior or current experience [VI]. Different microfoundations will, of course, change the properties of the entropy function, just as in physics where different microscopic properties of a gas (for example, whether it approximates an ideal gas in which molecules do not interact or whether the gas molecules are subject to van der Waals forces) determine the entropy function. Crucially, though, the macro-level analysis can proceed and macroscopic quantities such as prices, temperature and entropy can be measured, even when the microfoundations are not known or are too complex to model.

query: What is the difference in matching efficiency between private and public job search platforms?
golden_answer: The study found that matching efficiency on a private job search platform for high-skill workers is more volatile but generally higher than on a public platform. This suggests an increasing reliance on private platforms for high-skill job searches.
source_title:
Nonparametric Estimation of Matching Efficiency and Elasticity on a
  Private On-the-Job Search Platform: Evidence from Japan, 2014-2024
source_text:
# 6 Conclusion 

This paper uses proprietary data from BizReach, an online job scouting platform in Japan, spanning from 2014 to 2024, to estimate the matching function for high-skill employed workers in a private on-the-job search platform. The results are compared to a public off-the-job search platform, specifically targeting unemployed workers seeking full-time jobs. Findings suggest that matching efficiency on the private platform is more volatile but generally higher than on the public platform, highlighting the increasing reliance on private platforms for high-skill job searches. Furthermore, the private platform demonstrates a higher matching elasticity with respect to unemployment (between 0.6 and 0.8 ) compared to the public platform, while the elasticity with respect to vacancies is similar (between 0.8 and 1.1). This indicates a more balanced responsiveness to changes in both users and vacancies on the private platform, compared to the more stable but less dynamic public platform, Hello Work.

Additionally, industry-level heterogeneity is evident across both platforms, reflecting differing labor market dynamics by sector. However, while this paper provides key insights into the matching function for on-the-job searches, the analysis may not fully represent the broader on-the-job search labor market, particularly for non-high-skill workers in Japan. Moreover, the standard assumption of homogeneity among workers and vacancies may overlook important nuances. Future research should focus on expanding this analysis to other private platforms and exploring individual-level behavior, as discussed in studies like Kambayashi et al. (2025) and Roussille and Scuderi (2023), to provide a more comprehensive understanding of labor market dynamics.

query: Can an upper or lower bound be considered best-possible in terms of its definition?
golden_answer: Yes, an upper or lower bound can be considered best-possible if no valid bounds exist beyond them within any small positive increment or decrement.

  a problem of Kolmogorov with application to Individual Treatment Effects
source_text:
# 3 Sharpness of the bounds 

To investigate the tightness of the bounds, we first distinguish three notions of sharpness.
For two random variables $X, Y$ with fixed marginals $F, G$, respectively, let $J(\cdot)$ be the distribution function of $X+Y$ and let $J_{\ell}(\cdot)$ and $J^{u}(\cdot)$ be bounding functions such that $J_{\ell}(z) \leq J(z) \leq J^{u}(z)$ for all $z \in \mathbb{R}$.

Definition 7 (Achievability at a point). We say the lower bound $J_{\ell}(\cdot)$ is achievable at $z=z_{0}$ if there exists a joint distribution $H$ of $X, Y$ satisfying the marginals such that under $H, J\left(z_{0}\right)=J_{\ell}\left(z_{0}\right)$. The upper bound $J^{u}(\cdot)$ is achievable at $z=z_{0}$ if there exists a joint distribution $H$ of $X, Y$ satisfying the marginals such that under $H, J\left(z_{0}\right)=J^{u}\left(z_{0}\right)$.

Definition 8 (Pointwise Best-Possible). We say the lower bound $J_{\ell}(\cdot)$ is pointwise best-possible if for all $z_{0} \in \mathbb{R}$ and $\varepsilon>0, J_{\ell}\left(z_{0}\right)+\varepsilon$ will not be a valid lower bound for $J\left(z_{0}\right)$. In other words, for all $z_{0} \in \mathbb{R}$ and $\varepsilon>0$, there exists a joint distribution $H$ of $X, Y$ satisfying the marginals such that under $H, J\left(z_{0}\right)<J_{\ell}\left(z_{0}\right)+\varepsilon$. The upper bound $J^{u}(\cdot)$ is pointwise sharp if for all $z_{0} \in \mathbb{R}$ and $\varepsilon>0$, $J^{u}\left(z_{0}\right)-\varepsilon$ will not be a valid lower bound for $F\left(z_{0}\right) .{ }^{5}$

Definition 9 (Uniformly Sharp). We say the lower bound $J_{\ell}(\cdot)$ is uniformly sharp of $H$ if there exists a single joint distribution $H$ of $X, Y$ satisfying the marginals such that under $H, J(z)=J_{\ell}(z)$ for all $z \in \mathbb{R}$. The upper bound $J^{u}(\cdot)$ is uniformly sharp if there exists a single joint distribution $H$ of $X, Y$ satisfying the marginals such that under $H, J(z)=J^{u}(z)$ for all $z \in \mathbb{R}$.

Following these definitions, if a bound is uniformly sharp, then it is achievable for all $z \in \mathbb{R}$ and also pointwise sharp. If a bound is achievable for all $z \in \mathbb{R}$, then it is pointwise sharp. However, a pointwise sharp bound may not be achievable for all $z \in \mathbb{R}$.

[^0]
[^0]:    ${ }^{4}$ In Appendix E, we discuss the relationship between the bounds in Rüschendorf (1982) and the Makarov bounds presented in this section.
    ${ }^{5}$ Unlike Firpo and Ridder (2019), we differentiate between achievability and pointwise sharpness because a bound can be pointwise sharp but not necessarily achievable.

query: Why might complex moments be relevant despite not being commonly used in econometrics?
golden_answer: Complex moments extend the applicability of moment calculations into areas like statistical mechanics and quantum physics. They offer additional insights that can be integrated with minimal adaptation into econometric models, potentially uncovering new relationships or identities within data.
source_title: Moments by Integrating the Moment-Generating Function
source_text:
# 1 Introduction 

Moments of random variables, including conditional moments, are central to much of economics, finance, and econometrics. In this paper, we introduce a new method for obtaining moments of random variables with a well-defined moment-generating function (MGF). The proposed method is general, computationally efficient, and can offer solutions to problems where standard methods are inadequate.

It is well known that the $k$-th integer moment of a random variable $X$, with MGF, $M_{X}(s)=\mathbb{E}\left[e^{s X}\right]$, is given by $\mathbb{E}\left[X^{k}\right]=M_{X}^{(k)}(0)$, where $M_{X}^{(k)}(s)$ is the $k$-th derivative of $M_{X}(s)$. Non-integer moments and fractional absolute moments, $\mathbb{E}\left|X^{r}\right|, r \in \mathbb{R}$, have more complicated expressions, typically integrals that involve derivatives of the MGF or derivatives of the characteristic function (CF). ${ }^{1}$ In this paper, we derive novel integral expressions for computing fractional moments, including fractional absolute moments, and fractional central moments. Unlike existing expressions, the new expressions do not involve derivatives (of the MGF or the CF). Thus, the new expressions are particularly useful when derivatives are prohibitively difficult to obtain. This is often the case in dynamic models, where the conditional MGF is defined from recursive non-linear expressions. The new method is labelled CMGF because it relies on a complex extension of the MGF, and provides expressions for complex moments, $\mathbb{E}|X|^{r}, r \in \mathbb{C}$. Although complex moments are not commonly used in econometrics, this generalization can be included with minimal adaptation. ${ }^{2}$ The new expressions can also be used for establishing new identities, such as the expression for the reciprocal Gamma function, which we infer from the absolute moment of a Gaussian random variable.

The new CMGF expressions involve integrals, and while these cannot be evaluated analytically in most cases, they facilitate new ways to compute moments numerically, which are fast and accurate. We demonstrate this with the normal-inverse Gaussian distribution. We also show that the CMGF method offers fast and accurate moments in dynamic models, where we are not aware of good alternative methods. Specifically, we use the CMGF method to compute moments of cumulative returns in the Heston-Nandi GARCH (HNG) model, to compute moments of realized volatilities in the Heterogeneous Autoregressive Gamma (HARG) model, and to compute conditional moments in

[^0]
[^0]:    ${ }^{1}$ Kawata (1972) provides an expression for $\mathbb{E}|X|^{r}$ that involves several derivatives of the CF and Laue (1980) provides an expression based on fractional derivatives, see also Wolfe (1975), Samko et al. (1993), Matsui and Pawlas (2016), and Tomovski et al. (2022). For fractional moments of non-negative variables, similar expressions were derived in Cressie et al. (1981), Cressie and Borkent (1986), Jones (1987), and Schürger (2002).
    ${ }^{2}$ Complex moments are commonly used other fields, including statistical mechanics, number theory, and quantum physics. In part, because complex moments are related to Mellin transforms.

the Autoregressive Poisson Model.
The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. We present the new moment expressions in Section 2. Theorem 1 has the expression for absolute fractional moments for general random variables, Theorem 2 has the expression for fractional moments of non-negative random variables, and Theorem 3 presents a new expression for integer moments. As an example, we apply CMGF to the normal-inverse Gaussian distribution. Section 3 presents three applications of the new expressions in dynamic models, and Section 4 concludes.

query: Is the index of an equilibrium component invariant to equivalent presentations of a game?
golden_answer: Yes.
source_title: Robust Equilibria in Generic Extensive form Games
source_text:
# 2.3. Index Theory 

The fixed point index contains information about the robustness of fixed points of a map when such a map is perturbed to a nearby map. Since Nash equilibria are fixed points, we can apply index theory to them (cf. Ritzberger, 1994). The classical introduction to index theory usually requires some concepts from algebraic topology. For the purposes of this paper, this can be bypassed without much hindrance. Results in this section can be found in McLennan (2018, pp 245-265) and Pahl (2023).

Let $\mathbb{G}$ be a normal-form game with mixed strategy $\Sigma$. Given a neighborhood $O$ of $\Sigma$ suppose $f: O \rightarrow \Sigma$ is a differentiable map. Let $d_{f}$ be the displacement of $f$, i.e., $d_{f}(\sigma)=\sigma-f(\sigma)$. Then the fixed points of $f$ are the zeros of $d_{f}$. Suppose now that the Jacobian of $d_{f}$ at a zero $\sigma$ of $f$ is nonsingular. We assign the index +1 to $\sigma$ if the determinant of the Jacobian of $d_{f}$ is positive or -1 if such a determinant is negative. For the next definition, given a subset $\mathscr{O}$ of $\Sigma$, we denote by $\operatorname{cl}_{\Sigma}(\mathscr{O})$ the closure of $\mathscr{O}$ with respect to $\Sigma$.

Definition 2.2. An open neighborhood $\mathscr{O} \subset \Sigma$ of a component of equilibria (in mixed strategies) $K$ of normal-form game $\mathbb{G}$ is admissible if every equilibrium of $\mathbb{G}$ in $\mathrm{cl}_{\Sigma}(\mathscr{O})$ belongs to $K$.

When a finite game $\mathbb{G}$ has a component of equilibria $K$ that consists of more than a single strategy profile, we extend the definition of the index as follows. Take a continuous map $g_{\mathbb{G}}$ : $\Sigma \rightarrow \Sigma$ such that the fixed points of $g_{\mathbb{G}}$ are the Nash equilibria of game $\mathbb{G}$ and $g_{\mathbb{G}}$ continuously depends on the payoffs of $\mathbb{G}$. An example of such a map is the map Nash (1951) constructed to prove existence of equilibria in mixed strategies. Consider a neighborhood $O$ of $\Sigma$ and $r: O \rightarrow \Sigma$ a retraction to the closest point in $\Sigma$. Let $\mathscr{O} \subset O$ be an open neighborhood of $K$ in the affine space generated by $\Sigma$, whose closure contains no other fixed point of $g$. We approximate $\left(g_{\mathbb{G}} \circ r\right)$ uniformly by a differentiable function $f: O \rightarrow \Sigma$ without fixed points on the boundary of $\mathscr{O}$ and such that the displacement of $f$ at any fixed point has nonsingular Jacobian. For any sufficiently close approximation, the sum of the indexes of the (isolated) fixed points of $f$ in $\mathscr{O}$ is constant and can be taken as the definition of the index of the component $K .{ }^{9}$

We can now define the index with respect to the best-reply correspondence of game $\mathbb{G}$ following the same procedure as in GW. Consider now $\mathscr{O} \cap \Sigma$. For notational convenience, we will denote this intersection from now on as $\mathscr{O}$. Let $W$ be an open neighborhood of $\operatorname{Graph}\left(\mathrm{BR}^{\mathbb{G}}\right)$ such that $W \cap\left\{(\sigma, \sigma) \in \Sigma \times \Sigma \mid \sigma \in \mathrm{cl}_{\Sigma}(\mathscr{O})-\mathscr{O}\right\}=\varnothing$. There exists $\bar{W} \subset W$ a neighborhood of $\operatorname{Graph}\left(\mathrm{BR}^{\mathbb{G}}\right)$ such that any two continuous functions $f_{0}$ and $f_{1}$ from $\Sigma$ to $\Sigma$ whose graphs are in the neighborhood $\bar{W}$ are homotopic by a homotopy $H:[0,1] \times \Sigma \rightarrow \Sigma$ with

[^0]
[^0]:    ${ }^{9}$ Under the continuous dependence of the payoffs of $\mathbb{G}$, this definition of index is independent of the particular map $g_{\mathbb{G}}$ used, it only depends on the game $\mathbb{G}$ (cf. DeMichelis and Germano (2000)).

Graph $(H(t, \cdot)) \subset \bar{W}$ for all $t \in[0,1]$ (cf. McLennan, 1989). Take a continuous map $f: \Sigma \rightarrow \Sigma$ with $\operatorname{Graph}(f) \subset \bar{W}$. We define the best-reply index of component $K$, denoted $\operatorname{Ind}_{\mathrm{BR}^{\mathrm{C}}}(K)$, as the fixed point index of the continuous map $\left.f\right|_{\mathscr{O}}: \mathscr{O} \rightarrow \Sigma$. The choice of the neighborhood $W$ and the homotopy property of the index (see Dold, 1972, Chapter VII, 5.15) imply that the index of the component is the same for any continuous map with graph in the neighborhood $\bar{W}$. We note that defining the index of a component from, say, the map that Nash used in (Nash, 1951) or from the best-reply correspondence are two distinct ways of defining the index, which can be shown to be equivalent (cf. GW). In addition, this process to define the index applies with insignificant changes if the correspondence between the simplices of strategies is contractible valued instead of convex valued (cf. McLennan, 1989). ${ }^{10}$ This fact will play an important role in Section 5.1, as we need to consider selections of a best-reply correspondence which are not necessarily convex-valued, but are contractible-valued.

One can generalize the definition of the best-reply index of a component of equilibria to the best-reply index of an admissible neighborhood, by using the exact same procedure as in the previous paragraph. This yields the index of a neighborhood by summing the indexes of the components of equilibria which are contained in it. For convenience, whenever we refer to the index of a component or an admissible neighborhood, it will be implicit that we refer to the best-reply index.

We are now ready to recall a few known properties of the index of equilibria which we will use in the proof of our main result. The proofs that the index satisfies such properties can be found in McLennan (2018) or GW.
I. 1 The index of an admissible neighborhood is locally constant with respect to payoff perturbations of the game. Formally, fix an admissible neighborhood $O$ in the mixed strategy set of a finite game $\mathbb{G}$. Then there exist $\bar{\delta}>0$, such that for any $0 \leq \delta \leq \bar{\delta}$ and a $\delta$-payoff-perturbation $\mathbb{G}^{\delta}$ of game $\mathbb{G}$, the index of $O$ (with respect to $\mathbb{G}^{\delta}$ ) is constant.
I. 2 The index of an equilibrium component is invariant to equivalent presentations of a game. If $K$ is a component of equilibria of $\mathbb{G}$ with index $c$, then for any equivalent game $\bar{G}$, the index of the equivalent component $\bar{K}$ is also $c$.
I. 3 The index of a component is invariant to the deletion of strictly inferior replies to the component. If $K$ is a component of equilibria with index $c$ of game $\mathbb{G}$, then deleting from the normal-form of game $\mathbb{G}$ the pure strategies of player $n$ which are strictly inferior replies to every profile in the component $K$ yields a new game $\mathbb{G}^{\prime}$ with the same component $K$ as an equilibrium component in $\mathbb{G}^{\prime}$ and with the same index $c$.
We also need three well-known properties of the index. For our purposes, we particularize their statements as follows:
I. 4 Multiplication: Let $\mathrm{BR}^{\mathbb{G}}: \Sigma \Rightarrow \Sigma$ and $\mathrm{BR}^{\mathbb{G}^{\prime}}: \Sigma^{\prime} \Rightarrow \Sigma^{\prime}$ be the best-reply correspondences of (respectively) games $\mathbb{G}$ and $\mathbb{G}^{\prime}$. Let $\mathrm{BR}^{\mathbb{G}} \times \mathrm{BR}^{\mathbb{G}^{\prime}}$ be the correspondence taking $(\sigma, \tau) \in$ $\Sigma \times \Sigma^{\prime}$ to $\mathrm{BR}^{\mathbb{G}}(\sigma) \times \mathrm{BR}^{\mathbb{G}^{\prime}}(\tau)$. If $O \times O^{\prime} \subset \Sigma \times \Sigma^{\prime}$ contains no fixed points of $\mathrm{BR}^{\mathbb{G}} \times \mathrm{BR}^{\mathbb{G}^{\prime}}$ in its boundary, then $O$ (respectively $O^{\prime}$ ) has no fixed points of $\mathrm{BR}^{\mathbb{G}}$ (respectively $\mathrm{BR}^{\mathbb{G}^{\prime}}$ ) in its boundary, and the index of $O \times O^{\prime}$ with respect to $\mathrm{BR}^{\mathbb{G}} \times \mathrm{BR}^{\mathbb{G}^{\prime}}$ is the multiplication of the indexes of $O$ (with respect to $\mathrm{BR}^{\mathbb{G}}$ ) and of $O^{\prime}$ (with respect to $\mathrm{BR}^{\mathbb{G}^{\prime}}$ ).

[^0]
[^0]:    ${ }^{10}$ A topological space $X$ is contractible if there exists a continuous map $T:[0,1] \times X \rightarrow X$ and $x_{0} \in X$ such that $T(0, \cdot)=\operatorname{id}_{X}$ and $T(1, \cdot)=x_{0}$.

I. 5 Commutativity: Let $F: \Sigma \Rightarrow \Sigma$ be an upper hemicontinuous correspondence that is nonempty, compact and convex valued. Let $e: \Sigma \rightarrow \Sigma^{\prime}$ be a continuous map with leftinverse $q: \Sigma^{\prime} \rightarrow \Sigma$. If $X$ is a component of fixed points of $e \circ F \circ q: \Sigma^{\prime} \Rightarrow \Sigma^{\prime}$ then $q(X)$ is a component of fixed points of $F$ and their indexes agree.
I. 6 Excision: Let $F: \Sigma \Rightarrow \Sigma$ be an upper hemicontinuous correspondence that is nonempty, compact and convex valued. Suppose $\tilde{\mathscr{O}}$ and $\mathscr{O}$ are both admissible neighborhoods in $\Sigma$ whose closures in $\Sigma$ contain the same fixed points of $F$. Then the index of $\mathscr{O}$ and that of $\tilde{\mathscr{O}}$ with respect to $F$ are identical.

We conclude this section with the following result. In particular, it implies that if a component has zero index, then some ending node is reached with probability zero.

Proposition 2.3. If an equilibrium outcome $Q$ induced by a component of equilibria in mixed strategies $K$ has full support, then $K$ has non-zero index.

Proof. See Appendix A.

# 4.2 Bounded Sub-Cluster LP Relaxation for Preclustered Instances 

Following [CLLN23], we form an LP relaxation aiming at finding the good clustering $\mathcal{C}_{1}^{*}$. In the LP, we have a variable $y_{S}^{*}$, for every $s \in[n]$, and $S \subseteq V$ of size at most $r$ (recall that $r=\Theta\left(1 / \varepsilon^{12}\right)$ ), that denotes the number of clusters in $\mathcal{C}_{1}^{*}$ of size $s$ containing $S$ as a subset. When $S \neq \emptyset$, there is at most one such cluster and thus $y_{S}^{*} \in\{0,1\}$ indicates if $S$ is a subset of a cluster of size $s$ in $\mathcal{C}_{1}^{*}$. For every $S \subseteq V$ of size at most $r$,

let $y_{S}:=\sum_{s} y_{S}^{*}$ denote the number of clusters (of any size) in $\mathcal{C}_{1}^{*}$ containing $S$ as a subset. Again, if $S \neq \emptyset$, then $y_{S} \in\{0,1\}$ indicates if $S$ is a subset of a cluster in $\mathcal{C}_{1}^{*}$. For every $u v \in\binom{V}{2}$, we have a variable $x_{u v}$ indicating if $u$ and $v$ are separated or not in $\mathcal{C}_{1}^{*}$. We call the LP the bounded sub-cluster LP relaxation, as we have variables indicating if a small set $S$ is a subset of a cluster or not.

We use the following type of shorthand: $y_{u}^{s}$ for $y_{\{u\}}^{s}, y_{u v}^{s}$ for $y_{\{u, v\}}^{s}$, and $y_{S u}^{s}$ for $y_{S \cup\{u\}}^{s}$. The bounded sub-cluster LP is defined as follows. In the description, we always have $s \in[n], u \in V$ and $u v \in\binom{V}{2}$. For convenience, we omit the restrictions. By default, any variable of the form $y_{S}$ or $y_{S}^{s}$ has $|S| \leq r$; if not, we do not have the variable and the constraint involving it.

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \min \quad \operatorname{obj}(x) \\
& \sum_{s=1}^{n} y_{S}^{s}=y_{S} \quad \forall S \\
& y_{u}=1 \quad \forall u \\
& y_{u v}+x_{u v}=1 \quad \forall u v \\
& \frac{1}{s} \sum_{u} y_{S u}^{s}=y_{S}^{s} \quad \forall s, S \\
& y_{S}^{s} \geq 0 \quad \forall s, S
\end{aligned}
$$

(bounded sub-cluster LP)

$$
\begin{aligned}
& x_{u v}=0 \quad \forall u, v \text { in a same } K \in \mathcal{K} \\
& x_{u v}=1 \quad \forall \text { non-admissible edge } u v \\
& y_{u}^{s}=0 \quad \forall u, s \in\left[k_{u}-1\right] \cup\left[k_{u}+1, k_{u}+\varepsilon_{1}\left|N_{\text {adm }}(u)\right|\right] \\
& \sum_{T^{\prime} \subseteq T}(-1)^{\left|T^{\prime}\right|} y_{S \cup T^{\prime}}^{s} \in\left[0, y_{S}^{s}\right] \quad \forall s, S \cap T=\emptyset \\
& y_{S}^{s} \geq 0 \quad \forall s, S
\end{aligned}
$$

(6) gives the definition of $y_{S}$, (7) requires $u$ to be contained in some cluster, and (8) gives the definition of $x_{u v}$. (9) says if $y_{S}^{s}=1$, then there are exactly $s$ elements $u \in V$ with $y_{S u}^{s}=1$. (An exception is when $S=\emptyset$; but the equality also holds.) (10) is the non-negativity constraint. (11) and (12) follows from that $\mathcal{C}_{1}^{*}$ is a good clustering, and (13) follows from (A1). The left side of (14) is the number of clusters of size $s$ containing $S$ but does not contain any vertex in $T$. So the inequality holds. This corresponds to a SheraliAdams relaxation needed for the correlated rounding [RT12], see Lemma 16. The running time for solving the LP is $n^{O(r)}=n^{O\left(1 / \varepsilon^{12}\right)}$.

# 2.3. Generically stable groups. 

Definition 2.4. [PT11, Definition 2.1] A type-definable group $G(x)$ is generically stable if there is a generically stable $p \in S_{G}(\mathcal{U})$ which is left $G(\mathcal{U})$ invariant (we might use " $G(\mathcal{U})$-invariant" and " $G$-invariant" interchangeably when talking about global types).

Fact 2.5. [PT11, Lemma 2.1] Suppose that $G$ is a generically stable typedefinable group in an arbitrary theory, witnessed by a generically stable type $p \in S_{G}(\mathcal{U})$. Then we have:
(1) $p$ is the unique left $G(\mathcal{U})$-invariant and also the unique right $G(\mathcal{U})$ invariant type;
(2) $p=p^{-1}$ (where $p^{-1}:=\operatorname{tp}\left(g^{-1} / \mathcal{U}\right)$ for some/any $g \models p$ in a bigger monster model $\left.\mathcal{U}^{\prime} \succ \mathcal{U}\right)$.

By Fact 2.4 and its symmetric version, we get:
Corollary 2.6. A type-definable group $G(x)$ is generically stable if and only if there is a generically stable $p \in S_{G}(\mathcal{U})$ which is right $G(\mathcal{U})$-invariant.

query: What does it mean for two stable groups to be principal?
golden_answer: Two stable groups are said to be principal if they have the same connected components, i.e., $G_{1}^{0} = G_{2}^{0}$.

  theories
source_text:
# 3. DEFINABLE HULLS IN STABLE GROUPS 

3.1. General results. In this subsection, we will present some results of Wagner on groups and their subgroups in stable theories. We work in a sufficiently saturated model of a stable theory (with elimination of imaginaries). The results presented below remain valid for type-definable stable groups but for the sake of the presentation, we will assume that ambient model is the universe of a group $(G, \cdot)$. Moreover, we identify a formula with the corresponding definable subset.

Recall that a definable subset $\varphi(x, \bar{a})$ is generic in the stable group $G$ if $G$ is covered by finitely many bi-translates of the form $g^{-1} \cdot \varphi(x, \bar{a}) \cdot h^{-1}$ with $g$ and $h$ elements of $G$. Since the order property does not hold in stable theories, we always have that either a definable subset or its complement is generic in $G$. This yields the existence of generic types of $G$,

i.e. types that only contain generic formulae. Note that the type $p=\operatorname{tp}(g / A)$ is generic if $(\circ)$ for every $h$ in $G$ independent from $g$ the product $g \cdot h$ is independent from $h$.

The connected component of $G$, denoted by $G^{0}$, is the intersection of all definable subgroups of finite index. The (left-) stabilizer of a stationary type $p=\operatorname{tp}(g / A)$ is the set

$$
\operatorname{Stab}_{G}(p)=\{h \in G \mid h \cdot \mathfrak{p}=\mathfrak{p}\}
$$

where $\mathfrak{p}$ is the unique global non-forking extension of $p$ and $g \cdot \mathfrak{p}$ is given by the natural action of $G$ on the space of types induced by left translation. Using the definability of types in stable theories, the stabilizer of $p$ can be written as the intersection of the definable subgroups

$$
\operatorname{Stab}_{G}(p, \varphi)=\{g \in G \mid \models \forall \bar{z}\left(d_{p} \varphi(g x, \bar{z}) \leftrightarrow d_{p} \varphi(x, \bar{z})\right)\}
$$

A type is generic in $G$ if and only if its stabilizer equals $G^{0}$. We refer the reader to Poizat's volume on stable groups [24] for proofs and details.
Remark 3.1. In Section 4 we will also consider generic types and stabilizers for groups definable in simple theories. In this case, there is no notion of generic formula but a type is called generic if it satisfies the condition in (o). Since types are not necessarily stationary, the left-stabilizer $\operatorname{Stab}_{G}(p)$ of a type $p$ is defined as the subgroup generated by the set

$$
\operatorname{St}(p)=\{h \in G \mid \exists g \models p \text { with } g \underset{A}{\perp} h \text { such that } h \cdot g \models p\}
$$

Right-stabilizers are defined analogously. More details and proofs can be found in [7].
Wagner showed in [27] that the notions for stable groups extend to non-definable subgroups of $G$.
Definition 3.2. ([28, Definitions 1.1.2, 2.1.1, 2.1.2 and 2.1.3]) Let $H$ be a (possibly nondefinable) subgroup of the stable group $(G, \cdot)$.
(1) A definable subset $\varphi(x, \bar{a})$ of $G$ is called generic for $H$ if $H$ is covered by finitely many bitranslates of $\varphi(x, \bar{a})$ by elements from $H$; that is, there are elements $g_{1}, \ldots, g_{n}$ and $h_{1}, \ldots, h_{n}$ of $H$ such that for every $h$ in $H$ holds $\bigvee_{i=1}^{n} \varphi\left(g_{i} \cdot h \cdot h_{i}, \bar{a}\right)$.
(2) A type $p$ in $S_{1}(A)$ with $A \supset H$ is generic for $H$ if all its formulae are generic for $H$.
(3) The definable hull of $H$ (in $G$ ), denoted $\operatorname{dc}_{G}(H)$, is the intersection of all definable subgroups (with parameters) of $G$ containing $H$.

As in the case of stable groups, generic types for $H$ always exist and a definable set is generic for $H$ if and only if $H$ is covered by left translates.

Consider the subspace $S_{1}^{H}(A)$ which consists of the types in $S_{1}(A)$ that are finitely satisfiable in $H$. By coheirness, each type in $S_{1}^{H}(A)$ does not fork over $H$ and its restriction to $H$ is stationary. Every generic type for $H$ lies in $S_{1}^{H}(A)$, since we considered translates by elements from $H$ in the definition of genericity for $H$ in $G$.
Fact 3.3. ([27, Lemma 25, Lemma 26, Remark 27 and Lemma 28])
(1) The groups $\mathrm{dc}_{G}(H)$ and $\mathrm{dc}_{G}(H)^{0}$ are type-definable over $H$, and hence do not depend on the ambient model.

(2) A type $p$ in $S_{1}^{H}(A)$ is generic for $H$ if and only if $\operatorname{Stab}_{G}(p)=\operatorname{dc}_{G}(H)^{0}$. In particular, every type that is generic for $H$ in $G$ is also generic in the typedefinable group $\operatorname{dc}_{G}(H)$.

The first part follows from the Baldwin-Saxl condition for definable groups in stable theories. For the second part, Wagner uses that a definable subgroup $H^{\prime}$ contains $\operatorname{dc}_{G}(H)^{0}$ if and only if the index $\left[H: H \cap H^{\prime}\right]$ is finite. The general structure of proofs is as in the definable case.

Before exploring how Wagner's results can be used in the setting of the criterion given in the next section, we first introduce the following notion:

Definition 3.4. Consider two stable groups $\left(G_{2}, \cdot\right) \subset\left(G_{1}, \cdot\right)$. We say that $G_{2}$ is principal in $G_{1}$ if they have the same connected components, i.e. $G_{1}^{0}=G_{2}^{0}$.

In his lecture notes [7], Casanovas refers to this notion as being generic since it is equivalent to the partial type defining $G_{2}$ being generic in $G_{1}$ by part (ii) of the next remark.

Remark 3.5. Let $\left(G_{2}, \cdot\right) \subset\left(G_{1}, \cdot\right)$ be two stable groups, both defined over $A$. The following conditions are equivalent:
(i) The group $G_{2}$ is principal in $G_{1}$.
(ii) Every generic type of $G_{2}$ (over $A$ ) is also a generic type of $G_{1}$.
(iii) There is some element $g$ of $G_{2}$ such that $\operatorname{tp}(g / A)$ is generic in $G_{1}$.

The equivalences follow from basic facts about connected components. We will give a short proof for the sake of completeness.

Proof. $(i) \Rightarrow(i i)$ : Take a generic type $p$ of $G_{2}$, so its stabilizer $\operatorname{Stab}_{G_{2}}(p)$ equals $G_{2}^{0}=G_{1}^{0}$ by assumption. Since $G_{1}$ is a supergroup of $G_{2}$, we have $\operatorname{Stab}_{G_{1}}(p) \supset \operatorname{Stab}_{G_{2}}(p)=G_{1}^{0}$ which implies that $p$ is generic in $G_{1}$.
(ii) $\Rightarrow$ (iii): This implication is trivial.
(iii) $\Rightarrow(i)$ : We may assume that $A=\operatorname{acl}(A)$. First note that $G_{2}^{0} \subset G_{1}^{0} \cap G_{2}$ since $G_{2}$ is a subgroup of $G_{1}$. Let $g$ be as in the assumption of (iii) and take $g_{1} \equiv_{A} g$ with $g_{1} \downarrow_{A} g$. Since $G_{2}$ is definable over $A$, the type $\operatorname{tp}(g / A)$ determines a coset of the connected component $G_{2}^{0}$. In particular, the product $g_{1}^{-1} \cdot g$ lies in $G_{2}^{0}$. By the independence $g_{1} \downarrow_{A} g$ and genericity of $g$ in $G_{1}$ we also get that $g_{1}^{-1} \cdot g$ is generic in $G_{1}$. Hence, the group $G_{2}^{0}$ contains a generic element of $G_{1}$ which implies that $G_{1}^{0} \subset G_{2}^{0}$.

We use the remark as follows:
Corollary 3.6. Let $G$ and $H$ be as in Definition 3.2. If the definable hull $\operatorname{dc}_{G}(H)$ is principal in $G$, then for every $A \supset H$ there exists a type $p$ in $S_{1}^{H}(A)$ which is generic in $G$.

Proof. Choose $p$ to be a generic type for $H$ over $A$, then $p$ is generic in $\operatorname{dc}_{G}(H)$ by Fact 3.3 (2) and thus in $G$ by Remark 3.5.

3.2. Back to our Setting. We return to the assumptions of Section 1 and fix a sufficiently saturated model $\mathcal{M}_{0}$ of the stable $\mathcal{L}_{0}$-theory $T_{0}$ which eliminates imaginaries and quantifiers. As in Section 3.1, we assume that $\mathcal{M}_{0}$ is the universe of a group $(G, \cdot)$. In addition, we now consider a simple $\mathcal{L}$-theory $T$ with $\mathcal{L}_{0} \subset \mathcal{L}$ such that $T_{0}^{\varphi} \subset T$ (see Remark 1.1).

Inside $\mathcal{M}_{0}$, we fix a sufficiently saturated model $\mathcal{M}$ of $T$ and work either in $\mathcal{M}$ or $\mathcal{M}_{0}$. Furthermore, let $\mathcal{N}$ be a small elementary substructure of $\mathcal{M}$ and $H$ an $\mathcal{L}(N)$-definable subset of $M$. We now suppose that $(H, \cdot)$ is a group in $\mathcal{M}$ (i.e. closed under $\cdot$ and inverses).

In particular, both the $N$-points $(H(N), \cdot)$ and the $M$-points $(H(M), \cdot)$ form (possibly non-definable) subgroups of $(G, \cdot)$.
Remark 3.7. In the just described setting, the definable hulls of $H(M)$ and $H(N)$ in $\mathcal{M}_{0}$ coincide, that is $\operatorname{dc}_{G}(H(M))=\operatorname{dc}_{G}(H(N))$.
Proof. Since $H(N) \subset H(M)$, we have $\operatorname{dc}_{G}(H(N)) \subset \operatorname{dc}_{G}(H(M))$ as type-definable sets.
On the other hand, if $\psi(x)$ is an $\mathcal{L}_{0}(N)$-formula such that $H(N) \subset \psi\left(M_{0}\right)$, then (by quantifier elimination of $T_{0}$ ) $\mathcal{N} \models \forall x(H(x) \rightarrow \psi(x))$. Since $\mathcal{N} \prec \mathcal{M}$ we thus have that $H(M) \subset \psi\left(M_{0}\right)$, so $\operatorname{dc}_{G}(H(M)) \subset \operatorname{dc}_{G}(H(N))$ by Fact 3.3 (1).

Warning: Since $(H, \cdot)$ is an $\mathcal{L}(N)$-definable group in the simple theory $T$, we now have two different notions of genericity for elements in $H$. A type is said to be ( $\mathcal{L}$-)generic in $H$ if it is generic in the simple theory $T$ and generic for $H(M)$ as in Definition 3.2 if we view $(H(M), \cdot)$ as a subgroup of $(G, \cdot)$.

However, these notions are related if $T$ is stable:
Remark 3.8. Let $(G, \cdot)$ and $(H, \cdot)$ be as above and suppose that $T$ is stable. An element $g$ of $H(M)$ is generic for $H(M)$ (working in $\mathcal{M}_{0}$ ) if it is $\mathcal{L}$-generic in $H$ over $N$ (working in $\mathcal{M})$.

In particular, such an element $g$ is $\mathcal{L}_{0}$-generic over $N$ in $\operatorname{dc}_{G}(H(M))$ by Fact 3.3 (2).
Proof. First work in $\mathcal{M}$. Since $T$ is stable and $\operatorname{tp}_{\mathcal{L}}(g / N)$ is generic in $H$, we find for every formula $\varphi(x)$ in $\operatorname{tp}_{\mathcal{L}}(g / N)$ elements $g_{1}, \ldots, g_{n}$ and $h_{1}, \ldots, h_{n}$ of $H(M)$ such that $\mathcal{M} \models \bigvee_{i=1}^{n} \varphi\left(g_{i} \cdot h \cdot h_{i}\right)$ for every element $h$ of $H(M)$.

If $\varphi$ is a quantifier-free $\mathcal{L}_{0}$-formula, we then also have $\mathcal{M}_{0} \models \bigvee_{i=1}^{n} \varphi\left(g_{i} \cdot h \cdot h_{i}\right)$ since $\mathcal{M}$ is a substructure of $\mathcal{M}_{0}$. In particular, this is true for all formulas in $\operatorname{tp}_{0}(g / N)$ by quantifier elimination of $T_{0}$. Hence, working in $\mathcal{M}_{0}$, the type $\operatorname{tp}_{0}(g / N)$ is generic for $H(M)$.

We will now consider the definable hulls in $\mathcal{M}_{0}$ of two different subsets of $\mathcal{M}$, one being contained in the other.

Lemma 3.9. Given two $\mathcal{L}(N)$-definable sets $H_{1}$ and $H_{2}$ such that $\left(H_{1}, \cdot\right)$ and $\left(H_{2}, \cdot\right)$ are groups and $\left(H_{2}, \cdot\right) \subset\left(H_{1}, \cdot\right)$, the following two conditions are equivalent:
(i) The definable hull $\operatorname{dc}_{G}\left(H_{2}(N)\right)$ is principal in the definable hull $\operatorname{dc}_{G}\left(H_{1}(N)\right)$.
(ii) There exists an element $h$ of $H_{2}(M)$ that is $\mathcal{L}_{0}$-generic over $N$ in $\operatorname{dc}_{G}\left(H_{1}(N)\right)$.

Proof. Suppose that $\operatorname{dc}_{G}\left(H_{2}(N)\right)$ is principal in the definable hull $\operatorname{dc}_{G}\left(H_{1}(N)\right)$. Working in $\mathcal{M}_{0}$, there exists an $\mathcal{L}_{0}$-Type $p$ that is finitely satisfiable in $H_{2}(N)$ and generic in

$\operatorname{dc}_{G}\left(H_{1}(N)\right)$ by Remark 3.6 applied to $H_{2}(N)$ as a subgroup of $\operatorname{dc}_{G}\left(H_{1}(N)\right)$. By quantifier elimination of $T_{0}$, the $\mathcal{L}_{0}$-type $p$ yields a partial $\mathcal{L}$-type over $N$ in $\mathcal{M}$ which is still finitely satisfiable in $H_{2}(N)$. This means that the partial type $p \cup\left\{H_{2}(x)\right\}$ over $N$ is consistent in $\mathcal{M}$ and thus realized by an element $h$. Hence, we have found an element as in (ii).

On the other hand, an element $h$ as in (ii) lies in $\operatorname{dc}_{G}\left(H_{2}(M)\right)$ which by Remark 3.7 equals $\operatorname{dc}_{G}\left(H_{2}(N)\right)$. Remark 3.5 yields that $\operatorname{dc}_{G}\left(H_{2}(N)\right)$ is principal in $\operatorname{dc}_{G}\left(H_{1}(N)\right)$.

query: What are the key components for controlling emotions in text-to-speech systems?
golden_answer: The key components include controlling the dimensions of pleasure, arousal, and dominance. These elements are derived from established emotion theories and are integrated into language model-based speech generation to produce varied emotional expressions.
source_title:
Emotional Dimension Control in Language Model-Based Text-to-Speech:
  Spanning a Broad Spectrum of Human Emotions
source_text:
## 4. Conclusion

In this paper, we proposed an emotional TTS framework that integrates established emotion theory with language model-based speech generation. By controlling pleasure, arousal, and dominance, our proposed system synthesizes a wide range of emotional speech without relying on large-scale emotion-labeled data, while preserving naturalness in zero-shot scenarios. This work highlights the value of combining psychological insights with data-driven modeling. query: What role do HDAC inhibitors play in differentiation therapy for blood cancers?
golden_answer: HDAC inhibitors are predicted to increase $\beta$, resulting in differentiation, and they help restore normal differentiation by increasing $\beta$ further to facilitate differentiation.
source_title:
Hierarchical cell identities emerge from animal gene regulatory
  mechanisms
source_text:
# Pathways to dysregulation in cancer and implications for differentiation therapy 

The hierarchical cell identity model provides a framework for analyzing and predicting the dysregulation of cell identity in cancer. A hallmark of many cancers is the profound disruption of cellular identity, often driven by failures in differentiation processes [96]. This phenomenon is particularly evident in the blood system, where numerous blood cancers arise from the inability of progenitor states to undergo proper maturation [97].

Our analysis shows that, at a given level of $\beta$, progenitor states represent stable cell types with long-term persistence. Differentiation requires an increase in $\beta$ that results

in appropriate cell fate bifurcations. Consequently, failures in differentiation can result from two distinct forms of dysregulation: either $\beta$ is maintained at an inappropriately low level, or the critical threshold of $\beta$ required for differentiation is elevated. Both mechanisms appear to play significant roles in cancer development.

The model predicts that inhibiting HDACs will increase $\beta$, while inhibiting HATs will decrease it. These predictions are consistent with experimental observations [48, 98-102]. Broad inhibition of HDACs directly induces differentiation in cancers characterized by maturation failures, as well as in multipotent progenitors, resulting in cell cycle arrest and the upregulation of lineage-specific gene expression [102-109]. Within our modelling framework, HDAC inhibitors are predicted to decrease $\kappa_{-1}$ and therefore increase $\beta$, resulting in differentiation.

In addition to the dysregulation of epigenetic processes, many cancers-particularly blood cancers-are driven by mutations that disrupt the activity of transcription factors governing cell identity [110]. These mutations often involve deletions or regulatory changes caused by chromosomal translocations. Consistent with the predictions of the model, transcription factor alterations linked to differentiation failures frequently occur in factors that are strongly and differentially expressed between cell fates. Notable examples include Pu. 1 and Gata2, which are strongly and differentially expressed in myeloid lineages [111-113], and Pax5, which is uniquely expressed in B cells [114, 115]. Similarly, certain transcription factors are highly expressed in stem cells compared to differentiated lineages, and their dysregulation can lead to the aberrant stabilisation of a mixed stem-differentiated state. For instance, Lmo2 and Tal1, which are strongly expressed in hematopoietic stem cells but downregulated in lymphocytes, can drive lymphoblastic leukemias when mis-expressed [116-118]. Erg, another key transcription factor, is typically downregulated during stem cell differentiation, but its upregulation promotes a mixed stem/differentiated state in both myeloid $[37,119]$ and lymphoblastic leukemias $[119,120]$.

Our analysis suggests that a critical mechanism underlying transformation following transcription factor dysregulation is a change in the persistence length of associated progenitor states, which follows from a larger overlap between their transcriptional profiles following mutation. This perspective provides a straightforward explanation for the effectiveness of HDAC inhibitors in differentiation therapy for blood cancers $[103,104,106,121,122]$, as they may help restore normal differentiation by increasing $\beta$ further to facilitate differentiation.

query: How does the recursive algorithm ensure that all agents receive their preferred objects in a hierarchy of monarchies and diarchies?
golden_answer: The recursive algorithm uses supply vectors, partial allocations, and generalized mechanisms to map preferences to feasible allocations. It tracks progress through histories and applies sequencing rules to allocate objects based on priority order until all are distributed.
source_title: Unambiguous Efficiency of Random Allocations
source_text:
# B Formal Definition of Hierarchies of Monarchies and Diarchies
## B. 1 A Recursive Algorithm

Before defining the general algorithm, we give some preliminary definitions. A supply vector is $s \in S=[0,1]^{A}$. Denote by $A(s)$ the set of objects available in positive amounts at $s$ and by $\underline{A}(s)$ those that are only fractionally available. That is, $A(s)=\left\{a \in A: s_{a}>0\right\}$ and $\underline{A}(s)=\left\{a \in A: 0<s_{a}<1\right\}$. A partial allocation is an $|N| \times|N|$ substochastic matrix $\pi$ such that every agent receives an allocation in $\Pi$ or nothing. That is, for each $i \in N$, either $\pi_{i}=\overrightarrow{0}$ or $\sum_{a \in A} \pi_{i a}=1$ and for each $a \in A, \sum_{i \in N} \pi_{i a} \leq 1$. Let $\overline{\boldsymbol{\Pi}}$ be the set of all partial allocations. A partial allocation $\pi \in \overline{\Pi}$ is feasible at $s$ if $\sum_{i \in N} \pi_{i} \leq s$.

A generalized mechanism is a mapping $f: S \times \mathcal{P}^{N} \rightarrow \overline{\Pi}$ such that for each $s \in S$ and $P \in \mathcal{P}^{N}, f(s, P) \in \overline{\Pi}$ is feasible at $s$. Let $\mathcal{F}$ be the set of all generalized mechanisms.

If we start with a supply vector $s \in S$, the residual supply after allocating $\pi \in \overline{\Pi}$ is $r(s, \pi) \in S$ such that for each $a \in A, \boldsymbol{r}_{\boldsymbol{a}}(\boldsymbol{s}, \boldsymbol{\pi})=s_{a}-\sum_{i \in N} \pi_{i a}$.

The algorithm uses generalized mechanisms to compute a complete allocation part by part. It keeps track of these parts via a history, which is a (possibly empty) list of partial allocations $\eta=\left(\pi^{1}, \ldots, \pi^{K}\right)$ such that for each $k=1, \ldots K, \pi^{k} \in \overline{\Pi}$ and $\sum_{k=1}^{K} \pi^{k} \in \overline{\Pi}$. Let $\boldsymbol{N}(\eta)=\left\{i \in N\right.$ : there is $k$ such that $\left.\pi_{i}^{k} \neq \overrightarrow{0}\right\}$ be the set of agents allocated to along the history $\eta$. Having collected the history $\eta$, the next partial allocation can be any $\pi^{K+1} \in \overline{\Pi}$ such that for each $i \in N(\eta), \pi_{i}^{K+1}=\overrightarrow{0}$. That is, only partial allocations that allocate to agents not allocated to by any part of $\eta$ can occur after $\eta$. We append $\pi^{K+1}$ to form a new history $\left(\pi^{1}, \ldots, \pi^{K}, \pi^{K+1}\right)$ and denote it by $\eta \leftrightarrow \pi^{K+1}$. Let $\mathcal{H}$ be the set of all histories. The set of terminal histories is $\mathcal{H}^{T}=\left\{\eta \in \mathcal{H}: N(\eta)=N\right\}$. Note that for each $\left(\pi^{1}, \ldots, \pi^{K}\right) \in$ $\mathcal{H}^{T}, \sum_{k=1}^{K} \pi^{k} \in \Pi$ is an allocation, and not just a partial one. The set of non-terminal histories is $\mathcal{H}^{N T}=\mathcal{H} \backslash \mathcal{H}^{T}$. A sequencing rule, $\sigma: \mathcal{H}^{N T} \rightarrow \mathcal{F}$, maps each non-terminal history to a partial mechanism. We require that for each $\eta \in \mathcal{H}^{N T}$, each $i \in N(\eta)$, and each $\pi \in \operatorname{range}(\sigma(\eta)), \pi_{i}=\overrightarrow{0}$. That is, $\sigma(\eta)$ does not allocate to agents who have already been allocated to along $\eta$.

To summarize:

1. Each $f \in \mathcal{F}$ solves a part of the allocation problem.
2. A history $\eta \in \mathcal{H}$ keeps track of accumulated parts of the solution.
3. The sequencing rule $\sigma$ tells us what partial mechanism solves the next part.

We now put these components together to recursively compute an allocation for any preference profile. Define the function $\Psi: \mathcal{H} \times S \times \mathcal{P}^{N} \rightarrow \overline{\Pi}$ by setting, for each $(\eta, s, P) \in$ $\mathcal{H} \times S \times \mathcal{P}^{N}$,

$$
\Psi(\eta, s, P)= \begin{cases}\overrightarrow{0} & \text { if } \eta \in \mathcal{H}^{T} \\ \pi+\Psi(\eta++\pi, r(s, \pi), P) \text { where } \pi=\sigma(\eta)(s, P) & \text { if } \eta \in \mathcal{H}^{N T}\end{cases}
$$

If we start with the empty history and the full supply vector and then we have a mechanism for each sequencing rule $\sigma$. We denote this mechanism by $\varphi^{\sigma}$, which we define by setting for each $P \in \mathcal{P}^{N}, \varphi^{\sigma}(P)=\Psi((), \vec{1}, P)$.

To fix ideas, we demonstrate how one can describe a serial dictatorship in the recursive language we have laid out above.

Example 5 (Recursive formulation of serial dictatorship). In Section 2.3.3, we described serial dictatorship allocations where agents select their best objects according to a priority order. We now articulate these as mechanisms in the language of this section.

Consider $>\in \mathcal{O}$ and let $1, \ldots, n$ be a labeling of the agents in decreasing order of their priority according to $>$. For each history $\eta \in \mathcal{H}$, let length $(\eta)$ be the length of $\eta$. That is, length $(())=0$ and length $\left(\pi^{1}, \ldots, \pi^{K}\right)=K$. Let $\sigma: \mathcal{H}^{N T} \rightarrow \mathcal{F}$ be such that for each $\eta \in \mathcal{H}^{N T}$, $\sigma(\eta)=f$ where $f(s, P)$ allocates to $i=\operatorname{length}(\eta)+1$ the best possible lottery according to $P_{i}$ given the supply $s$.

As a concrete example, take $N=\{1,2,3,4\}$ and $A=\{a, b, c, d\}$ and the following preference profile $P \in \mathcal{P}^{N}$ :
