query: What type of processes do individual idiosyncratic noises form in classical mean field games?
golden_answer: In classical mean field games, individual idiosyncratic noises form a sequence of independent real-valued Brownian motions.
source_title:
Hilbert Space-Valued LQ Mean Field Games: An Infinite-Dimensional
  Analysis
source_text:
# 3. Coupled Controlled Stochastic Evolution Equations in Hilbert Space 

In classical mean field games (MFGs), the dynamics of the relevant $N$-player game is modeled as a system of finite-dimensional SDEs, the regularities of which are well-studied in the literature. However, in this paper, the dynamics of the $N$-player game will be modeled as $N$ coupled infinitedimensional stochastic equations. To be more specific, the state of each agent satisfies an infinitedimensional stochastic equation which is involved with the states of all agents. The well-posedness of such a system has not been rigorously established in the literature. Thus, we aim to address it in this section. For this purpose, we first discuss the existence of a sequence of independent $Q$-Wiener processes. Next, we prove the existence and uniqueness of the solution to a system of $N$ coupled infinite-dimensional stochastic equations.

More precisely, in the classic setup of MFGs, the individual idiosyncratic noises form a sequence of independent real-valued Brownian motions. In the current context, however, we require a sequence of independent $Q$-Wiener processes. The following proposition examines the existence of such a sequence.

Proposition 3.1. Let $(\Omega, \mathfrak{F}, \mathbb{P})$ be a probability space and $Q$ be a positive trace class operator on the separable Hilbert space $V$. Then, there exists a sequence of independent $V$-valued $Q$-Wiener processes $\left\{W_{i}\right\}_{i \in \mathbb{N}}$ defined on the given probability space.

Proof. Let $W,\left\{\beta_{j}\right\}_{j \in \mathbb{N}}$ be the processes defined in (2.1), and the corresponding natural filtrations be defined as $\mathcal{F}^{W}=\left\{\mathcal{F}_{t}^{W}: t \in \mathcal{T}\right\}$ and $\mathcal{F}^{\beta}=\left\{\mathcal{F}_{t}^{\beta}: t \in \mathcal{T}\right\}$, where $\mathcal{F}_{t}^{W}=\sigma(W(s), 0 \leq s \leq t)$, $\mathcal{F}_{t}^{\beta}=\sigma\left(\beta_{j}(s), 0 \leq s \leq t, j \in \mathbb{N}\right)=\sigma\left(\bigcup_{j \in \mathbb{N}} \sigma\left(\beta_{j}(s), 0 \leq s \leq t\right)\right)$. Subsequently, the augmented filtrations $\overline{\mathcal{F}}^{W}=\left\{\overline{\mathcal{F}}_{t}^{W}: t \in \mathcal{T}\right\}$ and $\overline{\mathcal{F}}^{\beta}=\left\{\overline{\mathcal{F}}_{t}^{\beta}: t \in \mathcal{T}\right\}$ consist of $\overline{\mathcal{F}}_{t}^{W}=\sigma\left(\mathcal{F}_{t}^{W} \cup \mathcal{N}\right)$ and $\mathcal{F}_{t}^{\beta}=\sigma\left(\mathcal{F}_{t}^{\beta} \cup \mathcal{N}\right)$. It is evident that $\overline{\mathcal{F}}_{t}^{W}=\mathcal{F}_{t}^{\beta}$. By applying the enumeration of $\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N}$ to the sequence of mutually independent Brownian motions $\left\{\beta_{j}\right\}_{j \in \mathbb{N}}$, we can obtain infinitely many distinct sequences of Brownian motions $\left\{\beta_{j}^{i}\right\}_{j \in \mathbb{N}}=\left\{\beta_{1}^{i}, \beta_{2}^{i}, \ldots, \beta_{j}^{i}, \ldots\right\}$, each sequence indexed by $i$. The real-valued Brownian motions $\beta_{j}^{i}$ are mutually independent for all indices $i, j \in \mathbb{N}$. Now we construct a sequence of Q-Wiener processes $\left\{W_{i}\right\}_{i \in \mathbb{N}}$, where $W_{i}(t)$ is defined by

$$
W_{i}(t)=\sum_{j \in \mathbb{N}} \sqrt{\lambda_{j}} \beta_{j}^{i}(t) e_{j}, \quad t \in \mathcal{T}
$$

For our purpose, it is enough to show that the augmented filtrations $\left\{\overline{\mathcal{F}}^{\beta^{\prime}}\right\}_{i \in \mathbb{N}}$ are independent. Recall that $\mathcal{F}^{\beta^{\prime}}=\left\{\mathcal{F}_{t}^{\beta^{\prime}}: t \in \mathcal{T}\right\}$, where $\mathcal{F}_{t}^{\beta^{\prime}}=\sigma\left(\bigcup_{j \in \mathbb{N}} \sigma\left(\beta_{j}^{i}(s), 0 \leq s \leq t\right)\right)$ and $\left\{\beta_{j}^{i}\right\}_{j, i \in \mathbb{N}}$ are independent Brownian motions. Then the independence of $\left\{\mathcal{F}_{t}^{\beta^{\prime}}\right\}_{i \in \mathbb{N}}, \forall t \in \mathcal{T}$, follows from the standard results in measure theory (see for instance [44, Proposition 10.1.7]), and hence $\left\{\overline{\mathcal{F}}_{t}^{\beta^{\prime}}\right\}_{i \in \mathbb{N}}, \forall t \in \mathcal{T}$ are also independent.

It is straightforward to verify that the sequence of processes $\left\{W_{i}\right\}_{i \in \mathbb{N}}$, constructed in Proposition 3.1, are (mutually independent) $Q$-Wiener processes with respect to $\mathcal{F}$. This measurability arises because each $W_{i}$ is constructed using a subsequence of real-valued Brownian motions generating the original $Q$-Wiener process $W$ given by (2.1). Usually, this "universal" filtration $\mathcal{F}$ is larger than necessary. Below, we construct a reduced filtration.
Reduced Filtration $\mathcal{F}^{[N]}=\left\{\mathcal{F}_{t}^{[N]}, t \in \mathcal{T}\right\}$ : Consider a set $\mathcal{N}=\{1,2, \ldots, N\}$ and let $\left\{W_{i}\right\}_{i \in \mathcal{N}}$ be $N$ independent $Q$-Wiener processes constructed in Proposition 3.1. A reduced filtration $\mathcal{F}^{[N]}$ may be constructed under which these processes are independent $Q$-Wiener processes. Note that the processes $\left\{W_{i}\right\}_{i \in \mathcal{N}}$ are constructed as described in (3.1) using $N$ sequences of mutually independent Brownian motions $\left\{\beta_{j}^{i}\right\}_{j \in \mathbb{N}, i \in \mathcal{N}}$. These $N$ sequences may be combined to form a new sequence of mutually independent Brownian motions. We then construct a new $Q$-Wiener process $W^{N}$ using this resulting sequence as in (2.1) and define $\mathcal{F}^{[N]}$ as the normal filtration that makes $W^{N}$ a $Q$ Wiener process. Clearly, this filtration only makes the processes $\left\{W_{i}\right\}_{i \in \mathcal{N}}$ independent $Q$-Wiener processes and can be smaller than $\mathcal{F}$.

We are now ready to introduce a system of coupled infinite-dimensional stochastic equations defined on $\left(\Omega, \mathfrak{F}, \mathcal{F}^{[N]}, \mathbb{P}\right)$ describing the temporal evolution of the vector process $\mathbf{x}=\{\mathbf{x}(t)=$ $\left.\left(x_{1}(t), x_{2}(t), \ldots, x_{N}(t)\right), t \in \mathcal{T}\right\}$. Note that $\mathbf{x}$ is an $H^{N}$-valued stochastic process, where $H^{N}$ denotes the $N$-product space of $H$, equipped with the product norm $|\mathbf{x}(t)|_{H^{N}}=\left(\sum_{i \in \mathcal{N}}\left|x_{i}(t)\right|_{H}^{2}\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}$. Subsequently, $\mathcal{M}^{2}\left(\mathcal{T} ; H^{N}\right)$ and $\mathcal{H}^{2}\left(\mathcal{T} ; H^{N}\right)$ are defined as the spaces of all $H^{N}$-valued progressively measurable processes $\mathbf{x}$, respectively, satisfying $|\mathbf{x}|_{\mathcal{M}^{2}\left(\mathcal{T} ; H^{N}\right)}<\infty$ and $|\mathbf{x}|_{\mathcal{H}^{2}\left(\mathcal{T} ; H^{N}\right)}<\infty$.

The differential form of a system of coupled infinite-dimensional stochastic equations can be represented by

$$
\begin{aligned}
& d x_{i}(t)=\left(A x_{i}(t)+F_{i}\left(t, \mathbf{x}(t), u_{i}(t)\right)\right) d t+B_{i}\left(t, \mathbf{x}(t), u_{i}(t)\right) d W_{i}(t) \\
& x_{i}(0)=\xi_{i}
\end{aligned}
$$

where, as defined in (2.6), $A$ is a $C_{0}$-semigroup generator. Moreover, the control action $u_{i}, i \in \mathcal{N}$, is a $U$-valued progressively measurable process, and the initial condition $\xi_{i}, i \in \mathcal{N}$, is $H$-valued and $\mathcal{F}_{0}^{[N]}$-measurable. Moreover, $\left\{W_{i}\right\}_{i \in \mathcal{N}}$ is a set of mutually independent $Q$-Wiener processes, each constructed as in Proposition 3.1 and applied to the filtration $\mathcal{F}^{[N]}$. Furthermore, the family of maps $F_{i}: \mathcal{T} \times H^{N} \times U \rightarrow H$ and $B_{i}: \mathcal{T} \times H^{N} \times U \rightarrow \mathcal{L}_{2}\left(V_{Q}, H\right), \forall i \in \mathcal{N}$, are defined for all $i \in \mathcal{N}$.
A3.1. For each $i \in \mathcal{N}$, the initial condition $\xi_{i}$ belongs to $L^{2}(\Omega ; H)$ and is $\mathcal{F}_{0}^{[N]}$-measurable.
We focus on the solution of (3.2) in a mild sense, which is defined below.
Definition 3.1. (Mild Solution of Coupled Infinite-Dimensional SDEs) A process $\boldsymbol{x} \in \mathcal{H}^{2}\left(\mathcal{T} ; H^{N}\right)$, where $\boldsymbol{x}=\left\{\boldsymbol{x}(t)=\left(x_{1}(t), x_{2}(t), \ldots, x_{N}(t)\right), t \in \mathcal{T}\right\}$, is said to be a mild solution of (3.2) if, for each $i \in \mathcal{N}$, the process $x_{i}$ is defined $\mathbb{P}$-almost surely by the integral equation

$$
x_{i}(t)=S(t) \xi_{i}+\int_{0}^{t} S(t-r) F_{i}\left(r, \boldsymbol{x}(r), u_{i}(r)\right) d r+\int_{0}^{t} S(t-r) B_{i}\left(r, \boldsymbol{x}(r), u_{i}(r)\right) d W_{i}(r), \quad \forall t \in \mathcal{T}
$$

where $S(t)$ is the $C_{0}$-semigroup generated by $A$.

We make the following assumptions on the system of coupled stochastic evolution systems described by (3.2) for every $i \in \mathcal{N}$.
A3.2. $u_{i} \in \mathcal{M}^{2}(\mathcal{T} ; U)$.
A3.3. The mapping $F_{i}: \mathcal{T} \times H^{N} \times U \rightarrow H$ is $\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{T}) \otimes \mathcal{B}\left(H^{N}\right) \otimes \mathcal{B}(U) / \mathcal{B}(H)$-measurable.
A3.4. The mapping $B_{i}: \mathcal{T} \times H^{N} \times U \rightarrow \mathcal{L}_{2}\left(V_{Q}, H\right)$ is $\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{T}) \otimes \mathcal{B}\left(H^{N}\right) \otimes \mathcal{B}(U) / \mathcal{B}\left(\mathcal{L}_{2}\left(V_{Q}, H\right)\right)$ measurable, where the Hilbert space $V_{Q}$ is as defined in Section 2.
A3.5. There exists a constant $C$ such that, for every $t \in \mathcal{T}, u \in U$ and $\boldsymbol{x}, \boldsymbol{y} \in H^{N}$, we have

$$
\begin{gathered}
\left|F_{i}(t, \boldsymbol{x}, u)-F_{i}(t, \boldsymbol{y}, u)\right|_{H}+\left\|B_{i}(t, \boldsymbol{x}, u)-B_{i}(t, \boldsymbol{y}, u)\right\|_{\mathcal{L}_{2}} \leq C|\boldsymbol{x}-\boldsymbol{y}|_{H^{N}} \\
\left|F_{i}(t, \boldsymbol{x}, u)\right|_{H}^{2}+\left\|B_{i}(t, \boldsymbol{x}, u)\right\|_{\mathcal{L}_{2}}^{2} \leq C^{2}\left(1+|\boldsymbol{x}|_{H^{N}}^{2}+|u|_{U}^{2}\right)
\end{gathered}
$$

The following theorem establishes the existence and uniqueness of a mild solution to the coupled stochastic evolution equations given by (3.2). This result extends Theorem 7.2 in [16], which addresses the existence and uniqueness of a mild solution for a single stochastic evolution equation without coupling.
Theorem 3.2. (Existence and Uniqueness of a Mild Solution) Under A3.2-A3.5, the set of coupled stochastic evolution equations given by (3.2) admits a unique mild solution in the space $\mathcal{H}^{2}\left(\mathcal{T} ; H^{N}\right)$.
Proof. The existence and uniqueness of a mild solution can be established through the classic fixedpoint argument for a mapping from $\mathcal{H}^{2}\left(\mathcal{T} ; H^{N}\right)$ to $\mathcal{H}^{2}\left(\mathcal{T} ; H^{N}\right)$. To this end, for any given element $\mathbf{x} \in \mathcal{H}^{2}\left(\mathcal{T} ; H^{N}\right)$, the operator $\Gamma$ is defined component-wise as

$$
\Gamma \mathbf{x}(t)=\left(\Gamma_{1} \mathbf{x}(t), \Gamma_{2} \mathbf{x}(t), \ldots, \Gamma_{N} \mathbf{x}(t)\right)
$$

where each component $\Gamma_{i} \mathbf{x}(t)$ is represented by the integral equation

$$
\Gamma_{i} \mathbf{x}(t)=S(t) \xi_{i}+\int_{0}^{t} S(t-r) F_{i}\left(r, \mathbf{x}(r), u_{i}(r)\right) d r+\int_{0}^{t} S(t-r) B_{i}\left(r, \mathbf{x}(r), u_{i}(r)\right) d W_{i}(r)
$$

We show that $\Gamma$ indeed maps $\mathcal{H}^{2}\left(\mathcal{T} ; H^{N}\right)$ into itself. The measurability of (3.4) as an $H$-valued process is established using the standard argument found in [16] and [17], based on our assumptions. This is because $F_{i}$ and $B_{i}$ are progressively measurable processes, valued in $H$ and $\mathcal{L}_{2}\left(V_{Q}, H\right)$, respectively. We use the inequality $|a+b+c|^{2} \leq 3|a|^{2}+3|b|^{2}+3|c|^{2}$, for each $i \in \mathcal{N}$ and $t \in \mathcal{T}$, to get

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{E}\left|\Gamma_{i} \mathbf{x}(t)\right|_{H}^{2} \leq & 3 \mathbb{E}\left|S(t) \xi_{i}\right|_{H}^{2}+3 \mathbb{E}\left[\left|\int_{0}^{t} S(t-r) F_{i}\left(r, \mathbf{x}(r), u_{i}(r)\right) d r\right|_{H}^{2}\right] \\
& +3 \mathbb{E}\left[\left|\int_{0}^{t} S(t-r) B_{i}\left(r, \mathbf{x}(r), u_{i}(r)\right) d W_{i}(r)\right|_{H}^{2}\right]
\end{aligned}
$$

For the Bochner integral in (3.5), we have

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{E}\left[\left|\int_{0}^{t} S(t-r) F_{i}\left(r, \mathbf{x}(r), u_{i}(r)\right) d r\right|_{H}^{2}\right] & \leq T \mathbb{E}\left[\int_{0}^{t}\left|S(t-r) F_{i}\left(r, \mathbf{x}(r), u_{i}(r)\right)\right|_{H}^{2} d r\right] \\
& \leq T \mathbb{E}\left[\int_{0}^{t}\|S(t-r)\|_{\mathcal{L}(H)}^{2}\left|F_{i}\left(r, \mathbf{x}(r), u_{i}(r)\right)\right|_{H}^{2} d r\right] \\
& \leq T M_{T}^{2} C^{2} \mathbb{E}\left[\int_{0}^{t}\left(\left|(\mathbf{x}(r))_{H^{N}}^{2}+\left|u_{i}(r)\right|_{U}^{2}+1\right) d r\right]
\end{aligned}
$$

where the first inequality results from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality. For the stochastic integral in (3.5), we have

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{E}\left[\left|\int_{0}^{t} S(t-r) B_{i}\left(r, \mathbf{x}(r), u_{i}(r)\right) d W_{i}(r)\right|_{H}^{2}\right] & \leq C^{\prime} \mathbb{E}\left[\int_{0}^{t}\left\|B_{i}\left(r, \mathbf{x}(r), u_{i}(r)\right)\right\|_{\mathcal{L}_{2}}^{2} d r\right] \\
& \leq C^{2} C^{\prime} \mathbb{E}\left[\int_{0}^{t}\left(|\mathbf{x}(r)|_{H^{N}}^{2}+\left|u_{i}(r)\right|_{U}^{2}+1\right) d r\right]
\end{aligned}
$$

where the first inequality is obtained by the standard approximation technique for stochastic convolutions (see e.g. [16, Theorem 4.36] and [17, Corollary 3.2]) in the current context for every $t \in \mathcal{T}$ and $i \in \mathcal{N}$. Note that the constant $C^{\prime}$ only depends on $T$ and $M_{T}$ (defined in (2.7)). Substituting (3.6) and (3.7) in (3.5), we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{E}\left|\Gamma_{i} \mathbf{x}(t)\right|_{H}^{2} & \leq 3 \mathbb{E}\left|S(t) \xi_{i}\right|_{H}^{2}+3\left(C^{2} C^{\prime}+T M_{T}^{2} C^{2}\right) \mathbb{E}\left[\int_{0}^{t}\left(|\mathbf{x}(r)|_{H^{N}}^{2}+\left|u_{i}(r)\right|_{U}^{2}+1\right) d r\right] \\
& \leq 3 \mathbb{E}\left|S(t) \xi_{i}\right|_{H}^{2}+3\left(C^{2} C^{\prime}+T M_{T}^{2} C^{2}\right) \mathbb{E}\left[\int_{0}^{T}\left(|\mathbf{x}(r)|_{H^{N}}^{2}+\left|u_{i}(r)\right|_{U}^{2}+1\right) d r\right], \forall t \in \mathcal{T}
\end{aligned}
$$

Hence,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{i \in \mathcal{N}} \mathbb{E}\left|\Gamma_{i} \mathbf{x}(t)\right|_{H}^{2} \leq & 3 M_{T}^{2} \sum_{i \in \mathcal{N}} \mathbb{E}\left|\xi_{i}\right|_{H}^{2}+3\left(C^{2} C^{\prime}+T M_{T}^{2} C^{2}\right) \sum_{i \in \mathcal{N}} \mathbb{E}\left[\int_{0}^{T}\left(\left|u_{i}(r)\right|_{U}^{2}\right) d r\right] \\
& +3 N\left(C^{2} C^{\prime}+T M_{T}^{2} C^{2}\right) \mathbb{E}\left[\int_{0}^{T}\left(|\mathbf{x}(r)|_{H^{N}}^{2}+1\right) d r\right], \quad \forall t \in \mathcal{T}
\end{aligned}
$$

From (3.9), we have

$$
\left|\Gamma \mathbf{x}\right|_{\mathcal{H}^{2}\left(\mathcal{T} ; H^{N}\right)}=\left(\sup _{t \in \mathcal{T}} \sum_{i \in \mathcal{N}} \mathbb{E}\left|\Gamma_{i} \mathbf{x}(t)\right|_{H}^{2}\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}<\infty
$$

Thus, the transformation $\Gamma$ is well-defined and maps $\mathcal{H}^{2}\left(\mathcal{T} ; H^{N}\right)$ into itself. The remaining part of the proof is to show that the mapping $\Gamma$ is a contraction, that is, for any two elements $\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y} \in$ $\mathcal{H}^{2}\left(\mathcal{T} ; H^{N}\right)$, it holds that

$$
\left|\Gamma \mathbf{y}-\Gamma \mathbf{x}\right|_{\mathcal{H}^{2}\left(\mathcal{T} ; H^{N}\right)}<\left|\mathbf{y}-\mathbf{x}\right|_{\mathcal{H}^{2}\left(\mathcal{T} ; H^{N}\right)}
$$

Using the inequlity $|a+b|^{2} \leq 2|a|^{2}+2|b|^{2}$, for each $i \in \mathcal{N}$ and $t \in \mathcal{T}$, we can write

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{E}\left|\Gamma_{i} \mathbf{y}(t)-\Gamma_{i} \mathbf{x}(t)\right|_{H}^{2} \leq & 2 \mathbb{E}\left[\left|\int_{0}^{t} S(t-r)\left(F_{i}\left(r, \mathbf{x}(r), u_{i}(r)\right)-F_{i}\left(r, \mathbf{y}(r), u_{i}(r)\right)\right) d r\right|_{H}^{2}\right] \\
& +2 \mathbb{E}\left[\left|\int_{0}^{t} S(t-r)\left(B_{i}\left(r, \mathbf{x}(r), u_{i}(r)\right)-B_{i}\left(r, \mathbf{y}(r), u_{i}(r)\right)\right) d W_{i}(r)\right|_{H}^{2}\right]
\end{aligned}
$$

For the first term on the RHS of (3.10), $\forall t \in \mathcal{T}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{E}\left[\left|\int_{0}^{t} S(t-r)\left(F_{i}\left(r, \mathbf{x}(r), u_{i}(r)\right)-F_{i}\left(r, \mathbf{y}(r), u_{i}(r)\right)\right) d r\right|_{H}^{2}\right] & \leq C^{2} M_{T}^{2} T \mathbb{E}\left[\int_{0}^{T}|\mathbf{x}(t)-\mathbf{y}(t)|_{H^{N}}^{2} d t\right] \\
& \leq C^{2} M_{T}^{2} T^{2} \sup _{t \in \mathcal{T}} \mathbb{E}|\mathbf{x}(t)-\mathbf{y}(t)|_{H^{N}}^{2} \\
& \leq C^{2} M_{T}^{2} T^{2}|\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{y}|_{\mathcal{H}^{2}\left(\mathcal{T}, H^{N}\right)}^{2}
\end{aligned}
$$

Similarly, for the second term on the RHS of (3.10) we have

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \mathbb{E}\left[\left|\int_{0}^{t} S(t-r)\left(B_{i}(r, \mathbf{x}(r), u_{i}(r))-B_{i}(r, \mathbf{y}(r), u_{i}(r))\right) d W_{i}(r)\right|_{H}^{2}\right] \\
& \leq C^{\prime} \mathbb{E}\left[\int_{0}^{T}\left\|B_{i}(r, \mathbf{x}(r), u_{i}(r))-B_{i}(r, \mathbf{y}(r), u_{i}(r))\right\|_{\mathcal{L}_{2}}^{2} d r\right] \\
& \leq M_{T}^{2} C^{\prime} C^{2} T\left(\sup _{t \in \mathcal{T}} \mathbb{E}|\mathbf{x}(t)-\mathbf{y}(t)|_{H^{N}}^{2}\right) \\
& \leq M_{T}^{2} C^{\prime} C^{2} T|\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{y}|_{\mathcal{H}^{2}\left(\mathcal{T} ; H^{N}\right)}^{2}, \quad \forall t \in \mathcal{T}
\end{aligned}
$$

Based on (3.10) to (3.12), we obtain

$$
\sum_{i \in \mathcal{N}} \mathbb{E}\left|\Gamma_{i} \mathbf{y}(t)-\Gamma_{i} \mathbf{x}(t)\right|_{H}^{2} \leq 2 N M_{T}^{2} C^{2} T\left(C^{\prime}+T\right)|\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{y}|_{\mathcal{H}^{2}\left(\mathcal{T} ; H^{N}\right)}^{2}, \quad \forall t \in \mathcal{T}
$$

and subsequently

$$
\left|\Gamma \mathbf{y}-\Gamma \mathbf{x}\right|_{\mathcal{H}^{2}\left(\mathcal{T} ; H^{N}\right)}^{2} \leq 2 N M_{T}^{2} C^{2} T\left(C^{\prime}+T\right)|\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{y}|_{\mathcal{H}^{2}\left(\mathcal{T} ; H^{N}\right)}^{2}
$$

By employing the same argument as in Theorem 7.2 of [16], if $T$ is sufficiently small, then the mapping $\Gamma$ is a contraction. We apply this reasoning on the intervals $[0, \widetilde{T}],[\widetilde{T}, 2 \widetilde{T}], \cdots,[(n-$ $1) \widetilde{T}, T]$, where $\widetilde{T}$ satisfies (3.13) and $n \widetilde{T}=T$.

Remark 3. An alternative approach to prove Theorem 3.2 could involve formulating the set of $N$ stochastic evolution equations as a single $H^{N}$-valued equation. This requires defining appropriate operators between the associated spaces and verifying that a valid $H^{N}$-valued Wiener process can be constructed using $\left\{W_{i}\right\}_{i \in \mathcal{N}}$. Such a reformulation also involves technical considerations. Following this, the existence and uniqueness of the solution may be established by adapting existing results related to single stochastic evolution equations.

# 6. BOOLEANNESS 

We finally concentrate on when the four completions are Boolean. Janowitz [Jan68, Thm. 3.11] gives a characterization for the Dedekind-MacNeille completion to be Boolean. We obtain his result as a corollary to our characterization of when the Bruns-Lakser completion is Boolean. This requires using the notion of $\wedge$-subfitness (see the introduction). Since $A$ is $\wedge$-subfit iff its order-dual is $\vee$-subfit, Proposition 4.1 immediately yields:
Proposition 6.1. For $\mathrm{A} \in$ DLat and X its Priestley dual, the following are equivalent:
(1) $A$ is $\wedge$-subfit.
(2) $a \nless b$ implies there is a maximal filter $F$ with $a \in F$ and $b \notin F$.
(3) Every principal filter is an intersection of maximal filters.
(4) $\max X$ is dense in $X$.

Corollary 6.2. Let $\mathrm{A} \in$ DLat with Priestley space X .
(1) If max $X$ is closed, then $A$ is $\wedge$-subfit iff $A$ is Boolean.
(2) If A is a frame, then A is $\wedge$-subfit iff A is Boolean.

Proof. (1) Suppose $A$ is $\wedge$-subfit. By Proposition 6.1, max $X$ is dense in $X$. But max $X$ is closed, so $\max X=X$, and hence $A$ is Boolean (see, e.g., [Gra11, p. 119]). The other implication is always true.
(2) If $A$ is a frame then max $X$ is closed (see, e.g., [Esa19, p. 47]) and hence (1) applies.

We utilize the above two results to characterize when the Bruns-Lakser completion of a distributive lattice is Boolean.

Theorem 6.3. For $A \in$ DLat, the following are equivalent.
(1) $\mathcal{B} \mathcal{L} A$ is Boolean.
(2) $A$ is $\wedge$-subfit.
(3) $p \mathcal{O}(A$ is Boolean.

Proof. $(1) \Rightarrow(2)$ : Let $a, b \in A$ with $a \nless b$. Since $\mathcal{B} \mathcal{L} A$ is Boolean, it is $\wedge$-subfit, so there is $u \in \mathcal{B} \mathcal{L} A$ such that $b \wedge u=0$ and $a \wedge u \neq 0$. Because $A$ is join-dense in $\mathcal{B} \mathcal{L} A, u=\bigvee S$ for some $S \subseteq A$. Therefore, since $\mathcal{B} \mathcal{L} A$ is a frame, $b \wedge s=0$ for each $s \in S$ and there is $t \in S$ with $a \wedge t \neq 0$. Thus, $b \wedge t=0$ but $a \wedge t \neq 0$, and hence $A$ is $\wedge$-subfit.
$(2) \Rightarrow(3)$ : Since $p \mathcal{O}(A$ is generated as a distributive lattice by relative annihilators, it is enough to show that each relative annihilator has a complement in $p \mathcal{O}(A$. By Lemma 3.14(1) and Proposition 3.15, it is sufficient to show that $X \backslash \downarrow(\mathrm{U} \backslash \mathrm{V})$ has a complement in $\mathrm{pH}(\mathrm{X})$ for any clopen upsets $U, V$ of $X$. Specifically, we show that $X \backslash \downarrow\left(U^{\mathrm{C}} \cup V\right)$ is the complement of $X \backslash \downarrow(U \backslash V)$ in $p H(X)$. Since $U^{c} \cup V$ is clopen, $X \backslash \downarrow\left(U^{c} \cup V\right) \in p H(X)$ by Lemma 3.14(2). Moreover, it is straightforward to see that

$$
[X \backslash \downarrow(U \backslash V)] \cap\left[X \backslash \downarrow\left(U^{c} \cup V\right)\right]=\varnothing
$$

Furthermore, since $A$ is $\wedge$-subfit, max $X$ is dense in $X$ by Proposition 6.1. But

$$
\max X \subseteq[X \backslash \downarrow(U \backslash V)] \cup\left[X \backslash \downarrow\left(U^{c} \cup V\right)\right]
$$

so $[X \backslash \downarrow(U \backslash V)] \cup\left[X \backslash \downarrow\left(U^{c} \cup V\right)\right]$ is dense in $X$, and hence

$$
[X \backslash \downarrow(U \backslash V)] \vee_{p H(X)}\left[X \backslash \downarrow\left(U^{c} \cup V\right)\right]=X
$$

Thus, $X \backslash \downarrow(U \backslash V)$ has a complement in $p H(X)$, finishing the proof that $p \mathcal{O}(A$ is Boolean.
$(3) \Rightarrow(1)$ : By Theorem 3.12, $\mathcal{B} \mathcal{L} A \cong \mathcal{D} M(p \mathcal{O}(A)$. Therefore, $p \mathcal{O}(A$ Boolean implies that so is $\mathcal{B} \mathcal{L} A$ because the Dedekind-MacNeille completion of a Boolean algebra is a Boolean algebra (see, e.g., [BD74, p. 239]).

As a consequence, we obtain:
Corollary 6.4. [Jan68, Thm. 3.11] For $A \in$ DLat, $\mathcal{D} M A$ is Boolean iff $A$ is $\vee$-subfit and $\wedge$-subfit.

Proof. First suppose $\mathcal{D} M A$ is Boolean. Then $\mathcal{D} M A$ is $\vee$-subfit, so $A$ is $\vee$-subfit by Corollary 4.3. Moreover, $\mathcal{D} M A$ is a frame (since every complete Boolean algebra is a frame; see, e.g., [BD74, p. 53]), so $\mathcal{D} M A \cong \mathcal{B} \mathcal{L} A$ by Proposition 3.7. Therefore, $\mathcal{B} \mathcal{L} A$ is Boolean, so $A$ is $\wedge$-subfit by Theorem 6.3.

Conversely, suppose $A$ is $\vee$-subfit and $\wedge$-subfit. Since $A$ is $\vee$-subfit, $A$ is proHeyting by Lemma 4.6, so $\mathcal{D} M A \cong \mathcal{B} \mathcal{L} A$ by Proposition 3.7. Because $A$ is $\wedge$-subfit, $\mathcal{B} \mathcal{L} A$ is Boolean by Theorem 6.3. Thus, $\mathcal{D} M A$ is Boolean.

We conclude this section by characterizing when the ideal and canonical completions are Boolean. As we will see, the condition for the ideal completion to be Boolean is more restrictive.

Proposition 6.5. For $\mathrm{A} \in$ DLat, $\mathcal{M}$ is Boolean iff A is finite and Boolean.
Proof. If A is finite, then $\mathcal{M} \cong \mathrm{A}$, so A Boolean implies that $\mathcal{M}$ is Boolean. Conversely, suppose $\mathcal{M}$ is Boolean. Then every ideal, being complemented, is principal, so again $\mathcal{M} \cong \mathrm{A}$. Since every infinite boolean algebra has an infinite pairwise disjoint set [Kop89, Prop. 3.4], it must also have a nonprincipal ideal. Thus, $A$ is finite.
Proposition 6.6. For $\mathrm{A} \in$ DLat, $A^{\sigma}$ is Boolean iff A is Boolean.
Proof. Let $X$ be the Priestley space of $A$. Then $A$ is Boolean iff the order on $X$ is discrete (see, e.g., [Gra11, p. 119]), which happens iff $\mathrm{Up}(\mathrm{X})=\mathcal{P}(\mathrm{X})$, which is equivalent to $\mathrm{A}^{\sigma}$ being Boolean.

The situation summarizes as follows:
Summary 6.7. Let $\mathrm{A} \in$ DLat.
(1) $\mathcal{B} \mathcal{L} A$ (resp. $p \mathcal{O}(A)$ is Boolean iff $A$ is $\wedge$-subfit iff max $X$ is dense in $X$.
(2) $\mathcal{D} M A$ is Boolean iff $A$ is both $\vee$ - and $\wedge$-subfit iff both $\min X$ and $\max X$ are dense in $X$.
(3) $A^{\sigma}$ is Boolean iff $A$ is Boolean iff $\max X$ is $X$.
(4) $\mathcal{M}$ is Boolean iff $A$ is finite and Boolean iff $\max X$ is $X$ and $X$ is finite.

query: What role do Bayesian models play in mitigating bias from spatial confounding?
golden_answer: Bayesian models mitigate bias from spatial confounding by using reduced-rank regression approaches with principal kriging functions. These models incorporate non-local spike-and-slab priors for basis coefficients, allowing simultaneous variable and model selection without needing separate smoothing parameter selection.
source_title: Regularized Principal Spline Functions to Mitigate Spatial Confounding
source_text:
# 1 Introduction 

In many observational studies, an important statistical problem lies in inferring the effects of one or more predictors, also known as treatments or exposures, on a response variable, while accounting for confounders, i.e. factors associated with both exposures and response (see, e.g., Lawson, 2018). However, adjusting for relevant confounders can be challenging if these variables are unknown. This limitation poses a significant hurdle as standard estimators are often biased and inconsistent. Hence, a major concern in estimating exposure effects is how to account for unmeasured confounders. In spatially structured data, this challenge is known as spatial confounding, first identified by Clayton et al. (1993).

In a regression framework, various methodological approaches have been advanced to mitigate the bias stemming from spatial confounding. For recent literature reviews see, for example, Reich et al. (2021), Khan and Berrett (2023), and Urdangarin et al. (2023). To adjust for unobserved covariates and improve model fitting, it is possible to include a spatially correlated random effect in the model. Nevertheless, research has demonstrated that this strategy does not necessarily alleviate the unmeasured confounding bias (Clayton et al., 1993, Paciorek, 2010, Page et al., 2017). In particular, Hodges and Reich (2010) demonstrated that this approach can actually increase bias relative to fitting a non-spatial model, due to the collinearity between the spatial term and the exposure. As a result, Reich et al. (2006) and Hodges and Reich (2010) propose the restricted spatial regression (RSR) model, wherein a spatial random effect (SRE) is included but is restricted to the orthogonal complement of the space spanned by other observed covariates. Various revisions and enhancements to RSR have been proposed in subsequent studies (Azevedo et al., 2021, Dupont et al., 2022, Hanks et al., 2015, Hughes and Haran, 2013, Nobre et al., 2021, Prates et al., 2019). However, research has shown that approaches based on RSR are not effective in mitigating spatial confounding (Khan and Calder, 2022, Zimmerman and Ver Hoef, 2022).

In parallel with the development of RSR, Paciorek (2010) explored further scenarios where fitting a spatial model may lead to changes in bias. In the context of Gaussian processes, the author provides an inequality condition for bias reduction (with respect to a non-spatial model that ignores confounding), where the variability of the exposure must be confined within a smaller spatial

range compared to that of the unmeasured confounder. Reversing this inequality, confounding bias becomes amplified. Besides, the non-spatial variation in the exposure is also found to be impactful on the bias (Bobb et al., 2022). These results, confirmed also by Page et al. (2017), guided the development of several solutions, based on different reparametrizations of a spatial linear model (Bobb et al., 2022, Dupont et al., 2022, Guan et al., 2023, Keller and Szpiro, 2020, Marques et al., 2022, Prates et al., 2015, Thaden and Kneib, 2018, Urdangarin et al., 2024).

A popular approach involves modelling the random effect component as a smooth function of spatial locations using spline basis functions (Dupont et al., 2022, Guan et al., 2023, Keller and Szpiro, 2020, Paciorek, 2010). This is motivated by the versatility of splines to address spatial scale and smoothness issues in both measured and unmeasured variables. However, given the potential for increased bias, a critical question in data analysis is to determine the "optimal" adjustment. Proposed approaches involve utilizing information criteria to determine the number of basis functions (Guan et al., 2023, Keller and Szpiro, 2020), or employing generalized crossvalidation to select a smoothing parameter (Dupont et al., 2022).

Central to our analysis is the formulation of the spatial model as a reduced-rank Bayesian regression model, where we approximate the unmeasured spatial confounder, conditioned on the exposure, using an expansion matrix of principal kriging functions. Notably, these basis functions are data-adaptive and can be organized from coarse to fine scales of spatial variation (Fontanella et al., 2013, Kent et al., 2001, Mardia et al., 1998). For a specific parametrization, we demonstrate that the principal kriging functions lead to principal thin-plate splines functions, thus establishing a connection between splines and kriging. Within the Bayesian paradigm, we then impose non-local spike-and-slab priors on the basis coefficients (Johnson and Rossell, 2012, Rossell and Telesca, 2017). Unlike the sequential selection of bases obtained via information criteria, the proposed methodology conducts variable and model selection simultaneously, thereby avoiding issues associated with truncating the basis matrix or selecting a smoothing parameter.

We envision spatial confounding as a "data generation" problem, that is the problematic relationship is between the processes generating exposure and unmeasured confounder (Khan and Berrett, 2023). To investigate the mechanism of spatial confounding within the proposed reduced-rank model, we provide a theoretical expression of the bias of the adjusted ordinary least squares estimator which clearly shows how the spatial scale of the involved spatial processes and the selection of the basis functions can either mitigate or exacerbate the bias.

The paper is structured as follows. Section 2 reviews the theoretical framework. Section 3 introduces the spatial linear model and its representation based on principal kriging and spline functions. Section 4 discusses the circumstances under which confounding bias can be alleviated. Section 5 discusses the proposed Bayesian model regularization approach. Section 6 illustrates the results from a wide range of simulated scenarios, where the proposed approach is also compared to most of the recently published methods. Section 7 applies these methods to real data concerning tropospheric ozone, Section 8 concludes with a discussion.

query: In what way do transformers outperform traditional methods like two-stage least squares under endogeneity conditions?
golden_answer: Transformers provide more robust and reliable predictions and coefficient estimates than the two-stage least squares method due to their ability to inherently handle endogeneity through an emulation of gradient-based optimization processes.
source_title: Transformers Handle Endogeneity in In-Context Linear Regression
source_text:
#### Abstract

We explore the capability of transformers to address endogeneity in in-context linear regression. Our main finding is that transformers inherently possess a mechanism to handle endogeneity effectively using instrumental variables (IV). First, we demonstrate that the transformer architecture can emulate a gradient-based bi-level optimization procedure that converges to the widely used two-stage least squares (2SLS) solution at an exponential rate. Next, we propose an in-context pretraining scheme and provide theoretical guarantees showing that the global minimizer of the pre-training loss achieves a small excess loss. Our extensive experiments validate these theoretical findings, showing that the trained transformer provides more robust and reliable in-context predictions and coefficient estimates than the 2SLS method, in the presence of endogeneity.

query: Is the beta-Poisson approximation valid for all values of \(\beta\) and \(\alpha\)?
golden_answer: No, the beta-Poisson approximation is valid for \(\beta \gg \alpha\) and \(\beta \gg 1\).

Impact of heterogeneity on infection probability: Insights from
  single-hit dose-response models
source_text:
# 4.5.1. Example $C_{1}^{\prime}$ : Beta-distributed infectivity and Poisson-distributed dose 

Here, it is assumed that the dose is $n_{h} \sim \operatorname{Pois}\left(\mu_{n}\right)$ so that model $C_{1}^{\prime}$ can be interpreted as an extension of model $A_{1}^{\prime}$ (Sec. 4.2.1) to include a betadistributed infectivity. Using Eq. (18) to set $P^{\left(A^{\prime}\right)}(x, \boldsymbol{\xi})=P^{\left(A_{1}^{\prime}\right)}\left(x, \mu_{n}\right)$ in Eq. (47) leads to the following expected probability of infection:

$$
P^{\left(C_{1}^{\prime}\right)}\left(\alpha, \beta, \mu_{n}\right)=1-{ }_{1} F_{1}\left(\alpha, \alpha+\beta,-\mu_{n}\right)
$$

Here, ${ }_{1} F_{1}$ is the Kummer confluent function [36]. Eq. (48) is the exact beta-Poisson model proposed by Furumoto and Mickey [16]. In the same work, the authors derived the beta-Poisson approximation,

$$
P^{\left(C_{1}^{\prime}\right)}\left(\alpha, \beta, \mu_{n}\right) \simeq P^{\left(\hat{C_{1}}^{\prime}\right)}\left(\alpha, \beta, \mu_{n}\right) \equiv 1-\left(1+\frac{\mu_{n}}{\beta}\right)^{-\alpha}
$$

which is valid for $\beta \gg \alpha$ and $\beta \gg 1$, i.e. for $\mu_{x} \ll 1$ and $v_{x} \ll \mu_{x}$ (cf. Eq. (33)).

The functional relationship between $P^{\left(\hat{C_{1}}^{\prime}\right)}$ and $\mu_{n}$ mirrors that of $P^{\left(\hat{C_{1}}\right)}$ and $n$ (compare Eqs. (49) and (40)). Consequently, Proposition 4.4, established for model $C_{1}$, directly extends to model $C_{1}^{\prime}$ through the expression of the median dose in terms of $\mu_{n}$. While this proposition may bear resemblance

to previous demonstrations expressing $P^{\left(\hat{C}_{1}{ }^{\prime}\right)}$ as a function of $\alpha$ and the median dose [8], it is essential to highlight a crucial distinction. Proposition 4.4 elucidates the decline in the slope of $P^{\left(\hat{C}_{1}{ }^{\prime}\right)}$ with increasing $v_{x}$ while holding $\mu_{x}$ constant. Such delineation between the variance and mean of infectivity cannot be achieved by parameterising $P^{\left(\hat{C}_{1}{ }^{\prime}\right)}$ in terms of $\alpha$ and the median dose.

Despite the formal similarity between Eqs. (40) and (49) and the fact that both are valid in the limit of low and relatively homogeneous infectivity, $P^{\left(\hat{C}_{1}^{\prime}\right)}$ does not result by using $P^{\left(\hat{C}_{1}\right)}$ and the Poisson probability mass function in Eq. (46). Irrespective of that, the deviations of $P^{\left(\hat{C}_{1}{ }^{\prime}\right)}$ from the exact probability $P^{\left(C_{1}^{\prime}\right)}$ are analogous to those described in Sec. 4.4.1 for $P^{\left(\hat{C}_{1}\right)}$ compared to $P^{\left(C_{1}\right)}$.

query: How is the index assigned to a zero of $f$ if the determinant of its Jacobian is positive?
golden_answer: The index +1 is assigned if the determinant of the Jacobian at a zero $\sigma$ is positive.
source_title: Robust Equilibria in Generic Extensive form Games
source_text:
# 2.3. Index Theory 

The fixed point index contains information about the robustness of fixed points of a map when such a map is perturbed to a nearby map. Since Nash equilibria are fixed points, we can apply index theory to them (cf. Ritzberger, 1994). The classical introduction to index theory usually requires some concepts from algebraic topology. For the purposes of this paper, this can be bypassed without much hindrance. Results in this section can be found in McLennan (2018, pp 245-265) and Pahl (2023).

Let $\mathbb{G}$ be a normal-form game with mixed strategy $\Sigma$. Given a neighborhood $O$ of $\Sigma$ suppose $f: O \rightarrow \Sigma$ is a differentiable map. Let $d_{f}$ be the displacement of $f$, i.e., $d_{f}(\sigma)=\sigma-f(\sigma)$. Then the fixed points of $f$ are the zeros of $d_{f}$. Suppose now that the Jacobian of $d_{f}$ at a zero $\sigma$ of $f$ is nonsingular. We assign the index +1 to $\sigma$ if the determinant of the Jacobian of $d_{f}$ is positive or -1 if such a determinant is negative. For the next definition, given a subset $\mathscr{O}$ of $\Sigma$, we denote by $\operatorname{cl}_{\Sigma}(\mathscr{O})$ the closure of $\mathscr{O}$ with respect to $\Sigma$.

Definition 2.2. An open neighborhood $\mathscr{O} \subset \Sigma$ of a component of equilibria (in mixed strategies) $K$ of normal-form game $\mathbb{G}$ is admissible if every equilibrium of $\mathbb{G}$ in $\mathrm{cl}_{\Sigma}(\mathscr{O})$ belongs to $K$.

When a finite game $\mathbb{G}$ has a component of equilibria $K$ that consists of more than a single strategy profile, we extend the definition of the index as follows. Take a continuous map $g_{\mathbb{G}}$ : $\Sigma \rightarrow \Sigma$ such that the fixed points of $g_{\mathbb{G}}$ are the Nash equilibria of game $\mathbb{G}$ and $g_{\mathbb{G}}$ continuously depends on the payoffs of $\mathbb{G}$. An example of such a map is the map Nash (1951) constructed to prove existence of equilibria in mixed strategies. Consider a neighborhood $O$ of $\Sigma$ and $r: O \rightarrow \Sigma$ a retraction to the closest point in $\Sigma$. Let $\mathscr{O} \subset O$ be an open neighborhood of $K$ in the affine space generated by $\Sigma$, whose closure contains no other fixed point of $g$. We approximate $\left(g_{\mathbb{G}} \circ r\right)$ uniformly by a differentiable function $f: O \rightarrow \Sigma$ without fixed points on the boundary of $\mathscr{O}$ and such that the displacement of $f$ at any fixed point has nonsingular Jacobian. For any sufficiently close approximation, the sum of the indexes of the (isolated) fixed points of $f$ in $\mathscr{O}$ is constant and can be taken as the definition of the index of the component $K .{ }^{9}$

We can now define the index with respect to the best-reply correspondence of game $\mathbb{G}$ following the same procedure as in GW. Consider now $\mathscr{O} \cap \Sigma$. For notational convenience, we will denote this intersection from now on as $\mathscr{O}$. Let $W$ be an open neighborhood of $\operatorname{Graph}\left(\mathrm{BR}^{\mathbb{G}}\right)$ such that $W \cap\left\{(\sigma, \sigma) \in \Sigma \times \Sigma \mid \sigma \in \mathrm{cl}_{\Sigma}(\mathscr{O})-\mathscr{O}\right\}=\varnothing$. There exists $\bar{W} \subset W$ a neighborhood of $\operatorname{Graph}\left(\mathrm{BR}^{\mathbb{G}}\right)$ such that any two continuous functions $f_{0}$ and $f_{1}$ from $\Sigma$ to $\Sigma$ whose graphs are in the neighborhood $\bar{W}$ are homotopic by a homotopy $H:[0,1] \times \Sigma \rightarrow \Sigma$ with

[^0]
[^0]:    ${ }^{9}$ Under the continuous dependence of the payoffs of $\mathbb{G}$, this definition of index is independent of the particular map $g_{\mathbb{G}}$ used, it only depends on the game $\mathbb{G}$ (cf. DeMichelis and Germano (2000)).

Graph $(H(t, \cdot)) \subset \bar{W}$ for all $t \in[0,1]$ (cf. McLennan, 1989). Take a continuous map $f: \Sigma \rightarrow \Sigma$ with $\operatorname{Graph}(f) \subset \bar{W}$. We define the best-reply index of component $K$, denoted $\operatorname{Ind}_{\mathrm{BR}^{\mathrm{C}}}(K)$, as the fixed point index of the continuous map $\left.f\right|_{\mathscr{O}}: \mathscr{O} \rightarrow \Sigma$. The choice of the neighborhood $W$ and the homotopy property of the index (see Dold, 1972, Chapter VII, 5.15) imply that the index of the component is the same for any continuous map with graph in the neighborhood $\bar{W}$. We note that defining the index of a component from, say, the map that Nash used in (Nash, 1951) or from the best-reply correspondence are two distinct ways of defining the index, which can be shown to be equivalent (cf. GW). In addition, this process to define the index applies with insignificant changes if the correspondence between the simplices of strategies is contractible valued instead of convex valued (cf. McLennan, 1989). ${ }^{10}$ This fact will play an important role in Section 5.1, as we need to consider selections of a best-reply correspondence which are not necessarily convex-valued, but are contractible-valued.

One can generalize the definition of the best-reply index of a component of equilibria to the best-reply index of an admissible neighborhood, by using the exact same procedure as in the previous paragraph. This yields the index of a neighborhood by summing the indexes of the components of equilibria which are contained in it. For convenience, whenever we refer to the index of a component or an admissible neighborhood, it will be implicit that we refer to the best-reply index.

We are now ready to recall a few known properties of the index of equilibria which we will use in the proof of our main result. The proofs that the index satisfies such properties can be found in McLennan (2018) or GW.
I. 1 The index of an admissible neighborhood is locally constant with respect to payoff perturbations of the game. Formally, fix an admissible neighborhood $O$ in the mixed strategy set of a finite game $\mathbb{G}$. Then there exist $\bar{\delta}>0$, such that for any $0 \leq \delta \leq \bar{\delta}$ and a $\delta$-payoff-perturbation $\mathbb{G}^{\delta}$ of game $\mathbb{G}$, the index of $O$ (with respect to $\mathbb{G}^{\delta}$ ) is constant.
I. 2 The index of an equilibrium component is invariant to equivalent presentations of a game. If $K$ is a component of equilibria of $\mathbb{G}$ with index $c$, then for any equivalent game $\bar{G}$, the index of the equivalent component $\bar{K}$ is also $c$.
I. 3 The index of a component is invariant to the deletion of strictly inferior replies to the component. If $K$ is a component of equilibria with index $c$ of game $\mathbb{G}$, then deleting from the normal-form of game $\mathbb{G}$ the pure strategies of player $n$ which are strictly inferior replies to every profile in the component $K$ yields a new game $\mathbb{G}^{\prime}$ with the same component $K$ as an equilibrium component in $\mathbb{G}^{\prime}$ and with the same index $c$.
We also need three well-known properties of the index. For our purposes, we particularize their statements as follows:
I. 4 Multiplication: Let $\mathrm{BR}^{\mathbb{G}}: \Sigma \Rightarrow \Sigma$ and $\mathrm{BR}^{\mathbb{G}^{\prime}}: \Sigma^{\prime} \Rightarrow \Sigma^{\prime}$ be the best-reply correspondences of (respectively) games $\mathbb{G}$ and $\mathbb{G}^{\prime}$. Let $\mathrm{BR}^{\mathbb{G}} \times \mathrm{BR}^{\mathbb{G}^{\prime}}$ be the correspondence taking $(\sigma, \tau) \in$ $\Sigma \times \Sigma^{\prime}$ to $\mathrm{BR}^{\mathbb{G}}(\sigma) \times \mathrm{BR}^{\mathbb{G}^{\prime}}(\tau)$. If $O \times O^{\prime} \subset \Sigma \times \Sigma^{\prime}$ contains no fixed points of $\mathrm{BR}^{\mathbb{G}} \times \mathrm{BR}^{\mathbb{G}^{\prime}}$ in its boundary, then $O$ (respectively $O^{\prime}$ ) has no fixed points of $\mathrm{BR}^{\mathbb{G}}$ (respectively $\mathrm{BR}^{\mathbb{G}^{\prime}}$ ) in its boundary, and the index of $O \times O^{\prime}$ with respect to $\mathrm{BR}^{\mathbb{G}} \times \mathrm{BR}^{\mathbb{G}^{\prime}}$ is the multiplication of the indexes of $O$ (with respect to $\mathrm{BR}^{\mathbb{G}}$ ) and of $O^{\prime}$ (with respect to $\mathrm{BR}^{\mathbb{G}^{\prime}}$ ).

[^0]
[^0]:    ${ }^{10}$ A topological space $X$ is contractible if there exists a continuous map $T:[0,1] \times X \rightarrow X$ and $x_{0} \in X$ such that $T(0, \cdot)=\operatorname{id}_{X}$ and $T(1, \cdot)=x_{0}$.

I. 5 Commutativity: Let $F: \Sigma \Rightarrow \Sigma$ be an upper hemicontinuous correspondence that is nonempty, compact and convex valued. Let $e: \Sigma \rightarrow \Sigma^{\prime}$ be a continuous map with leftinverse $q: \Sigma^{\prime} \rightarrow \Sigma$. If $X$ is a component of fixed points of $e \circ F \circ q: \Sigma^{\prime} \Rightarrow \Sigma^{\prime}$ then $q(X)$ is a component of fixed points of $F$ and their indexes agree.
I. 6 Excision: Let $F: \Sigma \Rightarrow \Sigma$ be an upper hemicontinuous correspondence that is nonempty, compact and convex valued. Suppose $\tilde{\mathscr{O}}$ and $\mathscr{O}$ are both admissible neighborhoods in $\Sigma$ whose closures in $\Sigma$ contain the same fixed points of $F$. Then the index of $\mathscr{O}$ and that of $\tilde{\mathscr{O}}$ with respect to $F$ are identical.

We conclude this section with the following result. In particular, it implies that if a component has zero index, then some ending node is reached with probability zero.

Proposition 2.3. If an equilibrium outcome $Q$ induced by a component of equilibria in mixed strategies $K$ has full support, then $K$ has non-zero index.

Proof. See Appendix A.

query: How does magneto-optical trapping differ from other methods used in creating Cs+ ion beams?
golden_answer: Magneto-optical trapping uses laser cooling techniques to create an intense atomic beam that is then photoionized into Cs+ ions with high brightness and low energy spread. source_title: Molten salt ion source using glass capillaries as emitter
source_text:
## I. INTRODUCTION

In Secondary Ion Mass Spectrometry (SIMS), charged particles are ejected from a sample surface when bombarded by a primary beam. Those charged particles form a secondary ion beam that is analyzed with appropriate electrostatic lenses to derive the charge-to-mass ratio of the particles. The molecular mass spectrum of the pulverized area on the sample allows then for highly sensitive detection and imaging. As a primary beam source and depending on the analysis requirements, typically $\mathrm{O}^{2+}, \mathrm{O}^{-}, \mathrm{Cs}^{+}, \mathrm{Ga}^{+}$ions or clusters such as $\mathrm{Bi}_{3}^{+}$are used. While gallium ion sources are vastly used in high lateral resolution SIMS when there is a need for fine image resolution, their excellent optical characteristics come unfortunately at a cost of ionization yield, i.e. the amount of secondary ions generated per pulverized atom: typical orders of magnitude for applications in metallurgy are around $10^{-5}$ with a $\mathrm{Ga}^{+}$beam, while yields of $10^{-3}$ using $\mathrm{O}^{2+}$ or even $10^{-2}$ using $\mathrm{Cs}^{+}$beams are commonly achieved ${ }^{1,2}$.

An ideal primary ion source for Secondary Ion Mass Spectrometry (SIMS), would combine the brightness and low energy spread of a Liquid Metal Ion Source (LMIS), i.e., the emitted ion current per unit solid angle, with the availability of reactive elements as primary ions like $\mathrm{Cs}^{+}$beam or nonmetallic ones like Oxygen or reactive clusters. Additionally, having the versatility of a duoplasmatron to produce both positive and negative ions would also be appreciated. From there, adapting LMIS source designs to work with other liquids containing different ion species naturally comes to mind.

In order to focus ion beams into a spot size less than 10 nm , the beam needs to be emitted from a very small area into a limited solid angle. To meet this demand, several LMIS-type sources using a needle or a capillary with micrometer tips have been proposed. In both cases, the conducting liquid at the tip of the emitter forms a Taylor cone under a strong electric field. The high field at the cone's apex extracts the ions and
accelerates them, producing a bright beam. To sustain a steady beam, the liquid is fed passively to the tip, relying on capillary action along externally wetted needles, inside capillaries, or through bulk porous media. The needle-type emitter is most commonly used in Focused Ion Beam (FIB) instruments.

Few Cs-based LMIS designs have been reported ${ }^{3-6}$, arguably due to the chemical activity, low surface tension, and high vapor pressure of cesium, as opposed to the successful Ga-LMIS. In fact, liquid caesium has to be supplied to the emitter / reserve by breaking a cesium vial under ultra-high vacuum (UHV) to prevent oxidation of $\mathrm{Cs}^{4,6}$, so that Cs-LMIS designs are difficult to handle or suffer a short lifetime and therefore are mainly suited for academic purposes.

Instead of pure liquid metals, Liquid Alloy Ion Sources (LAIS) use liquid alloys based, for example, on gold-silicon eutectics to produce ion beams of different species, see L. Bischoff et al. for an extensive review ${ }^{7}$. While LAIS sources are able to emit numerous ions like $\mathrm{Li}, \mathrm{Be}, \mathrm{Ge} \ldots, \mathrm{Cs}$-emitting LAIS sources have, to our knowledge, not been reported, probably because they are as challenging to operate as the pure Cs-LMIS.

Liquid metals are not the only substances from which ion beams can be obtained. Ionic liquids (IL) have been investigated as alternatives to LMIS due to their low vapor pressure, chemical stability, low operating temperature and tunability via selection of cation/anion pairs. In the pioneering work by Romero-Sanz et al. ${ }^{8}$, it was shown that positively charged solvated ions could be extracted from the ionic liquid $[\mathrm{EMI}]^{+}$ $\left[\mathrm{BF}_{4}\right]^{-}$in a pure ion evaporation regime using silica capillaries as emitters. Martino et al. demonstrated using the capillary rise method that both hydrophilic and hydrophobic ionic liquids can wet borosilicate glass in dry conditions ${ }^{9}$. Hence, ILs should also be suitable for use with borosilicate glass capillaries as emitters.

Ionic Liquid Ion Sources (ILIS) using a tungsten emitter tip wetted by room temperature ionic liquids were investigated

among others by Lozano and Martinez-Sanchez ${ }^{10-15}$. ILIS share qualities with LMIS sources necessary for focused ion beams (FIB) operation, such as pure ion emission and low energy spreads. These sources work at lower currents, room temperature, and are able to produce both positive and negative ions from many ionic liquids.

However, organic ILs present specific issues in SIMS: large organic fragments can lead to complex, overlapping peaks in mass spectra, making data interpretation harder. Larger organic ions may not efficiently sputter sample material or may fragment unpredictably. Also, ILIS operation in a single polarity is limited by the formation of a charge double layer at the surface of the tungsten needle that is wetted by the ionic liquid, leading to emission degradation within a few minutes ${ }^{11}$. In the particular case of a porous tungsten emitter needle, continuous DC operation leads even to the degradation of the emitter tip ${ }^{16}$. Now, the electrochemical degradation of a porous needle was mitigated by using a distal electrode that polarizes the liquid, while the emitter is electrically floating ${ }^{16}$. The formation of a charge double layer could be avoided by alternating the polarity of the source at a rate of $1 \mathrm{~Hz}^{11}$. This way, the beam could be stabilized for over 200 h , but such a mode is generally not compatible with FIB operation. More recently, Fujiwara reported that a negative cluster ion beam could be produced continuously using hydrophilic ionic liquid, propylammonium nitrate, and that electrochemical reduction of the ionic liquids forms volatile products, enabling continuous negative ion beam production ${ }^{17}$. Irradiating the surface of an electrically insulated material, Fujiwara et al. showed that the charging voltage is as low as 1 V , so that secondary ion mass spectrometry of an insulated organic sample is possible using the negative ion beam without charge compensation ${ }^{18}$. While ILIS may potentially enhance the capabilities in FIB applications, the integration of ILIS into FibSIMS systems is still under development.

Some cesium salts with bulky organic anions, such as $\left[\mathrm{Tf}_{2} \mathrm{~N}\right]^{-}$are known to form low melting $\left(125^{\circ} \mathrm{C}\right)$ ionic salts ${ }^{19}$ and can even be mixed with other alkali organic salts sharing the same anion to lower the melting temperature of the eutectic mixture ${ }^{20}$. They can also be mixed with organic ionic liquids containing, for example, organic cations like imidazolium, to form room temperature ionic liquids ${ }^{21}$. While there seems to be no published work about a ILIS based on organic Cs salts, this may be a promising way to produce $\mathrm{Cs}^{+}$ions with an ILIS.

Alternatively, a bright $\mathrm{Cs}^{+}$ion source, which is not based on the field evaporation mechanism from an emitter tip, has been developed in the last years. Low-temperature ion sources (LoTIS) use magneto-optical trapping with laser cooling to create an intense atomic beam, which is then photoionised to produce a beam with a high brightness and a low energy spread ${ }^{22-24}$. Such a $\mathrm{Cs}^{+}$has been recently integrated with SIMS instruments ${ }^{25}$. However, compared to ILIS-type sources (including the one presented here), LoTIS systems generally produce much lower ion currents compared to ILIS. This limitation makes them less suitable for applications that demand high throughput for fast imaging time or for highdose ion implantation. Also, implementing magneto-optical
trapping requires complex laser systems, precise frequency stabilization, and carefully aligned optics. These components add to the system's complexity, cost, and maintenance compared to the relatively straightforward setup of LAIS or ILIS. Finally, LoTIS works exclusively in positive emission mode.

Compared to organic ionic liquids, molten salts have a significantly higher electrical conductivity and surface tension, albeit at the cost of a higher melting temperature. Based on the finding of Garoz et al. that the purely ionic regime in ILIS is achieved merely for liquids with high surface tension and high electrical conductivity ${ }^{26}$, molten salts should be promising alternatives, if purely ionic regimes are required. Using several eutectic salt mixtures in their ILIS source, mostly alkalichlorides but also a few alkali-nitrates and akali-bromides, R. Sailer and P. Sudraud ${ }^{27}$ achieved stable beam emissions with a lifetime of typically 20 hours, the lifetime being limited mostly by the evaporation rates of the ionic compounds. The emitter tip was a $500 \mu \mathrm{~m}$ alumina fiber machined into a conical shape with typical curvature radii below $50 \mu \mathrm{~m}$. The source could be operated for several dozens of hours in a single polarity without noticing any change in the emitter or emission characteristics. Time of flight measurements showed that the beam contained a variety of singly charged ions or small clusters.

Tajmar et al., manufactured and tested an indium liquid metal ion source using a tapered silicate glass capillary with a sub-micrometer tip as an emitter tip ${ }^{28}$. They demonstrated that a pure glass-based LMIS may form the basis for future LMIS-chips with very high current densities. From the current voltage curve, they deduced a source impedance of 19 $\mathrm{M} \Omega$ and a tip radius of about $0.5 \mu \mathrm{~m}$, which was the outer diameter of the glass tip. However, because the liquid metal does not wet the silicate glass, they had to apply an overpressure of 20 bar to the liquid to push it into the capillary tip. When an electric field was applied at the tip, they succeeded in emitting a stable beam of $20 \mu \mathrm{~A}$ from the liquid meniscus anchored at the tip of the capillary for about 800 s before the tip of the capillary was destroyed by the overpressure of the liquid and the Coulomb pressure applied by the electric field at the tip of the capillary.

Following the idea of Tajmar, we present a proof of concept of a tapered glass capillary ion source, intended for SIMS applications using a molten salt mixture rich in $\mathrm{Cs}^{+}$ions and negative oxygen complexes like $\mathrm{NO}_{2}^{-}$. In contrast to an "open" source design in which the conducting liquid covers the surface of a tungsten needle, the presented setup uses a closed design which should avoid the problem of limited flow supply to the tip and also limit the surface of molten salt that is exposed to the vacuum. We also discuss in this work the fusion temperature, evaporation, wetting behavior and hygroscopicity of the molten salt mixture in vacuum conditions and how those properties influenced the design of the ion source body.

query: How does the DMVC-Tracker improve multi-agent trajectory planning for aerial tracking?
golden_answer: The DMVC-Tracker enhances multi-agent trajectory planning by utilizing Dynamic Buffered Voronoi Cells (DBVC) and Dynamic Inter-Visibility Cells (DIVC). These time-variant spaces help prevent collisions and occlusions among agents while maintaining optimal distances from a moving target. This approach is combined with a Bernstein polynomial motion primitive-based method to generate efficient tracking trajectories.
source_title:
DMVC-Tracker: Distributed Multi-Agent Trajectory Planning for Target
  Tracking Using Dynamic Buffered Voronoi and Inter-Visibility Cells
source_text:
#### Abstract

This letter presents a distributed trajectory planning method for multi-agent aerial tracking. The proposed method uses a Dynamic Buffered Voronoi Cell (DBVC) and a Dynamic Inter-Visibility Cell (DIVC) to formulate the distributed trajectory generation. Specifically, the DBVC and the DIVC are time-variant spaces that prevent mutual collisions and occlusions among agents, while enabling them to maintain suitable distances from the moving target. We combine the DBVC and the DIVC with an efficient Bernstein polynomial motion primitive-based tracking trajectory generation method, which has been refined into a less conservative approach than in our previous work. The proposed algorithm can compute each agent's trajectory within several milliseconds on an Intel i7 desktop. We validate the tracking performance in challenging scenarios, including environments with dozens of obstacles.


Index Terms—Path planning for multiple mobile robots, distributed robot systems, aerial tracking.

query: Does the probabilistic counter use more than $\mathcal{O}(1)$ bits to detect if it has exceeded a threshold?
golden_answer: No, it uses only $\mathcal{O}(1)$ bits.
source_title: Regular Languages in the Sliding Window Model
source_text:
# 4.3 The Bernoulli counter 

The crucial algorithmic tool for the proof of Theorem 4.3(3) is a simple probabilistic counter. It is inspired by the approximate counter by Morris [36, 76], which uses $\mathcal{O}(\log \log n)$ bits. For our purposes, it suffices to detect whether the counter has exceeded a certain threshold, which can be accomplished using only $\mathcal{O}(1)$ bits.

Formally, a probabilistic counter is a probabilistic automaton

$$
\mathfrak{Z}=(C,\{\operatorname{inc}\}, \iota, \rho, F)
$$

over the unary alphabet $\{$ inc $\}$. States in $F$ are called high and states in $C \backslash F$ are called low. We make the restriction that there is a low state $c_{0} \in C$ such that $\iota\left(c_{0}\right)=1$ (and hence $\iota(c)=0$ for all $c \in C \backslash\left\{c_{0}\right\}$ ); thus $\mathfrak{Z}$ has a unique initial state $c_{0}$ (which must be low) and we write $\mathfrak{Z}=\left(C,\{\right.$ inc $\left.\}, c_{0}, \rho, F\right)$. This restriction is not really important (and can in fact be achieved for every probabilistic automaton by adding a new state), but it will simplify our constructions.

In the following we write $\mathfrak{Z}(k, c)$ for $\mathfrak{Z}\left(\right.$ inc $\left.^{k}, c\right)(k \geqslant 0, c \in C)$, which is the probability that $\mathfrak{Z}$ arrives in state $c$ after $k$ increments. Moreover, $\mathfrak{Z}^{\text {hi }}(k)$ is the probability that $\mathfrak{Z}$ is in a high state after $k$ increments (this is the same as $\operatorname{Pr}\left[\mathfrak{Z}\right.$ accepts inc $\left.^{k}\right]$ ). Given numbers $0 \leqslant \ell<h$ we say that $\mathfrak{Z}$ is an $(h, \ell)$-counter with error probability $\lambda<\frac{1}{2}$ if for all $k \in \mathbb{N}$ we have:
— If $k \leqslant \ell$, then $\mathfrak{Z}^{\text {hi }}(k) \leqslant \lambda$.

- If $k \geqslant h$, then $\mathfrak{Z}^{\text {hi }}(k) \geqslant 1-\lambda$.

In other words, a probabilistic counter can distinguish with high probability between values below $\ell$ and values above $h$ but does not give any guarantees for counter values strictly between $\ell$ and $h$. A Bernoulli counter is a probabilistic counter $\mathfrak{Z}_{p}$ that is parameterized by a probability $0<p<1$ and that has the state set $\{0,1\}$, where 0 is a low state and 1 is a high state. Initially the counter is in the state $x=0$. On every increment we set $x=1$ with probability $p$; the state remains unchanged with probability $1-p$. We have

$$
\mathfrak{Z}_{p}^{\mathrm{hi}}(k)=\mathfrak{Z}_{p}(k, 1)=1-(1-p)^{k}
$$

Let us first show the following claim.
LEMMA 4.5. For all $h>0,0<\xi<1$ and $0<\ell \leqslant(1-\xi) h$ there exists $0<p<1$ such that $\mathfrak{Z}_{p}$ is an $(h, \ell)$-counter with error probability $1 / 2-\xi / 8$.

PROOF. We need to choose $0<p<1$ such that
(i) $1-(1-p)^{(1-\xi) h} \leqslant 1 / 2-\xi / 8$, or equivalently, $1 / 2+\xi / 8 \leqslant(1-p)^{(1-\xi) h}$, and
(ii) $(1-p)^{h} \leqslant 1 / 2-\xi / 8$, or equivalently, $(1-p)^{(1-\xi) h} \leqslant(1 / 2-\xi / 8)^{1-\xi}$.

It suffices to show

$$
\frac{1}{2}+\frac{\xi}{8} \leqslant\left(\frac{1}{2}-\frac{\xi}{8}\right)^{1-\xi}
$$

Then one can take for instance $p=1-(1 / 2-\xi / 8)^{1 / h} \in(0,1)$, which satisfies (ii). Moreover, (i) is satisfied due to (6).

Taking logarithms shows that (6) is equivalent to

$$
\ln (4+\xi)-\ln 8 \leqslant(1-\xi) \cdot(\ln (4-\xi)-\ln 8)
$$

which can be rearranged to $\ln (4+\xi) \leqslant \ln (4-\xi)+\xi(\ln 8-\ln (4-\xi))$. Since $\ln 8-\ln (4-\xi) \geqslant$ $\ln 8-\ln 4=\ln 2$, it suffices to prove

$$
\ln (4+\xi) \leqslant \ln (4-\xi)+\xi \ln 2
$$

One can verify $3 \ln 2 \approx 2.0794 \geqslant 2$. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}
4+\xi & \leqslant 4+(3 \ln 2-1) \xi \\
& =4+(4 \ln 2-1) \xi-\xi \ln 2 \\
& \leqslant 4+(4 \ln 2-1) \xi-\xi^{2} \ln 2 \\
& =(4-\xi)(\xi \ln 2+1)
\end{aligned}
$$

By taking logarithms and plugging in $\ln x \leqslant x-1$ for all $x>0$, we obtain

$$
\ln (4+\xi) \leqslant \ln (4-\xi)+\ln (\xi \ln 2+1) \leqslant \ln (4-\xi)+\xi \ln 2
$$

This proves (7) and hence (6), and thus the lemma.
PROPOSITION 4.6. For all $h>0,0<\xi<1,0<\ell \leqslant(1-\xi) h$ and $0<\lambda^{\prime}<1 / 2$ there exists an $(h, \ell)$-counter $\mathcal{Z}$ with error probability $\lambda^{\prime}$ which uses $O\left(\log \log \left(1 / \lambda^{\prime}\right)+\log (1 / \xi)\right)$ bits.

PROOF. Take the $(h, \ell)$-counter $\mathcal{Z}_{p}$ from Lemma 4.5, whose error probability is $\lambda:=1 / 2-\xi / 8$. To $\mathcal{Z}_{p}$ we apply Lemma 4.1, which states that we need to run $k=O\left(\log \left(\frac{1}{\lambda^{\prime}}\right) \cdot \frac{1}{\xi^{\prime}}\right)$ independent copies to reduce the error probability to $\lambda^{\prime}$. The states of $\mathcal{Z}_{p}^{(k)}$ are multisets over $\{0,1\}$ of size $k$, which can be encoded with $O(\log k)=O\left(\log \log \frac{1}{\lambda^{\prime}}+\log \frac{1}{\xi}\right)$ bits by specifying the number of 1-bits in the multiset. Note that the unique initial state of $\mathcal{Z}_{p}^{(k)}$ is the multiset with $k$ occurrences of 0 .

  ideals

## QUICK OVERVIEW

Let $(X, 0)$ be a germ of complex space embedded in $\left(\mathbb{C}^{n}, 0\right)$. It is well known that the topological type of $(X, 0)$, that is its class of homeomorphism, determines and is determined by the homeomorphism class of its link $X^{(\epsilon)}=X \cap S_{\epsilon}^{2 n-1}$ for $\epsilon>0$ sufficiently small, where $S_{\epsilon}^{2 n-1}$ is the sphere of

[^0]
[^0]:    2020 Mathematics Subject Classification. Primary 32S05, 32S25, 32B10 Secondary 14J17, 14B05, 32S55.
    Key words and phrases. Complex Surface Singularities, Resolution Of Singularities, Polar Curves, Lipschitz Geometry, Non Archimedean Geometry.

radius $\epsilon$. Thanks to this result, the topology of germs of complex spaces is quite well understood; however, it is not the case for their metric type, and that is what we are going to investigate in this paper.

Let us first give some historical context: the standard metric of $\mathbb{C}^{n}$ induces two natural distances on $(X, 0)$. The outer metric, denoted $d_{o}$, is defined by restricting the Euclidean distance of $\mathbb{C}^{n}$ to $X$, and the inner metric, referred to as $d_{i}$, quantifies the lengths of arcs on $X$. There are many motivations to study these metrics. Among them is the fact that the biholomorphic class of the germ $(X, 0)$ determines the inner (resp. outer) Lipschitz geometry of $(X, 0)$ (see Definition 5.11). Another motivation arises from a result by Mostowski in [Mos85], which asserts that the set of complex germs up to bilipschitz equivalence with respect to the inner (resp. outer) metric is countable. This result was significantly generalized by Parusiński in [Par94] for the real case and then Nhan and Valette in [NV16] for more general O-minimal structures.

The complete classification of complex germs under bilipschitz equivalence is then more attainable compared to the analytic classification and, as expected, richer than the topological classification. However, in the case of germs of complex curves, the difference between Lipschitz geometry and topology does not appear. Indeed, a germ of curve $(C, 0)$ embedded in $\mathbb{C}^{n}$ is metrically conical, meaning that it is inner bilipschitz equivalent to the cone over its link $C^{\epsilon}=C \cap \mathbb{S}_{\epsilon}$. As for the outer metric, it follows from the work of Teissier in [Tei82] that any curve germ $(C, 0) \subset\left(\mathbb{C}^{n}, 0\right)$ is outer bilipschitz equivalent to a germ of a complex plane curve (embedded in $\mathbb{C}^{2}$ ). Later, Neumann and Pichon proved in [NP14] that the outer Lipschitz geometry of a plane curve germ $(C, 0) \subset\left(\mathbb{C}^{2}, 0\right)$ determines and is determined by the embedded topological type of the curve germ.

More recently, Neumann, Birbrair, and Pichon gave a complete classification of complex surface germs with isolated singularities up to bilipschitz equivalence with respect to the inner metric by means of the inner rates of complex surface germs (see Definition 2.18), a topic we elaborate on in this paper. Furthermore, Neumann and Pichon's work in [NP16] establishes a connection between the outer metric of a complex surface germ $(X, 0) \subset\left(\mathbb{C}^{n}, 0\right)$ and the families of generic hyperplane sections and generic polar curves of $(X, 0)$ (see Definitions 1.14 and 2.18). Their result roughly states that the outer Lipschitz geometry of $(X, 0)$ determines the relative position between these families of curves.

In an early study, Belotto, Fantini, Némethi, and Pichon proved in [BdSFNP22] that when the homeomorphism class of a normal surface germ $(X, 0)$ is fixed, there are, up to homeomorphism, only finitely many possible relative positions between the family of generic hyperplane sections and the family of polar curves associated with the generic projections on $(X, 0)$.

In this paper, we investigate what happens to the last mentioned result when we do not assume the normality of the complex surface germ $(X, 0)$. Our result (Theorem A) essentially states that when the homeomorphism class of the germ $(X, 0)$ and the analytic type of its normalization $(\bar{X}, 0)$ are fixed, there are, up to homeomorphism, infinitely many possible relative positions between the generic hyperplane sections and the generic polar curves of $(X, 0)$. In particular, it follows from our result and the work of Neumann and Pichon described earlier that there are infinitely many outer Lipschitz geometries on complex surface germs even when we fix the homeomorphism class of the germs and the analytic type of their normalization.

query: How is spontaneous symmetry breaking characterized for discrete symmetries?
golden_answer: Spontaneous symmetry breaking for discrete symmetries can be characterized by the behavior of the partition function in the presence of a symmetry defect, where it approaches zero in a broken phase and remains constant (non-zero) in an unbroken phase.
