Thus, by combining Theorem 3 and Lemma 1, truthful agents which choose to participate in PFL attain a reshaped and lower loss at the same optimum. Individually rational agents would therefore prefer to participate in PFL (Algorithm 1) over local training due to the reshaped optimum's lower loss. This optimum achieves the same data usage as local training, thereby eliminating the free-rider dilemma.

Remark 6 (Truthfulness Concerns). Participating in PFL, rational agents contribute as much as they would locally (Theorem 3) and attain more benefit (Lemma 1). The only issue that remains is truthfulness: agents may lie about their costs in order to contribute less to federated training under the guise of what looks like an "optimal amount" to the server (thereby avoiding large $P_{f r}$ ).

While PFL eliminates free riding when agents are truthful, this assumption is not realistic in practice. Untruthful agents can report inflated costs to the server in order to trick it into expecting smaller data usage. In effect, agents can lie about their costs to free ride. In the next section, we propose a mechanism which incentivizes agents to be truthful (i.e., their best strategy is not to lie).

query: What is the definition of concurrent composition for continual mechanisms (CMs)?
golden_answer: Concurrent composition for CMs allows an adversary to create new CMs or ask pairs of queries from existing ones, with constraints on the created mechanisms and their query pairs to limit the adversary's power.
source_title: Concurrent Composition for Differentially Private Continual Mechanisms
source_text:
# 4. Concurrent Composition of Continual Mechanisms 

Composition of NIMs. For $1 \leq i \leq k$, let $\mathcal{N}_{i}$ be an NIM with input domain $\mathcal{X}_{i}$, and let $\sim_{i}$ be a neighboring relation on $\mathcal{X}_{i}$. The composition of the NIMs $\mathcal{N}_{1}, \ldots, \mathcal{N}_{k}$ is represented by a non-interactive mechanism $\operatorname{Comp}\left[\mathcal{N}_{1}, \ldots, \mathcal{N}_{k}\right]$ with the domain $\mathcal{X}=\mathcal{X}_{1} \times \cdots \times \mathcal{X}_{k}$. This mechanism takes a tuple of datasets $x=\left(x_{1}, \ldots, x_{k}\right)$ as input and returns

$$
\operatorname{Comp}\left[\mathcal{N}_{1}, \ldots, \mathcal{N}_{k}\right](x)=\left(\mathcal{N}_{1}\left(x_{1}\right), \ldots, \mathcal{N}_{k}\left(x_{k}\right)\right)
$$

Define $\sim$ as a neighboring relation on $\mathcal{X}$, where two tuples $x=\left(x_{1}, \ldots, x_{k}\right)$ and $x^{\prime}=\left(x_{1}^{\prime}, \ldots, x_{k}^{\prime}\right)$ satisfy $x \sim x^{\prime}$ if and only if $x_{i} \sim_{i} x_{i}^{\prime}$ for all $1 \leq i \leq k$. The composition of NIMs $\mathcal{N}_{1}, \ldots, \mathcal{N}_{k}$ is said to be $(\epsilon, \delta)$-DP if the non-interactive mechanism $\operatorname{Comp}\left[\mathcal{N}_{1}, \ldots, \mathcal{N}_{k}\right]$ is $(\epsilon, \delta)$-DP w.r.t. $\sim$ (see Definition 2.2).

In the proofs of this section, we consider $\operatorname{Comp}\left[\mathcal{N}_{1}, \ldots, \mathcal{N}_{k}\right]$ not as a non-interactive, but instead as an interactive mechanism with initial state space $\mathcal{X}$ that receives $x=\left(x_{1}, \ldots, x_{k}\right)$ not as input, but instead as its first message. Immediately after receiving this message it executes $\operatorname{Comp}\left[\mathcal{N}_{1}, \ldots, \mathcal{N}_{k}\right]$ on its initial state and returns its output. Upon receiving a second message, this interactive mechanism halts the communication.
Concurrent Composition of IMs. Vadhan and Wang [20] extended the definition of the composition of NIMs to the concurrent composition of IMs, where an adversary interacts with $k$ interactive mechanisms $\mathcal{M}_{1}, \ldots, \mathcal{M}_{k}$ at the same time. In concurrent composition, the adversary generates a message and determines the receiver of this message (one of the $\mathcal{M}_{i} \mathrm{~s}$ ) adaptively based on all the previous messages exchanged between the adversary and the mechanisms $M_{1}, \ldots, M_{k}$. To

formalize this, Vadhan and Wang [20] introduced an interactive mechanism ConComp[ $\left.\mathcal{M}_{1}, \ldots, \mathcal{M}_{k}\right]$, which internally runs $\mathcal{M}_{1}, \ldots, \mathcal{M}_{k}$ and, upon receiving a message $(q, j)$, forwards the query $q$ to $\mathcal{M}_{j}$ and returns its response.

The initial state space of $\operatorname{ConComp}\left[\mathcal{M}_{1}, \ldots, \mathcal{M}_{k}\right]$ is $S_{\mathcal{M}_{1}}^{\text {init }} \times \cdots \times S_{\mathcal{M}_{k}}^{\text {init }}$, where $S_{\mathcal{M}_{i}}^{\text {init }}$ is the initial state space of $\mathcal{M}_{i}$. Let $\sim_{i}$ be a neighboring relation on each $S_{\mathcal{M}_{i}}^{\text {init }}$, and define the neighboring relation $\sim$ on $S_{\mathcal{M}_{1}}^{\text {init }} \times \cdots \times S_{\mathcal{M}_{k}}^{\text {init }}$ as follows: for any two initial states $s=\left(s_{1}, \ldots, s_{k}\right)$ and $s^{\prime}=\left(s_{1}^{\prime}, \ldots, s_{k}^{\prime}\right)$, we have $s \sim s^{\prime}$ if and only if $s_{i} \sim_{i} s_{i}^{\prime}$ for every $i \in[k]$.

Vadhan and Wang [20] show that if each IM $\mathcal{M}_{i}$ is $\epsilon_{i}$-DP w.r.t $\sim_{i}$, and if the composition of NIMs $\mathrm{RR}_{\epsilon_{1}, 0}, \ldots, \mathrm{RR}_{\epsilon_{k}, 0}$ is $(\epsilon, \delta)$-DP, then $\operatorname{ConComp}\left[\mathcal{M}_{1}, \ldots, \mathcal{M}_{k}\right]$ is also $(\epsilon, \delta)$-DP against an adaptive adversary. Lyu [18] extends this result for $\left(\epsilon_{i}, \delta_{i}\right)$-DP IMs.

In the concurrent composition of IMs, queries asked to each mechanism are chosen adaptively, not only based on that mechanism's previous responses but also using the responses of the other mechanisms up to that point. The results of [20] and [18] show that this concurrency and additional adaptivity do not compromise privacy guarantees. As a result, all $(\epsilon, \delta)$-DP composition theorems for NIMs, such as the basic [6], advanced [9], and optimal [15] composition theorems, can also be applied to the concurrent composition of IMs.
Concurrent Composition of CMs. We extend the definition of the concurrent composition for IMs to the concurrent composition of CMs, where an adversary can create new CMs or ask pairs of queries from the existing ones. Depending on the type of composition, the created mechanisms are constrained, and the sequence of query pairs asked from each CM satisfies certain properties. Based on a secret bit $b \in\{0,1\}$, each CM either receives the first element of every query pair asked from it or the second element. In Section 4.1, we generalize ConComp to ExtConComp and give a formal definition for the concurrent composition of CMs.

To extend Lyu's result on the privacy guarantee of the concurrent composition of IMs to the concurrent composition of CMs, we want to use the following intermediate lemma from their paper: For every $(\epsilon, \delta)$-DP interactive mechanism $\mathcal{M}$ and any pair of neighboring initial states $s$ and $s^{\prime}$ for $\mathcal{M}$, there exists an IPM $\mathcal{P}$ such that for each $b \in\{0,1\}$, the IMs $\mathcal{P} \circ^{*} \mathrm{RR}_{\epsilon, \delta}(b)$ and $\mathcal{M}(b)$ are equivalent. However, as we discuss in Section 4.2, there are hidden assumptions in the proof of this lemma. Additionally, we show there that the construction of $\mathcal{P}$ in [20], for $\epsilon_{i}$-DP IMs, satisfies a property, required for a later proof.

In Section 4.3, we analyze the privacy of the concurrent composition of $k$ fixed $\mathrm{CMs} \mathcal{M}_{1}, \ldots, \mathcal{M}_{k}$. In this composition, the adversary first creates the mechanisms $\mathcal{M}_{1}, \ldots, \mathcal{M}_{k}$ and then asks pairs of queries from each mechanism, ensuring that the sequence of query pairs for each mechanism is valid. In Section 4.4, we extend this composition by fixing $k$ privacy parameters $\left(\epsilon_{1}, \delta_{1}\right), \ldots,\left(\epsilon_{k}, \delta_{k}\right)$ and allowing the adversary to adaptively choose the $\left(\epsilon_{i}, \delta_{i}\right)$-DP mechanism $\mathcal{M}_{i}$ over time.
4.1. Formalization. We extend the definition of ConComp in [20] and introduce ExtConComp that allows the creation of new mechanisms in addition to queries to existing ones. A creation query $(\mathcal{M}, s, \epsilon, \delta, f)$ is a message that requests the creation of a continual mechanism $\mathcal{M}$ with the initial state $s$ and asserts that $\mathcal{M}$ is $(\epsilon, \delta)$-DP w.r.t. the verification function $f$. The mechanism ExtConComp accepts creation queries and messages of the form $(q, i)$, where $q$ is a query for the $i$-th created mechanism. The formal definition of ExtConComp is as follows:
Definition 4.1. Extended concurrent composition, ExtConComp, is a continual mechanism that receives two types of messages:

- A creation query $(\mathcal{M}, s, \epsilon, \delta, f)$, where $\mathcal{M}$ is a CM with a single initial state $s$ that is $(\epsilon, \delta)$-DP w.r.t. a verification function $f$, and
- a query-index pair $(q, i)$, where $i$ is a positive integer, and $q$ is any message.

Upon receiving $(\mathcal{M}, s, \epsilon, \delta, f)$, ExtConComp creates an instance of $\mathcal{M}$ with the initial state $s$, and when receiving $(q, i)$, it forwards $q$ to the $i$-th created mechanism and returns its response. If less than

$i$ mechanisms have been created, ExtConComp halts the communication. The state of ExtConComp is a sequence of pairs $\left(\mathcal{M}_{i}, s_{i}^{\prime}\right)$, where the $i$-th pair represents the $i$-th created mechanism $\mathcal{M}_{i}$ and its current state $s_{i}^{\prime}$. The single initial state space of ExtConComp is the empty sequence () . Both query set and answer set of ExtConComp are the universal message set $\mathcal{U}$ in Remark 3.4.

To define DP for the extended concurrent composition, we must impose constraints on the created mechanisms and their query pairs to limit the adversary's power. We force a set of constraints using a verifier $\mathcal{V}[f]$, where $f$ is a verification function returning $\perp$ whenever the adversary misbehaves. We define variants of the concurrent composition of CMs by choosing different verification functions $f$ :

Definition 4.2. For any verification function $f$, the $f$-concurrent composition of CMs is the interactive mechanism $\mathcal{V}[f] \circ^{*} \mathcal{I} \circ^{*}$ ExtConComp.

Differential privacy for the $f$-concurrent composition of CMs follows the standard definition for IMs:

Definition 4.3 (DP for $f$-Concurrent Composition of CMs). For a verification function $f$ and privacy parameter $\epsilon \geq 0$ and $0 \leq \delta \leq 1$, the $f$-concurrent composition of CMs is $(\epsilon, \delta)$-DP against adaptive adversaries if the interactive mechanism $\mathcal{V}[f] \circ^{*} \mathcal{I} \circ^{*}$ ExtConComp is $(\epsilon, \delta)$-DP w.r.t. $\sim_{01}$. Equivalently, this holds if the continual mechanism ExtConComp is $(\epsilon, \delta)$-DP w.r.t. $f$ against adaptive adversaries.

Although verification functions $f$ for ExtConComp vary for different compositions, they must all ensure that the format of the adversary's messages is compatible with $\mathcal{I} \circ^{*}$ ExtConComp. An adversary is expected to either create a new CM or send a pair of queries to an existing one. The creation of a new mechanism is independent of the initial state of $\mathcal{I}$. Thus, when requesting the creation of a new mechanism, the adversary must send a pair of identical creation queries to $\mathcal{V}[f]$. Moreover, due to the definition of $\mathcal{I}$ and ExtConComp, to request asking one of the queries $q_{0}$ and $q_{1}$ from the $i$-th created mechanism according to $\mathcal{I}$ 's initial state, the adversary must send the message $\left(\left(q_{0}, i\right),\left(q_{1}, i\right)\right)$ to $\mathcal{V}[f]$.

Next, we formalize these shared constraints by defining suitable message sequences. Later, when defining specific verification functions $f$ for different concurrent compositions, we set $f\left(m_{1}, \ldots, m_{k}\right)=$ $\perp$ whenever the sequence of messages $m_{1}, \ldots, m_{k}$ is not suitable.
Definition 4.4 (Suitable Sequence of Messages). A sequence of messages $m_{1}, \ldots, m_{k}$ is suitable if for every $1 \leq j \leq k$, (i) $m_{j}$ is of the form $\left(m_{j}^{0}, m_{j}^{1}\right)$, where $m_{j}^{0}$ and $m_{j}^{1}$ are either identical creation queries or messages of the forms $\left(q_{0}, \ell\right)$ and $\left(q_{1}, \ell\right)$ with the same index $\ell$; (ii) for each $b \in\{0,1\}$, if $m_{j}^{b}=(q, \ell)$, then there are at least $\ell$ creation queries in the sequence $m_{1}^{b}, \ldots, m_{j-1}^{b}$; (iii) for each $b \in\{0,1\}$, if $m_{j}^{b}=(q, \ell)$ and $\mathcal{M}_{\ell}$ is the $\ell$-th mechanism requested to be created in $m_{1}^{b}, \ldots, m_{j-1}^{b}$, then $q$ is in the query space of $\mathcal{M}_{\ell}$, i.e., $q \in Q_{\mathcal{M}_{\ell}}$; and (iv) if $m_{j}^{0}=m_{j}^{1}=(\mathcal{M}, s, \epsilon, \delta, f)$, then $\mathcal{M}$ is a CM with a single initial state $s$, and it is $(\epsilon, \delta)$-DP w.r.t. $f$.
4.2. $(\epsilon, \delta)$-DP IMs and $\mathrm{RR}_{\epsilon, \delta}$. Lyu [18] shows that for every $(\epsilon, \delta)$-DP IM $\mathcal{M}$ and every pair of neighboring initial states $s_{0}$ and $s_{1}$, there exists an IPM $\mathcal{T}$ (with a single initial state) such that for each $b \in\{0,1\}$, the mechanisms $\mathcal{T} \circ^{*} \mathrm{RR}_{\epsilon, \delta}(b)$ and $\mathcal{M}\left(s_{b}\right)$ are identical. Vadhan and Wang [20] show the same result in the special case where $\delta=0$.

Although not explicitly stated, the constructions of $\mathcal{T}$ proposed in both [18] and [20] require the answer distributions of $\mathcal{M}\left(s_{0}\right)$ and $\mathcal{M}\left(s_{1}\right)$ to be discrete. This assumption is formally defined as:
Definition 4.5. An IM $\mathcal{M}$ has discrete answer distributions if $A_{\mathcal{M}}$ is countable, and for every initial state $s$, integer $t \in \mathbb{N}$, history $\left(q_{1}, a_{1}, \ldots, q_{t-1}, a_{t-1}\right) \in\left(Q_{\mathcal{M}} \times A_{\mathcal{M}}\right)^{t-1}$, and new query $q_{t} \in Q_{\mathcal{M}}$, the distribution of $\mathcal{M}(s)$ 's answer in respond to $q_{t}$ conditioned on having the history $\left(q_{1}, \ldots, a_{t-1}\right)$ has a probability mass function (PMF).

This is generally not a restrictive assumption in differential privacy. In practice, the binary nature of computers and the fact that the total number of memory bits in the world is finite ensure that every distribution sampled computationally is inherently discrete. Theoretically, when dealing with real-valued outputs, one can enforce discrete answer distributions by rounding each output to the nearest multiple of a sufficiently small constant $\alpha$. This discretization post-processing preserves the privacy of the mechanism and has a negligible effect on the accuracy. An example of this approach will be provided in Section 7.

Lyu [18] additionally assumes that there exists a pre-fixed upper bound $c$ on the number of queries $\mathcal{M}$ answers. In Appendix A, we will modify their proof to remove this additional assumption. Let $\mathcal{M}^{\prime}$ be a continual mechanism that is $(\epsilon, \delta)$-DP w.r.t. a verification function $f$. By Corollary 3.8, $\mathcal{V}[f] \circ^{*} \mathcal{I} \circ^{*} \mathcal{M}^{\prime}$ is an IM that is $(\epsilon, \delta)$-DP w.r.t. $\sim_{01}$. Replacing $\mathcal{M}$ in Lemma A. 1 with $\mathcal{V}[f] \circ^{*} \mathcal{I} \circ^{*} \mathcal{M}^{\prime}$, we get:

Lemma 4.6 ([18]). For $\epsilon>0$ and $0 \leq \delta \leq 1$, let $\mathcal{M}$ be a CM that is $(\epsilon, \delta)$-DP w.r.t. a verification function $f$. Suppose $\mathcal{V}[f] \circ^{*} \mathcal{I} \circ^{*} \mathcal{M}$ has discrete answer distributions and responds to at most $c$ queries. Then, there exists an IPM $\mathcal{T}$ with a single initial state () such that for each $b \in\{0,1\}$, the IMs $\mathcal{T} \circ^{*} \mathrm{RR}_{\epsilon, \delta}(b)$ and $\mathcal{V}[f] \circ^{*} \mathcal{I}(b) \circ^{*} \mathcal{M}$ are equivalent.

Let $\mathcal{M}$ be an IM that is $\epsilon$-DP w.r.t. a neighbor relation $\sim$. For every pair of neighboring initial states $s_{0}$ and $s_{1}$, Vadhan and Wang [20] construct an IPM $\mathcal{T}$ (with a single initial state) such that for each bit $b \in\{0,1\}$, the mechanisms $\mathcal{T} \circ^{*} \mathrm{RR}_{\epsilon, 0}(b)$ and $\mathcal{M}\left(s_{b}\right)$ are identical. Appendix B, we will review their construction and show that for any query sequence $q_{1}, \ldots, q_{t}$, if the distributions of the $t$ answers of $\mathcal{M}\left(s_{0}\right)$ and $\mathcal{M}\left(s_{1}\right)$ to the queries $q_{1}, \ldots, q_{t}$ are identical, then $\mathcal{T}$ does not need to know the output of $\mathrm{RR}_{\epsilon, 0}(b)$ in the first $t$ steps. This observation allows us to delay the interaction of $\mathcal{T}$ and $\operatorname{RR}_{\epsilon, 0}(b)$ as much as possible.

Let $\mathcal{M}=\mathcal{V}[f] \circ^{*} \mathcal{I} \circ^{*} \mathcal{M}^{\prime}$, where $\mathcal{M}^{\prime}$ is an $\epsilon$-DP CM w.r.t. $f$. By definition, upon receiving a query sequence $q_{1}, \ldots, q_{t}$ where each $q_{j}=\left(q_{j}^{\prime}, q_{j}^{\prime}\right)$ is a pair of identical queries, $\mathcal{V}[f] \circ^{*} \mathcal{I}(0) \circ^{*} \mathcal{M}^{\prime}$ and $\mathcal{V}[f] \circ^{*} \mathcal{I}(1) \circ^{*} \mathcal{M}^{\prime}$ have the same answer distribution, implying the following lemma:

Lemma 4.7 ([20]). For $\epsilon \geq 0$, let $\mathcal{M}$ be a CM that is $\epsilon$-DP w.r.t. a verification function $f$. Suppose $\mathcal{V}[f] \circ^{*} \mathcal{I} \circ^{*} \mathcal{M}$ has discrete answer distributions. Then, there exists an IPM $\mathcal{T}$ with a single initial state () such that for each $b \in\{0,1\}$,

- the IMs $\mathcal{T} \circ^{*} \mathrm{RR}_{\epsilon, 0}(b)$ and $\mathcal{V}[f] \circ^{*} \mathcal{I}(b) \circ^{*} \mathcal{M}$ are equivalent, and
- as long as $\mathcal{T}$ receives pairs of identical queries, it does not interact with $\mathrm{RR}_{\epsilon, 0}(b)$.

Remark 4.8. Since $\mathrm{RR}_{\epsilon, \delta}$ is a NIM, in both Lemma 4.6 and Lemma 4.7, the IPM $\mathcal{T}$ interacts with $\mathrm{RR}_{\epsilon, \delta}$ at most once.
4.3. Concurrent Composition of CMs $\mathcal{M}_{1}, \ldots, \mathcal{M}_{k}$. For $1 \leq i \leq k$, let $\mathcal{M}_{i}$ be a CM with the initial state space $S_{i}=\left\{s_{i}\right\}$ such that $\mathcal{M}_{i}$ is $\left(\epsilon_{i}, \delta_{i}\right)$-DP w.r.t. a verification function $f_{i}$, and $\mathcal{V}\left[f_{i}\right] \circ^{*} \mathcal{I} \circ^{*} \mathcal{M}_{i}$ has discrete answer distributions. In the concurrent composition of $\mathcal{M}_{1}, \ldots, \mathcal{M}_{k}$, an adversary is restricted to the following steps: (1) It first creates the fixed mechanisms $\mathcal{M}_{1}, \ldots, \mathcal{M}_{k}$ and (2) then adaptively issues pairs of queries for them such that the sequences of query pairs for each $\mathcal{M}_{i}$ is $f_{i}$-valid. Note that creating the $\mathrm{CM} \mathcal{M}_{i}$ means creating an instance of $\mathcal{M}_{i}\left(s_{i}\right)$, where $s_{i}$ is the unique initial state of $\mathcal{M}_{i}$. Based on a secret bit $b \in\{0,1\}$, each CM either receives the first element of every query pair addressed to it or the second element, and the adversary tries to guess $b$ using the answers of all $k$ mechanisms.

To formalize this type of concurrent composition of CMs, we introduce the verification function $f^{\alpha_{1}, \ldots, \alpha_{k}}$. Intuitively, this verification function enforces that the adversary creates the mechanisms $\mathcal{M}_{1}, \ldots, \mathcal{M}_{k}$ in their first $k$ messages and then only sends messages containing pairs of queries for $\mathcal{M}_{i}$ s. Additionally, it ensures that the sequence of query pairs for each $\mathcal{M}_{i}$ is $f_{i}$-valid. The formal definition of $f^{\alpha_{1}, \ldots, \alpha_{k}}$ is as follows:

Definition 4.9 $\left(f^{\alpha_{1}, \ldots, \alpha_{k}}\right)$. For $i \in[k]$, let $\alpha_{i}=\left(\mathcal{M}_{i}, s_{i}, \epsilon_{i}, \delta_{i}, f_{i}\right)$ denote a creation query. For any input sequence of messages $m_{1}, \ldots, m_{t}$, the outcome of $f^{\alpha_{1}, \ldots, \alpha_{k}}$ returns $\top$ if and only if all of the following conditions hold:
(i) The sequence $m_{1}, \ldots, m_{k}$ is suitable. For $j \in[t]$, let $m_{j}=\left(m_{j}^{0}, m_{j}^{1}\right)$.
(ii) For $j \leq \min \{t, k\}$, the messages $m_{j}^{0}=m_{j}^{1}=\alpha_{j}$.
(iii) For $i \in[k]$, the sequence of $\left(q^{0}, q^{1}\right)$ s in the messages of the form $\left(\left(q^{0}, i\right),\left(q^{1}, i\right)\right)$ is $f_{i}$-valid.

With the above definition of $f^{\alpha_{1}, \ldots, \alpha_{k}}$, we refer to the $f^{\alpha_{1}, \ldots, \alpha_{k}}$-concurrent composition of CMs as the concurrent composition of the continual mechanisms $\mathcal{M}_{1}, \ldots, \mathcal{M}_{k}$. Therefore, the concurrent composition of $\mathcal{M}_{1}, \ldots, \mathcal{M}_{k}$ is $(\epsilon, \delta)$-DP against adaptive adversaries if ExtConComp is $(\epsilon, \delta)$-DP w.r.t. $f^{\alpha_{1}, \ldots, \alpha_{k}}$ against adaptive adversaries.

Recall that in Section 3, we generalized the notion of neighboring relations for interactive mechanisms to verification functions for continual mechanisms. The neighboring initial states for an interactive mechanism are chosen non-adaptively at initialization. However, the choice of messages forming a valid sequence w.r.t. a verification function is adaptive and happens over time. That is, an adversary generates two different query sequences for a CM, and the choice of differing sequences is made adaptively throughout the interaction.

In the concurrent composition of IMs, queries to each mechanism are chosen adaptively, not only based on that mechanism's previous responses but also using the responses of the other mechanisms up to that point. By definition, the choice of neighboring initial states for the interactive mechanisms is non-adaptive. However, in the concurrent composition of CMs, the choice of differences between query sequences, i.e., the neighboring query sequences is adaptive, based on not only the responses of the corresponding mechanism but also the responses of other mechanisms. (Note that, unlike IMs, CMs inherently have a single fixed initial state; hence, no choice of initial state is involved.) Despite this additional adaptivity, in the following theorem, we show that the privacy results of [18] for $\operatorname{ConComp}\left[\mathcal{M}_{1}, \ldots, \mathcal{M}_{k}\right]$ also hold for $\mathcal{V}\left[f^{\alpha_{1}, \ldots, \alpha_{k}}\right] \circ^{*} \mathcal{I} \circ^{*}$ ExtConComp.

Theorem 4.10. For $1 \leq i \leq k$, let $\mathcal{M}_{i}$ be a continual mechanism with initial state space $S_{\mathcal{M}_{i}}^{\text {init }}=\left\{s_{i}\right\}$ such that $\mathcal{M}_{i}$ is $\left(\epsilon_{i}, \delta_{i}\right)$-DP w.r.t. a verification function $f_{i}$ against adaptive adversaries, and $\mathcal{V}\left[f_{i}\right] \circ^{*} \mathcal{I} \circ^{*} \mathcal{M}_{i}$ has discrete answer distributions. For $\epsilon>0$ and $0 \leq \delta \leq 1$, if the composition of non-interactive mechanisms $\mathrm{RR}_{\epsilon_{1}, \delta_{1}}, \ldots, \mathrm{RR}_{\epsilon_{k}, \delta_{k}}$ is $(\epsilon, \delta)$-DP, then the concurrent composition of $\mathcal{M}_{1}, \ldots, \mathcal{M}_{k}$ is also $(\epsilon, \delta)$-DP against adaptive adversaries.

Proof. Let $\alpha_{i}=\left(\mathcal{M}_{i}, s_{i}, \epsilon_{i}, \delta_{i}, f_{i}\right)$ for each $i \in[k]$, and let $f$ denote $f^{\alpha_{1}, \ldots, \alpha_{k}}$ for simplicity. Our goal is to show that ExtConComp is $(\epsilon, \delta)$-DP w.r.t. $f$. To prove so, we construct an IPM $\mathcal{P}$ with a single initial state and show that for each $b \in\{0,1\}$, the mechanisms $\mathcal{V}[f] \circ^{*} \mathcal{I}(b) \circ^{*}$ ExtConComp and $\mathcal{V}[f] \circ^{*} \mathcal{P} \circ^{*} \operatorname{Comp}\left[\mathrm{RR}_{\epsilon_{1}, \delta_{1}}, \ldots, \mathrm{RR}_{\epsilon_{k}, \delta_{k}}\right]((b)_{\epsilon=1}^{k})$ are equivalent.

Since $\mathcal{V}[f] \circ^{*} \mathcal{P}$ is an IPM with a single initial state, Lemma 2.15 implies that if $\operatorname{Comp}\left[\mathrm{RR}_{\epsilon_{1}, \delta_{1}}, \ldots, \mathrm{RR}_{\epsilon_{k}, \delta_{k}}\right]$ is $(\epsilon, \delta)$-DP, then $\mathcal{V}[f] \circ^{*} \mathcal{P} \circ^{*} \operatorname{Comp}\left[\mathrm{RR}_{\epsilon_{1}, \delta_{1}}, \ldots, \mathrm{RR}_{\epsilon_{k}, \delta_{k}}\right]$ is also $(\epsilon, \delta)$ DP. Hence, for any adversary $\mathcal{A}$, the views of $\mathcal{A}$ when interacting with the mechanisms $\mathcal{V}[f] \circ^{*} \mathcal{P} \circ^{*} \operatorname{Comp}\left[\mathrm{RR}_{\epsilon_{1}, \delta_{1}}, \ldots, \mathrm{RR}_{\epsilon_{k}, \delta_{k}}\right]((0)_{\epsilon=1}^{k})$ and $\mathcal{V}[f] \circ^{*} \mathcal{P} \circ^{*} \operatorname{Comp}\left[\mathrm{RR}_{\epsilon_{1}, \delta_{1}}, \ldots, \mathrm{RR}_{\epsilon_{k}, \delta_{k}}\right]((1)_{\epsilon=1}^{k})$ are $(\epsilon, \delta)$-indistinguishable. As we will show below, by construction, these views are identical to those obtained by interacting with the original mechanisms $\mathcal{V}[f] \circ^{*} \mathcal{I}(b) \circ^{*}$ ExtConComp, implying that the concurrent composition of $\mathcal{M}_{1}, \ldots, \mathcal{M}_{k}$ is $(\epsilon, \delta)$-DP.

In $\mathcal{V}[f] \circ^{*} \mathcal{I}(b) \circ^{*}$ ExtConComp, when $\mathcal{I}(b)$ receives pairs of identical creation queries from $\mathcal{V}[f]$, it forwards one of them to ExtConComp, which then creates an instance of $\mathcal{M}_{i}$ and returns $\top$. Subsequently, when $\mathcal{I}(b)$ receives two queries for $\mathcal{M}_{i}$, it forwards them to $\mathcal{M}_{i}$ through ExtConComp and returns its response. This procedure can be equivalently represented by an IM $\operatorname{IECC}(b)$ as follows: when receiving pairs of identical creation queries from $\mathcal{V}[f], \operatorname{IECC}(b)$ creates an instance of $\mathcal{V}\left[f_{i}\right] \circ^{*} \mathcal{I}(b) \circ^{*} \mathcal{M}_{i}$ and returns $\top$. Subsequently, when receiving $\left(\left(q_{0}, i\right),\left(q_{1}, i\right)\right)$, it forwards $\left(q_{0}, q_{1}\right)$ to $\mathcal{V}\left[f_{i}\right] \circ^{*} \mathcal{I}(b) \circ^{*} \mathcal{M}_{i}$ and returns its response. By definition of $f$ and $\mathcal{I}$, the mechanisms

$\mathcal{V}[f] \circ^{*} \mathcal{I}(b) \circ^{*}$ ExtConComp and $\mathcal{V}[f] \circ^{*} \operatorname{IECC}(b)$ are equivalent. Next, we define $\mathcal{P}$ explicitly and show $\mathcal{V}[f] \circ^{*} \operatorname{IECC}(b)$ and $\mathcal{V}[f] \circ^{*} \mathcal{P} \circ^{*}$ Comp $\left[\mathrm{RR}_{\epsilon_{1}, \delta_{1}}, \ldots, \mathrm{RR}_{\epsilon_{k}, \delta_{k}}\right]((b)_{\epsilon=1}^{k})$ are equivalent.

Let $\mathcal{T}_{i}$ be the IPM for $\mathcal{M}_{i}$ given by Lemma 4.6, and let $t_{i}$ be its single initial state. The initial state of $\mathcal{P}$ is a pair of empty sequences. Let $\left(\sigma_{1}, \sigma_{2}\right)$ denote the state of $\mathcal{P}$. When receiving the first left message, $\mathcal{P}$ interacts with its right mechanism, Comp $\left[\mathrm{RR}_{\epsilon_{1}, \delta_{1}}, \ldots, \mathrm{RR}_{\epsilon_{k}, \delta_{k}}\right]((b)_{\epsilon=1}^{k})$, and sets $\sigma_{1}$ to its output sequence $\left(r_{1}, \ldots, r_{k}\right) . \mathcal{P}$ never interacts with its right mechanism again.

Upon receiving a left message $\left(\mathcal{M}_{i}, s_{i}, \epsilon_{i}, \delta_{i}, f_{i}\right)^{2}, \mathcal{P}$ adds $\left(\mathcal{T}_{i}, t_{i}\right)$ to $\sigma_{2}$ and returns $\top$. Moreover, upon receiving a left message $\left(\left(q_{0}, i\right),\left(q_{1}, i\right)\right), \mathcal{P}$ sends $\left(q_{0}, q_{1}\right)$ as a left message to $\mathcal{T}_{i}$ and returns its response. If $\mathcal{T}_{i}$ requests a sample from $\mathrm{RR}_{\epsilon_{i}, \delta_{i}}, \mathcal{P}$ provides it with the previously stored sample $r_{i}$. Formally, $\mathcal{P}$ executes $\left(t_{i}, v, m\right) \leftarrow \mathcal{T}_{i}\left(t_{i}, \mathrm{~L},\left(q_{0}, q_{1}\right)\right)$ and as long as $v=\mathrm{R}$, it runs $\left(t_{i}, v, m\right) \leftarrow \mathcal{T}_{i}\left(t_{i}, v, r_{i}\right)$. Once $v=\mathrm{L}, \mathcal{P}$ returns the message $m$ to $\mathcal{V}[f]$. (By Remark 4.8, $v=\mathrm{R}$ at most once.) By Lemma 4.6, each $\mathcal{T}_{i}$, provided with the sample $r_{i}$ from $\mathrm{RR}_{\epsilon_{i}, \delta_{i}}$, simulates $\mathcal{V}\left[f_{i}\right] \circ^{*} \mathcal{I}(b) \circ^{*} \mathcal{M}_{i}$ identically. Hence, by definition of IECC and $\mathcal{P}$, the mechanisms $\operatorname{IECC}(b)$ and $\mathcal{P} \circ^{*} \operatorname{Comp}\left[\mathrm{RR}_{\epsilon_{1}, \delta_{1}}, \ldots, \mathrm{RR}_{\epsilon_{k}, \delta_{k}}\right]((b)_{\epsilon=1}^{k})$ are equivalent, finishing the proof.
4.4. Concurrent Composition of CMs with Fixed Parameters. The concurrent composition of CMs with fixed parameters generalizes the concurrent composition of fixed CMs by allowing the adversary to select the CMs $\mathcal{M}_{1}, \ldots, \mathcal{M}_{k}$ adaptively over time, instead of forcing them to create a fixed set of mechanisms in their first $k$ messages. Each selected mechanism $\mathcal{M}_{i}$ must be $\left(\epsilon_{i}, \delta_{i}\right)$-DP w.r.t. a verification function $f_{i}$, where the multiset of privacy parameters $\left(\epsilon_{1}, \delta_{1}\right), \ldots,\left(\epsilon_{k}, \delta_{k}\right)$ is fixed in advance, but the verification functions $f_{i}$ are chosen by the adversary. Note that this implies that at most $k$ continual mechanism are created by the adversary. Moreover, due to the aforementioned technical reasons, each $\mathcal{V}\left[f_{i}\right] \circ^{*} \mathcal{I} \circ^{*} \mathcal{M}_{i}$ must have discrete answer distributions.

For instance, an adversary may first create a continual mechanism $\mathcal{M}_{3}$ that is $\left(\epsilon_{3}, \delta_{3}\right)$-DP w.r.t. a verification function $f_{3}$. Then, after interacting with $\mathcal{M}_{3}$ for some time and analyzing its responses, the adversary may then select a mechanism $\mathcal{M}_{1}$ from the class of $\left(\epsilon_{1}, \delta_{1}\right)$-DP CMs. Similar to the concurrent composition of fixed CMs, the adversary's sequence of query pairs for each $\mathcal{M}_{i}$ must be $f_{i}$-valid.

To formally define this composition, we introduce a verification function, $f^{\epsilon_{1}, \delta_{1}, \ldots, \epsilon_{k}, \delta_{k}}$ as follows:
Definition 4.11 $\left(f^{\epsilon_{1}, \delta_{1}, \ldots, \epsilon_{k}, \delta_{k}}\right)$. For any input sequence of messages $m_{1}, \ldots, m_{t}$, the function $f^{\epsilon_{1}, \delta_{1}, \ldots, \epsilon_{k}, \delta_{k}}$ returns $\top$ if and only if all of the following conditions hold:
(i) The sequence $m_{1}, \ldots, m_{t}$ is suitable.
(ii) There are at most $k$ pairs of identical creation queries in the sequence $m_{1}, \ldots, m_{t}$. Let $\mathcal{M}_{i}^{\prime}$ denote the $i$-th created mechanism and $\left(\epsilon_{i}^{\prime}, \delta_{i}^{\prime}\right)$ and $f_{i}^{\prime}$ be its privacy parameters and verification function, respectively. $\mathcal{V}\left[f_{i}^{\prime}\right] \circ^{*} \mathcal{I} \circ^{*} \mathcal{M}_{i}^{\prime}$ has discrete answer distributions. Moreover, the multiset of the privacy parameters $\left(\epsilon_{i}^{\prime}, \delta_{i}^{\prime}\right)$ of the created mechanisms is a sub-multiset of the fixed privacy parameters $\left(\epsilon_{1}, \delta_{1}\right), \ldots,\left(\epsilon_{k}, \delta_{k}\right)$. Note that $\left(\epsilon_{i}^{\prime}, \delta_{i}^{\prime}\right)$ is adaptively chosen by the adversary, while $\left(\epsilon_{i}, \delta_{i}\right)$ is a predetermined publicly-known parameter.
(iii) For each $i \in[k]$, the sequence of $\left(q^{0}, q^{1}\right)$ s in the messages of the form $\left(\left(q^{0}, i\right),\left(q^{1}, i\right)\right)$ is $f_{i}^{\prime}$-valid.

We refer to the $f^{\epsilon_{1}, \delta_{1}, \ldots, \epsilon_{k}, \delta_{k}}$-concurrent composition of CMs as the concurrent composition of CMs with privacy parameters $\left(\left(\epsilon_{i}, \delta_{i}\right)\right)_{i=1}^{k}$. A slight adaptation of the proof of Theorem 4.10 implies the following theorem.

Theorem 4.12. For $\epsilon, \epsilon_{1}, \ldots, \epsilon_{k}>0$ and $0 \leq \delta, \delta_{1}, \ldots, \delta_{k} \leq 1$, if the composition of non-interactive mechanisms $\mathrm{RR}_{\epsilon_{1}, \delta_{1}}, \ldots, \mathrm{RR}_{\epsilon_{k}, \delta_{k}}$ is $(\epsilon, \delta)$-DP, then the concurrent composition of $k$ CMs with the privacy parameters $\left(\left(\epsilon_{i}, \delta_{i}\right)\right)_{i=1}^{k}$ is also $(\epsilon, \delta)$-DP against adaptive adversaries.

Proof. The proof is identical to the proof of Theorem 4.10 with the following modification in the construction of $\mathcal{P}$ : Recall that $\left(r_{1}, \ldots, r_{k}\right)$ denotes the output of $\operatorname{Comp}\left[\mathrm{RR}_{\epsilon_{1}, \delta_{1}}, \ldots, \mathrm{RR}_{\epsilon_{k}, \delta_{k}}\right]$. In the proof of Theorem 4.10, the $i$-th creation query was known to be $\left(\mathcal{M}_{i}, s_{i}, \epsilon_{i}, \delta_{i}, f_{i}\right)$. Consequently, $\mathcal{T}_{i}$

expected $\mathrm{RR}_{\epsilon_{i}, \delta_{i}}$ as its right mechanism, and when $\mathcal{T}_{i}$ needed a response from its right mechanism, $\mathcal{P}$ sent $r_{i}$ to it. However, in the concurrent composition with fixed parameters, the IPM requesting the sample from $\mathrm{RR}_{\epsilon_{i}, \delta_{i}}$ need not necessarily be $\mathcal{T}_{i}$. To handle this, we modify $\mathcal{P}$ so that it maps each output sample $r_{i}$ to the appropriate IPM $\mathcal{T}_{j}$ needing a sample from $\mathrm{RR}_{\epsilon_{i}, \delta_{i}}$.

Let $\left(\mathcal{M}_{j}^{\prime}, s_{j}^{\prime}, \epsilon_{j}^{\prime}, \delta_{j}^{\prime}, f_{j}^{\prime}\right)^{2}$ denote the $j$-th pair of identical creation queries received by $\mathcal{P}$ from the verifier, and let $\mathcal{T}_{j}$ be the corresponding IPM given by Lemma 4.6. When $\mathcal{T}_{j}$ requests a sample from $\mathrm{RR}_{\epsilon_{j}^{\prime}, \delta_{j}^{\prime}}, \mathcal{P}$ iterates over $\sigma_{1}$ to find the smallest $i^{*} \in[k]$ such that the $i^{*}$-th element of $\sigma_{1}$ is not null and $\epsilon_{j}^{\prime}=\epsilon_{i^{*}}, \delta_{j}^{\prime}=\delta_{i^{*}}$. After sending $r_{i^{*}}$ to $\mathcal{T}_{j}, \mathcal{P}$ updates $\sigma_{1}$ and sets $r_{i}$ to null. This adjustment ensures that even when there are duplicate privacy parameters among $\left(\epsilon_{1}, \delta_{1}\right), \ldots,\left(\epsilon_{k}, \delta_{k}\right)$, each sample $r_{i}$ is sent to at most one $\mathcal{T}_{j}$. Note that by the definition of $f^{\epsilon_{1}, \delta_{1}, \ldots, \epsilon_{k}, \delta_{k}}, i^{*}$ always exists.

query: What are phase transitions in the context of signal detection and recovery using kernel PCA?
golden_answer: Phase transitions refer to changes in behavior regarding signal detection and recovery when using kernel PCA. Specifically, there exists a signal strength threshold above which kernel PCA becomes informative for detecting signals and recovering their support consistently. Below this threshold, kernel principal components become asymptotically orthogonal to the signal, making detection ineffective.
source_title: Sparse PCA: Phase Transitions in the Critical Regime
source_text:
#### Abstract

This work studies sparse principal component analysis (PCA) in high dimensions. Given $n$ independent $p$-dimensional Gaussian samples with covariance $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}:=(\lambda-1) \boldsymbol{v} \boldsymbol{v}^{\top}+\mathbf{I}_{p}$, our goal is to estimate $\boldsymbol{v}$ under the assumption of sparsity. On the one hand, if the sparsity level $m:=\|\boldsymbol{v}\|_{0}$ satisfies $m \lesssim \sqrt{n}$, algorithms such as covariance thresholding (Krauthgamer et al., 2015) consistently outperform PCA. On the other hand, if $m \gg \sqrt{n}$, it is conjectured that no polynomial-time algorithm can recover $\boldsymbol{v}$ below the detection threshold of PCA. We investigate the "critical" high-dimensional regime, where $n, p, m \rightarrow \infty$ with $m / \sqrt{n} \rightarrow \beta$ and $p / n \rightarrow \gamma$, and study estimators based on kernel PCA, generalizing covariance thresholding.

Within this framework, we achieve a fine-grained understanding of signal detection and recovery. Our main result establishes a detection phase transition, analogous to the Baik-Ben Arous-Péché (BBP) transition for PCA: above a signal strength threshold-depending on the kernel function, $\gamma$, and $\beta$-kernel PCA is informative. Conversely, below the threshold, kernel principal components are asymptotically orthogonal to the signal. Notably, (1) above this threshold, consistent support recovery is possible with high probability, (2) for all $\beta \in(0, \infty)$, kernel PCA strictly outperforms PCA, and (3) as $\beta \rightarrow \infty$, kernel PCA and PCA coincide. We identify optimal kernel functions for detection and support recovery, and numerical calculations suggest that soft thresholding is nearly optimal. Our key technical contribution is approximation guarantees for deterministic equivalents of kernel random matrices, which enable sharp estimates of coordinate fluctuations of kernel principal components.

query: How are new density and voltage variables defined for stretched domains?
golden_answer: New density and voltage variables are defined as $\mathcal{C}_{i}(\boldsymbol{\xi})=\tilde{c}_{i}(\boldsymbol{\xi} / \alpha)$ and $\mathcal{V}(\boldsymbol{\xi})=\tilde{v}(\boldsymbol{\xi} / \alpha)$.
source_title:
Voltage laws in nanodomains revealed by asymptotics and simulations of
  electro-diffusion equations
source_text:
# 3.2 Non-dimensionalization 

We show here how we use the dimensional spatial $\tilde{\boldsymbol{x}}$ and time $\tilde{t}$ variables:

$$
\tilde{\boldsymbol{x}}=\frac{\boldsymbol{x}}{R} \in \tilde{\Omega}, \quad \tilde{t}=\frac{D_{1}}{R^{2}} t
$$

where $D_{1}$ is the diffusion coefficient of the first ionic species, while $\tilde{\Omega}=\Omega / R$ is the rescaled domain. The weighted sum $\sum_{k=1}^{n} z_{k}^{2} C_{k}$ measures the conductivity of the electrolyte. By using this term and the thermal voltage $k_{B} \mathcal{T} / e$ we can define new density and voltage variables given by

$$
\tilde{c}_{i}(\tilde{\boldsymbol{x}}, \tilde{t})=\frac{c_{i}\left(R \tilde{\boldsymbol{x}}, \frac{R^{2}}{D_{1}} \tilde{t}\right)}{\sum_{k=1}^{n} z_{k}^{2} C_{k}}, \quad i=1, \ldots, n, \quad \tilde{v}(\tilde{\boldsymbol{x}}, \tilde{t})=\frac{e}{k_{B} \mathcal{T}} v\left(R \tilde{\boldsymbol{x}}, \frac{R^{2}}{D_{1}} \tilde{t}\right)
$$

as well as dimensionless electro-chemical gradients,

$$
\tilde{j}_{i}(\tilde{\boldsymbol{x}}, \tilde{t})=\frac{R j_{i}\left(R \tilde{\boldsymbol{x}}, \frac{R^{2}}{D_{1}} \tilde{t}\right)}{D_{i} \sum_{k=1}^{n} z_{k}^{2} C_{k}}=-\left(\nabla c_{i}(\tilde{\boldsymbol{x}}, \tilde{t})+z_{i} c_{i}(\tilde{\boldsymbol{x}}, \tilde{t}) \nabla \tilde{v}(\tilde{\boldsymbol{x}}, \tilde{t})\right), \quad i=1, \ldots, n
$$

Then, upon substituting within the PNP Eq. (3.2)-(3.4), we obtain

$$
\begin{gathered}
\tau_{i} \frac{\partial \tilde{c}_{i}(\tilde{\boldsymbol{x}}, \tilde{t})}{\partial t}+\nabla \cdot \tilde{j}_{i}(\tilde{\boldsymbol{x}}, \tilde{t})=0, \quad i=1, \ldots, n, \quad \tilde{\boldsymbol{x}} \in \tilde{\Omega} \\
\Delta \tilde{v}(\tilde{\boldsymbol{x}}, \tilde{t})+\alpha^{2} \sum_{i=1}^{n} z_{i} \tilde{c}_{i}(\tilde{\boldsymbol{x}}, \tilde{t})=0, \quad \tilde{\boldsymbol{x}} \in \tilde{\Omega}
\end{gathered}
$$

where $\tau_{i}=D_{1} / D_{i}$ is a diffusion coefficients ratio while $\alpha$ is given by

$$
\alpha=\frac{R}{\lambda_{D}}, \quad \text { with } \quad \lambda_{D}=\sqrt{\frac{k_{B} \mathcal{T} \varepsilon \varepsilon_{0}}{e \mathcal{F} \sum_{k=1}^{n} z_{k}^{2} C_{k}}}
$$

and thus it corresponds to the ratio of the domain length-scale $R$ over the Debye length $\lambda_{D}$ measuring electro-static interaction lengths in the absence of external flux. The boundary conditions Eq. (3.4) get reformulated as

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \boldsymbol{n} \cdot \tilde{j}_{1}(\tilde{\boldsymbol{x}}, \tilde{t})+\frac{J}{z_{1}}=0, \quad \boldsymbol{n} \cdot \tilde{c}_{i}(\tilde{\boldsymbol{x}}, \tilde{t})=0, \quad i=2, \ldots, n, \quad \boldsymbol{n} \cdot \tilde{v}(\tilde{\boldsymbol{x}}, \tilde{t})=0, \quad \tilde{\boldsymbol{x}} \in \partial \tilde{\Omega}_{a_{1}} \\
& \tilde{c}_{i}(\tilde{\boldsymbol{x}}, \tilde{t})=\nu_{i}, \quad i=1, \ldots, n, \quad \tilde{v}(\tilde{\boldsymbol{x}}, \tilde{t})=0, \quad \tilde{\boldsymbol{x}} \in \partial \tilde{\Omega}_{a_{2}} \\
& \boldsymbol{n} \cdot \tilde{j}_{i}(\tilde{\boldsymbol{x}}, \tilde{t})=0, \quad i=1, \ldots, n, \quad \boldsymbol{n} \cdot \tilde{v}(\tilde{\boldsymbol{x}}, \tilde{t})=0, \quad \tilde{\boldsymbol{x}} \in \partial \tilde{\Omega}_{r}
\end{aligned}
$$

where $\partial \tilde{\Omega}_{a_{1}}$ and $\partial \tilde{\Omega}_{a_{2}}$ are two small circular windows of radii $a_{1}=A_{1} / R$ and $a_{2}=A_{2} / R$, centered in $\tilde{\boldsymbol{x}}_{1}=\boldsymbol{x}_{1} / R$ and $\tilde{\boldsymbol{x}}_{2}=\boldsymbol{x}_{2} / R$. In Eq. (3.10) the parameter $J$ measures the strength of the influx current entering window $\partial \tilde{\Omega}_{a_{1}}$, while $\nu_{i}$ for each $i$ is proportional to the exit site $\partial \tilde{\Omega}_{a_{2}}$ constant ionic density:

$$
J=\frac{I R}{\mathcal{F} \pi A_{1}^{2} D_{1}\left(\sum_{k=1}^{n} z_{k}^{2} C_{k}\right)}, \quad \nu_{i}=\frac{C_{i}}{\sum_{k=1}^{n} z_{k}^{2} C_{k}}, \quad i=1, \ldots, n
$$

We seek solutions for the ionic densities $\tilde{c}_{i}(\tilde{\boldsymbol{x}})$ and voltage $\tilde{v}(\tilde{\boldsymbol{x}})$ distribution at steady-state, thus satisfying

$$
\begin{gathered}
\nabla \cdot \tilde{j}_{i}(\tilde{\boldsymbol{x}})=\Delta \tilde{c}_{i}(\tilde{\boldsymbol{x}})+z_{i} \nabla \cdot\left(\tilde{c}_{i}(\tilde{\boldsymbol{x}}) \nabla \tilde{v}(\tilde{\boldsymbol{x}})\right)=0, \quad \tilde{\boldsymbol{x}} \in \tilde{\Omega} \\
\Delta \tilde{v}(\tilde{\boldsymbol{x}})+\alpha^{2} \sum_{i=1}^{n} z_{i} \tilde{c}_{i}(\tilde{\boldsymbol{x}})=0, \quad \tilde{\boldsymbol{x}} \in \tilde{\Omega}
\end{gathered}
$$

for two different parameter regimes: first $\alpha \sim O(1)$, and then $\alpha \gg 1$. For the first case the Debye length is of the order of the domain length-scale, while for the latter $\lambda_{D}$ is much smaller than $R$. Lengthscales of neuronal nano-compartments are usually of the order of hundreds of nanometers (with $R=500$ nm for a typical dendritic spine head), while for a 1:1 binary electrolyte with steady-state ionic density $C_{1}=C_{2}=100 \mathrm{mM}$, we calculate $\lambda_{D} \approx 1 \mathrm{~nm}$. Thus in practice $\alpha \gg 1$, but we will show that our analysis can also treat the case $\alpha \sim O(1)$ corresponding to small interior charge densities. The two distinct cases can be handled by introducing the coordinate $\boldsymbol{\xi}=\alpha \tilde{\boldsymbol{x}}$ within the stretched domain $\Omega_{\boldsymbol{\xi}}=\alpha \tilde{\Omega}$, but we remark that this is the same as rescaling $\boldsymbol{x} \in \Omega$ by the Debye length, with $\boldsymbol{\xi}=\boldsymbol{x} / \lambda_{D}$. Upon defining new density and voltage variables as

$$
\mathcal{C}_{i}(\boldsymbol{\xi})=\tilde{c}_{i}(\boldsymbol{\xi} / \alpha), \quad i=1, \ldots, n, \quad \mathcal{V}(\boldsymbol{\xi})=\tilde{v}(\boldsymbol{\xi} / \alpha)
$$

we can reformulate (3.12) as

$$
\begin{gathered}
\Delta \mathcal{C}_{i}(\boldsymbol{\xi})+z_{i} \nabla\left(\mathcal{C}_{i}(\boldsymbol{\xi}) \nabla \mathcal{V}(\boldsymbol{\xi})\right)=0, \quad \boldsymbol{\xi} \in \Omega_{\boldsymbol{\xi}} \\
\Delta \mathcal{V}(\boldsymbol{\xi})+\sum_{i=1}^{n} z_{i} \mathcal{C}_{i}(\boldsymbol{\xi})=0, \quad \boldsymbol{\xi} \in \Omega_{\boldsymbol{\xi}}
\end{gathered}
$$

subject to the boundary conditions

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\partial \mathcal{C}_{1}(\boldsymbol{\xi})}{\partial \boldsymbol{n}}=\frac{J}{\alpha z_{1}}, \quad \frac{\partial \mathcal{C}_{i}(\boldsymbol{\xi})}{\partial \boldsymbol{n}} & =0, \quad i=2, \ldots, n, \quad \frac{\partial \mathcal{V}(\boldsymbol{\xi})}{\partial \boldsymbol{n}}=0, \quad \boldsymbol{\xi} \in \partial \Omega_{\boldsymbol{\xi}_{1}} \\
\mathcal{C}_{i}(\boldsymbol{\xi}) & =\nu_{i}, \quad i=1, \ldots, n, \quad \mathcal{V}(\boldsymbol{\xi})=0, \quad \boldsymbol{\xi} \in \partial \Omega_{\boldsymbol{\xi}_{2}} \\
\frac{\partial \mathcal{C}_{i}(\boldsymbol{\xi})}{\partial \boldsymbol{n}} & =0, \quad i=1, \ldots, n, \quad \frac{\partial \mathcal{V}(\boldsymbol{\xi})}{\partial \boldsymbol{n}}=0, \quad \boldsymbol{\xi} \in \partial \Omega_{\boldsymbol{\xi}_{r}}
\end{aligned}
$$

where $\partial \Omega_{\boldsymbol{\xi}_{j}}$ for $j=1,2$ are two circular boundary disks of radius $\alpha a_{j}$ centered in $\boldsymbol{\xi}_{j}$ on $\partial \Omega_{\boldsymbol{\xi}}$. Note that the ratio $\frac{J}{\alpha}$ is the single parameter controlling the strength of the influx and the electric potential due to ionic density disturbances.

golden_answer: Yes.

Mitigating the Stability-Plasticity Dilemma in Adaptive Train Scheduling
  with Curriculum-Driven Continual DQN Expansion
source_text:
### 5.1 FORMALISATION OF THE CONTINUAL REINFORCEMENT LEARNING PROBLEM

A continual reinforcement learning scenario is characterized by a sequence of $N$ tasks or instances. Each task $k$ is described through a Markov Decision Process (MDP) $M_{k}=\left\langle S_{k}, A_{k}, T_{k}, r_{k}, \gamma\right\rangle$, which encompasses a set of states $S_{k}$, a set of actions $A_{k}$, a transition function $T_{k}: S_{k} \times A_{k} \rightarrow \mathcal{P}\left(S_{k}\right)$, and a reward function $r_{k}: S_{k} \times A_{k} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$. We assume in our case that all tasks share identical state and action spaces.

A global Q-function $Q:[1 . . N] \times \mathcal{Z} \rightarrow(S \times A \rightarrow \mathbb{R})$ is defined. This function accepts a task identifier $k$ and a sequence of tasks $\mathcal{Z}$ as inputs, yielding a Q-value representing the expected future rewards for interacting with the environment of $k^{\text {th }}$ task. The output is a real-valued estimate of the expected return from taking action $A$ in state $S$.

For each new task, we reset the replay buffer. Meaning that upon transitioning to task $k+1$, the transitions from the previous MDP $M_{i}$ are no longer accessible to the agent.

query: Is Dicke superradiant emission transient or steady-state by nature?
golden_answer: Dicke superradiant emission is inherently transient by nature.
source_title: Dicke superradiant enhancement of the heat current in circuit QED
source_text:
## A. Steady-state density matrix and effective temperature

Since we are interested in computing the steady-state heat current flowing across the device, we start discussing the steady-state solution of the Lindblad master equation (9). In the case of a single reservoir, i.e. $\mathcal{D}(\hat{\rho})=\mathcal{D}_{i}(\hat{\rho})$ for $i=\mathrm{h}$ or $i=\mathrm{c}$, the steady-state solution corresponds to the thermal distribution (within each subspace with fixed $J$ ) characterized by the corresponding temperature $T_{i}$, since the rates satisfy the detailed balance condition

$$
\frac{\gamma_{i} n_{i}}{\gamma_{i}\left(1+n_{i}\right)}=\exp \left(-\frac{\hbar \omega_{0}}{k_{\mathrm{B}} T_{i}}\right)
$$

capturing the equilibrium relation between absorption and emission rates in each bath. This result, consistent with the laws of thermodynamics, comes from using a master equation written in terms of the global jump operators for the coupled qubits (see Refs. 73-75 for a discussion of this point). In the case of two baths, the total dissipator in Eq. (10) can be expressed as:

$$
\mathcal{D}(\hat{\rho})=\left[\gamma_{\mathrm{c}}\left(1+n_{\mathrm{c}}\right)+\gamma_{\mathrm{h}}\left(1+n_{\mathrm{h}}\right)\right]\left(\hat{J}_{-} \hat{\rho} \hat{J}_{+}-\frac{1}{2}\left\{\hat{J}_{+} \hat{J}_{-}, \hat{\rho}\right\}\right)+\left[\gamma_{\mathrm{c}} n_{\mathrm{c}}+\gamma_{\mathrm{h}} n_{\mathrm{h}}\right]\left(\hat{J}_{+} \hat{\rho} \hat{J}_{-}-\frac{1}{2}\left\{\hat{J}_{-} \hat{J}_{+}, \hat{\rho}\right\}\right)
$$

For clarity in this discussion, we introduce a temperature $T_{0}$ associated with the qubit frequency $\omega_{0}, T_{0} \equiv$ $\left(\hbar \omega_{0}\right) / k_{\mathrm{B}}$. The dissipator in Eq. (14) defines a detailed
balance equation

$$
\frac{\gamma_{\mathrm{c}} n_{\mathrm{c}}+\gamma_{\mathrm{h}} n_{\mathrm{h}}}{\gamma_{\mathrm{c}}\left(1+n_{\mathrm{c}}\right)+\gamma_{\mathrm{h}}\left(1+n_{\mathrm{h}}\right)}=\exp \left(-\frac{T_{0}}{T^{*}}\right)
$$

which, in turn, defines an effective temperature $T^{*}$, such that $T_{c} \leq T^{*} \leq T_{h}$. We can invert the previous equation to get an explicit expression for the effective temperature

$$
T^{*}=\frac{T_{0}}{\log \left[\frac{\gamma_{\mathrm{c}}\left(1+n_{\mathrm{c}}\right)+\gamma_{\mathrm{h}}\left(1+n_{\mathrm{h}}\right)}{\gamma_{\mathrm{c}} n_{\mathrm{c}}+\gamma_{\mathrm{h}} n_{\mathrm{h}}}\right]}
$$

The steady-state solution $\dot{\rho}^{(s)}$, determined setting $\mathcal{D}\left(\dot{\rho}^{(s)}\right)=0$, is thus a thermal state at temperature $T^{*}$ within each subspace with fixed $J$. However, since $\hat{J}^{2}$ is conserved, the relative occupation of different subspaces is fixed by the initial state. Assuming that the initial state does not contain any coherence between subspaces with different $J$, the stationary state $\dot{\rho}^{(s)}$ is given by

$$
\dot{\rho}^{(s)}=\sum_{J} P_{J} \sum_{m_{J}} P\left(m_{J}|J|\left|J, m_{J}\right\rangle\left\langle J, m_{J}\right|\right.
$$

where $m_{J}$ are the eigenvalues of $\hat{J}_{z}$ compatible with $J, P_{J}$ is the occupation probability of subspace $J$ determined by the initial state, and $\left|J, m_{J}\right\rangle$ are the Dicke states, given in Eq. (8). It should be noted that the summation over $J$ in Eq. (17) incorporates the degeneracies associated with $J$, as customary in angular momentum composition [76]. For example, considering a system composed of three qubits, each characterized by a spin of $\frac{1}{2}$, the resultant collective angular momentum can exhibit values of $J=1 / 2,1 / 2,3 / 2$, with the $J=1 / 2$ appearing twice. This is due to the composition rule that three spin- $\frac{1}{2}$ entities combine to yield collective angular momenta of $\frac{3}{2}$ and two instances of $\frac{1}{2}$. This composition rule is customarily represented as $\frac{1}{2} \otimes \frac{1}{2} \otimes \frac{1}{2}=\frac{3}{2} \oplus \frac{1}{2} \oplus \frac{1}{2}$. The dissipator in Eq. (14) fixes the occupation within each subspace $J$, i.e. it fixes the conditional probabilities $P\left(m_{J} \mid J\right)$ to be thermal at the effective temperature $T^{*}$ :

$$
P\left(m_{J} \mid J\right)=\frac{\exp \left(-\frac{m_{J} T_{0}}{T^{*}}\right)}{Z_{J, T^{*}}}
$$

where $Z_{J, T^{*}}=\sum_{m_{J}} \exp \left[-m_{J} T_{0} / T^{*}\right]$ is the partition function.

query: How do different memory window sizes affect the performance of translation models in terms of quality and consistency?
golden_answer: The performance of translation models is influenced by the size of memory windows. Short-Term Memory window size slightly improves consistency but at a high computational cost, while Long-Term Memory window size changes offer no significant benefits due to effective context capture by the Bilingual Summary component.

DelTA: An Online Document-Level Translation Agent Based on Multi-Level
  Memory
source_text:
## E Detailed Results of the Ablation Study

![table_10](table_10)

Table 11: Effect of the Short-Term and Long-Term window size.

![table_11](table_11)

Table 12: Evaluation results on the $\mathrm{Lt} \Rightarrow$ En low-resource test set.

Effect of Each Memory Component The ablation results for each individual memory component are presented in Table 10. The backbone model used in our experiments is GPT-3.5-Turbo, evaluated on the IWSLT2017 En $\Rightarrow$ Zh test set. We can observe that 1) Short-Term Memory enhances translation quality but negatively impacts consistency due to disruptions caused by the short-span context it introduces (Model 2). 2) Similarly, Long-Term Memory improves translation quality but also leads to a decline in consistency (Model 3). However, these two modules complement each other, as their integration leverages information from different spans, resulting in further quality enhancements while mitigating consistency issues (Model 6). 3) Proper Noun Records contribute to both translation quality and consistency, as improved accuracy in proper noun translation directly enhances overall quality (Model 4). 4) Bilingual Summary also positively impacts translation quality by introducing the document's main idea, which guides the generation of target sentences more effectively (Model 5).

Each module independently contributes to performance improvements. However, none surpass the combination of all modules working together. We also conducted an additional comparative test between DelTA and the context method augmented with Proper Noun Records. The results, presented as Model 7 in Table 10, reveal a large performance gap favoring DelTA. We attribute this to the DelTA architecture's ability to incorporate information across varying granularities and scales, enabling a synergistic enhancement of both translation quality and consistency within our framework.

Effect of Hyper-Parameters We perform experiments to evaluate the impact of different window sizes for Short-Term and Long-Term Memory (i.e. $k$ and $l$ introduced in §4). The results are presented in Table 11. Increasing the window size of Short-Term Memory results in a slight improvement in consistency but incurs a substantial additional computational cost, as two sentence pairs extend each sentence's translation prompt. Given the trade-off between computational cost, translation quality, and consistency, we opted to employ a Short-Term window size of 3. Further increasing the Long-Term Memory window does not yield significant benefits. To address the idea that the model might require longer context windows in the later stages of document translation, we also experimented with a dynamic window setting, where the window size increases by one sentence pair for every eight sentences translated. However, this approach does not lead to performance improvements. We attribute this to the Bilingual Summary component, which effectively captures key information from more distant contexts. The iterative process of summary generation and merging inherently functions as a form of context window growth, rendering additional adjustments to the Long-Term Memory window unnecessary.

query: What does the invariance principle involve in the context of multiview settings?
golden_answer: The invariance principle involves defining a joint overlapping index set where the value of the sharing partition remains invariant for all observables on a sample level.
source_title: Unifying Causal Representation Learning with the Invariance Principle
source_text:
# D. 1 Multiview CRL 

High-level overview. The multiview setting in CRL (Daunhawer et al., 2023; Yao et al., 2023) considers multiple observables that are concurrently generated by an overlapping subset of latent variables. Multiview scenarios are often found in a partially observable setup. For example, multiple devices on a robot measure different modalities, jointly monitoring the environment through these real-time measurements. While each device measures a distinct subset of latent variables, these subsets probably still overlap as they are measuring the same system at the same time. In addition to partial observability, another way to obtain multiple views is to perform an "intervention/perturbation" (Locatello et al., 2020; von Kügelgen et al., 2021; Ahuja et al., 2022b; Brehmer et al., 2022) and collect both pre-action and post-action views on the same sample. This setting is often improperly termed "counterfactual" ${ }^{1}$ in the CRL literature, and this type of data is termed "paired data". From another perspective, the paired setting can be cast in the partial observability scenario by considering the same latent before and after an action (mathematically modeled as an intervention) as two separate latent nodes in the causal graph, as shown by von Kügelgen et al. (2021, Fig. 1). Thus, both pre-action and post-action views are partial because neither of them can observe pre-action and post-action latents simultaneously. These works assume the latents that are not affected by the action remain constant, an assumption that is relaxed in temporal CRL works. See App. D. 3 for more discussion on temporal CRL.

Data generating process. In the following, we introduce the data-generating process of a multiview setting in the flavor of the invariance principle as introduced in $\S 2$. We consider a set of views $\left\{\mathbf{x}^{k}\right\}_{k \in[K]}$ with each view $\mathbf{x}^{k} \in \mathcal{X}^{k}$ generated from some latents $\mathbf{z}^{k} \in \mathcal{Z}^{k}$. Let $S_{k} \subseteq[N]$ be the index set of generating factors for the view $\mathbf{x}^{k}$, we define $\mathbf{z}_{j}^{k}=0$ for all $j \in[N] \backslash S_{k}$ to represent the uninvolved partition of latents. Each entangled view $\mathbf{x}^{k}$ is generated by a view-specific mixing function $f_{k}: \mathcal{Z}^{k} \rightarrow \mathcal{X}^{k}$ :

$$
\mathbf{x}^{k}=f_{k}\left(\mathbf{z}^{k}\right) \quad \forall k \in[K]
$$

Define the joint overlapping index set $A:=\bigcap_{k \in[K]} S_{k}$, and assume $A \subseteq[N]$ is a non-empty subset of $[N]$. Then the value of the sharing partition $\mathbf{z}_{A}$ remain invariant for all observables $\left\{\mathbf{x}^{k}\right\}_{k \in[K]}$ on a sample level. By considering the joint intersection $A$, we have one single invariance property $\iota: \mathbb{R}^{|A|} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^{|A|}$ in the invariance set $\mathcal{I}$; and this invariance property $\iota$ emerges as the identity map id on $\mathbb{R}^{|A|}$ in the sense that $\operatorname{id}\left(\mathbf{z}_{A}^{k}\right)=\operatorname{id}\left(\mathbf{z}_{A}^{k^{\prime}}\right)$ and thus $\mathbf{z}_{A}^{k} \sim_{\iota} \mathbf{z}_{A}^{k^{\prime}}$ for all $k, k^{\prime} \in[K]$. Note that Defn. 2.1 (ii) is satisfied because any transformation $h_{k}$ that involves other components $\mathbf{z}_{q}$ with $q \notin A$ violates the equality introduced by the identity map. For a subset of observations $V_{\iota} \subseteq[K]$ with at least two elements $\left|V_{\iota}\right|>1$, we define the latent intersection as $A_{\iota}:=\bigcap_{k \in V_{\iota}} S_{k} \subseteq[N]$, then for each non-empty intersection $A_{\iota}$, there is a corresponding invariance property $\iota_{\iota}: \mathbb{R}^{\left|A_{\iota}\right|} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^{\left|A_{\iota}\right|}$ which is the identity map specified on the subspace $\mathbb{R}^{\left|A_{\iota}\right|}$. By considering all these subsets $\mathcal{V}:=\left\{V_{\iota} \subseteq\right.$ $\left.[K]:\left|V_{\iota}\right|>1,\left|A_{\iota}\right|>0\right\}$, we obtain a set of invariance properties $\mathcal{I}:=\left\{\iota_{\iota}: \mathbb{R}^{\left|A_{\iota}\right|} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^{\left|A_{\iota}\right|}\right\}$ that satisfy Asm. 2.1.

Identification algorithms. Many multiview works (von Kügelgen et al., 2021; Daunhawer et al., 2023; Yao et al., 2023) employ the $L_{2}$ loss as a regularizer to enforce sample-level invariance on the invariant partition, cooperated with some sufficiency regularizer to preserve sufficient information about the observables (Constraint 3.2). Aligned with our theory (Thm. 3.1), these works have shown block-identifiability on the invariant partition of the latents across different views. Following the same principle, there are certain variations in the implementations to enforce the invariance principle, e.g. Locatello et al. (2020) directly average the learned representations from paired data $g\left(\mathbf{x}^{1}\right), g\left(\mathbf{x}^{2}\right)$ on the shared coordinates before forwarding them to the decoder; Ahuja et al. (2022b) enforces $L_{2}$ alignment up to a learnable sparse perturbation $\delta$. As each latent component constitutes a single invariant block in the training data, these two works element-identifies (Defn. C.2) the latent variables, as explained by Proposition C.2.

[^0]
[^0]:    ${ }^{1}$ Traditionally, counterfactual in causality refers to non-observable outcomes that are "counter to the fact" (Rubin, 2005). The works we refer to here represent pre- and post-actions that affect some latent variables but not all. This can be mathematically expressed as a counterfactual in an SCM but is conceptually different as both pre- and post-action outcomes are realized (Liu et al., 2023). The "counterfactual" terminology silently implies that this is a strong assumption, but nuance is needed and it can in fact be much weaker than an intervention.

query: Why might framing affect perceptions about appropriate levels of inequality aversion?
golden_answer: Framing affects perceptions because it influences how people interpret trade-offs between equality and efficiency. For instance, presenting scenarios as percentage changes rather than absolute amounts can make certain redistributions seem more reasonable or extreme depending on context. This highlights why understanding both mathematical implications and intuitive interpretations are important when discussing appropriate coefficients for policy-making purposes.
source_title: Protected Income and Inequality Aversion
source_text:
# 1 Introduction 

Since Atkinson's (1970) and Kolm's (1976) seminal works on inequality measurement, the notion of inequality aversion has been well understood, and applied to many different contexts. The concept of inequality aversion has been closely associated to the Pigou-Dalton transfer principle, according to which social welfare does not decrease (or inequality does not increase) when a given amount is taken from someone and given to someone else who is less well-off, without reversing the ranking between these two individuals. ${ }^{1}$

The empirical-experimental literature on people's social preferences ${ }^{2}$ has elicited the value of their inequality aversion about income by making respondents choose between distributions involving different levels of inequality and different levels of average income. For instance, Venmans and Groom (2021) find an average coefficient of inequality aversion of 2.9 in an empirical survey on a sample of students, while Hurley et al. (2020) find an average coefficient of 3.27 in a representative sample of the Ontario province of Canada. The underlying mechanism for such ethical preference elicitation is the leaky-bucket experiment: a distribution is less unequal than another, but has a lower average income, reflecting the classical equality-efficiency trade-off highlighted in Okun (1975). The meaning of the coefficient of inequality aversion is usually presented in this way: a coefficient of 3 means that it is worth giving a dollar to someone even if this requires taking $8\left(=2^{3}\right)$ dollars from a person who is twice as rich-thus losing 7 dollars, i.e., $87.5 \%$ of the amount levied from the donor.

A small literature (Fleurbaey and Michel 2001, Aboudi and Thon 2003, Thon and Wallace 2004, Dubois 2016) has explored the relationship between principles of transfer that allow for leakage and the value of the coefficient of inequality aversion in a social welfare criterion that endorses such leaky trans-

[^0]
[^0]:    ${ }^{1}$ Aboudi and Thon (2006) also study what they call the Muirhead-Dalton principle, in which transfers are allowed to reverse the ranking between the two individuals, but still leave the difference between them smaller than in the initial distribution. For authoritative reviews of this field, see Chakravarty (2009), Dutta (2002) and Cowell (2000).
    ${ }^{2}$ For a review, see Gaertner and Schokkaert (2012).

fers. ${ }^{3}$ For instance, Fleurbaey and Michel (2001) show that if the transfers are proportional to the initial level of the donor and recipient, the coefficient must be at least 2 , whereas if the transfers are proportional to the final levels, the coefficient must be at least 1 .

A coefficient of 2 , according to the common presentation (referring to a gift of 1 dollar costing $2^{2}=4$ ) means that wasting $75 \%$ of the transfer when the recipient has only half the level of the donor is acceptable, and this seems a lot. The principle of proportional transfers (on initial levels), however, suggests something less extreme, since when the recipient gets X , a donor who is initially twice as rich would only lose 2 X , which means that only half of the gift is lost in the transfer. This apparent contradiction is resolved by noting that the reasoning in terms of one dollar gifts is only true for infinitesimal gifts, whereas the principe of proportional transfers applies to transfers of any size (under the proviso that they do not reverse the order between the donor and the recipient).

This shows that the way in which the implications of the coefficient of inequality aversion are presented may influence the ethical choice of the coefficient. One may find that the principle of proportional transfers appears reasonable, since it is very common for people to think in terms of variations in percentage, while hesitating to condone the maxim that "a marginal transfer from a donor to someone who is half below can waste $75 \%$ and still improve social welfare"-and yet the two refer to the same coefficient of inequality aversion of 2 .

In this paper we discover a fundamental and previously unrecognized structure within the class of additively separable social welfare functions that makes it straightforward to fully characterize the social preferences of an inequality-averse evaluator. This characterization leads directly to the following elicitation procedure: Start from a perfectly equal distribution, and then imagine that an increment can be given to one individual. What is the maximal sacrifice that can be imposed on another individual for the sake of this increment? In other words, if one individual's level of income can become infinitely high, how much could justifiably be taken from another one in order to make this possible? It seems to us that this framing pushes people's intuition further toward high values of inequality aversion. In particular, a coefficient that is below 1 would justify depriving the sacrificed individual

[^0]
[^0]:    ${ }^{3}$ See also Bosmans (2014) for a similar analysis applied to rank-dependent poverty measures, involving transfers across the poverty threshold.

from everything. For a Kolm-Atkinson (scale-invariant) social welfare function, a coefficient of 2 or more means that it is never acceptable to bring the sacrificed individual below half of her initial level, which seems a rather generous (i.e., generously low) bound-the bound is $70 \%$ of the initial level when the coefficient is 3 . In addition to relating levels of protection of the sacrificed individual's income to coefficients of inequality, we actually characterize the classes of additively separable social welfare functions that guarantee specific (absolute or relative) levels of protection.

The paper is structured as follows. In section 2, we define the framework and the main notions. Section 3 determines the general conditions under which an additively separable social welfare function provides a strictly positive protected level to the sacrificed individual. In section 4, we characterize the class of social welfare functions which protect a fixed fraction of the initial level, against increments given to either one other individual, or two other individuals. Section 5 instead examines the case in which the protected level is always at a fixed absolute difference from the initial level. Section 6 explores how to obtain a protection that is, in proportion to the initial level, greater when the initial level is lower, reflecting the intuitively appealing thought that poor people deserve a relatively greater protection than rich people. We examine in section 7 the case in which the starting point is not perfect equality and generalize the results to this broader class of contexts. Section 8 concludes. We also created a companion website to the paper, available at https://osf.io/tnu2q/, which contains interactive visuals, apps and narratives that explain and motivate our results in simple and intuitive terms.

query: What happens when you integrate an analytic function \(f\) of \(\omega\) over all reals where \(x=0\)?
golden_answer: The integral equals \(f^{\prime}(a)+\frac{1}{\pi} \int_{a}^{\infty} f^{\prime \prime}(x) d x^{\prime}\), for arbitrary real \(a\).
source_title: Applying numerosity to surreal integration
source_text:
# 3. Integration of a surreal value over a subset of reals 

Generalizing relation (3) to any analytic function $f$ of $\omega$, we have:
$\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\left(\begin{cases}f(\tilde{\delta}(0)) & x=0 \\ 0 & x \neq 0\end{cases}\right) d x=f^{\prime}(a)+\frac{1}{\pi} \int_{a}^{\infty} f^{\prime \prime}(x) d x^{\prime}$
for arbitrary real $a$ where the expression converges. This is equal to $f^{\prime}(\tilde{\delta}(0))$, if $f^{\prime}(\tilde{\delta}(0)) \in \mathbb{J}$ according to the definition (1).

Noticing that our H-field is equipped with operation of derivation $\partial()$, we can re-write it like this:
$\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\left(\begin{cases}w & x=0 \\ 0 & x \neq 0\end{cases}\right) d x=\pi \partial(w)^{\prime}$

where $w \in \mathbb{J}$. But if we are integrating over a set where the expression under the integral can take surreal values at several points, it is natural to multiply this result by the numerosity of the support:
$\int_{S} w d t=\pi N(S) \partial(w)$
One can easily notice that surreal integration defined this way does not generally satisfy the linearity against an infinite factor $\alpha$ :
$\int_{S}(\alpha f) \neq \alpha \int_{S} f$
For instance, if $u(x)$ is a unit impulse function $\mathrm{u}(\mathrm{x})=\left\{\begin{array}{ll}1 & x=0 \\ 0 & x \neq 0\end{array}\right.$, then
$\int_{-1}^{1} \omega u(x) d x=\pi \neq \omega \int_{-1}^{1} u(x) d x=0$
In our opinion, the struggle to keep this rule intact is the reason for many failed attempts to define the surreal integration. Still, there are ongoing efforts by other authors to keep this rule [7].

As a consequence,
$\frac{1}{\pi} \int_{S} \omega d t=\int_{S} \bar{\delta}(0) d t=N(S)$.

query: Does the expected probability of infection decrease with increasing variance in dose?
golden_answer: Yes.
source_title:
Impact of heterogeneity on infection probability: Insights from
  single-hit dose-response models
source_text:
### 4.1. General results for the expected probability of infection

Theorem 4.1 gives a general result for the dependence of the expected probability of infection on the infectivity and/or dose variability across different hosts.

Theorem 4.1. Let us suppose that the following conditions hold:

(a) The probability of infection for a given infectivity and dose is given by $P^{(A)}(x, n)$ (Eq. 12).
(b) The between-host variation of infectivity is described by a continuous random variable defined on $[0,1]$ with expectation $\mu_{x}$ and variance $v_{x}$.
(c) The dose ingested by different hosts is a discrete random variable taking values in $\mathbb{Z}^{+}$(i.e., at least one microbe is ingested), with expectation $\mu_{n}$ and variance $v_{n}$.

Then, in the limit of small infectivity, the expected probability of infection, $\hat{P}$, is a decreasing function of both $v_{x}$ and $v_{n}$.

Proof. The proof essentially uses a cumulant expansion procedure [33]. From assumption (a), the expected probability of infection is given by

$$
\hat{P}=1-\mathrm{E}_{x}\left(\mathrm{E}_{n}\left((1-x)^{n}\right)\right)
$$

where $\mathrm{E}_{x}$ and $\mathrm{E}_{n}$ are the expectations corresponding to infectivity and dose, respectively.

The binomial power in Eq. (13) can be expanded to give $\mathrm{E}_{x}\left(\mathrm{E}_{n}((1-\right.$ $\left.\left.x)^{n}\right)\right)=1+y$, where
$y \equiv-\left(\mu_{x}+\frac{1}{2}\left(v_{x}+\mu_{x}^{2}\right)+O\left(x^{3}\right)\right) \mu_{n}+\frac{1}{2}\left(v_{x}+\mu_{x}^{2}+O\left(x^{3}\right)\right)\left(v_{n}+\mu_{n}^{2}\right)+O\left(x^{3} n^{3}\right)$.
Here, the identities $\mathrm{E}_{x}\left(x^{2}\right)=v_{x}+\mu_{x}^{2}$ and $\mathrm{E}_{n}\left(n^{2}\right)=v_{n}+\mu_{n}^{2}$ have been used to express $y$ as a function of expected values and variances of $x$ and $n$.

It is now convenient to express the expected value in Eq. (13) as $\mathrm{E}_{x}\left(\mathrm{E}_{n}((1-\right.$ $\left.\left.x)^{n}\right)\right)=\exp (\ln (1+y))$ and use the expansion $\ln (1+y)=y-y^{2} / 2+O\left(y^{3}\right)$. After introducing the expression (14) into this expansion and neglecting $O\left(x^{3}\right)$ terms in the resulting function of $x$, one obtains the following approximation:
$\hat{P} \simeq f_{1}\left(\mu_{x}, v_{x}, \mu_{n}, v_{n}\right) \equiv 1-\exp \left(-\mu_{x} \mu_{n}+\frac{\mu_{x}^{2}}{2}\left(v_{n}-\mu_{n}\right)+\frac{v_{x}}{2}\left(\mu_{n}^{2}-\mu_{n}+v_{n}\right)\right)$.
According to Eq. (15), $\hat{P}$ decreases with increasing $v_{n}$ for any $\mu_{x}>0 . \hat{P}$ also decreases with increasing $v_{x}$ since $\mu_{n}^{2}-\mu_{n}+v_{n} \geq 0$ for any reasonable dose with $\mu_{n} \geq 1$ and $v_{n} \geq 0$.

Corollary 4.1.1 establishes a general link between the slope of the doseresponse curve and the variance of the infectivity. This gives mathematical support to the ubiquitous flattening of the dose-response curve experimentally observed and modelled by assuming heterogeneous infectivity $[16,8]$.
Corollary 4.1.1. In the limit of small infectivity, the slope of $\hat{P}$ evaluated at the median dose-defined as the dose $\mu_{n}=\mu_{50}$ for which the expected probability of infection is $50 \%$-is an increasing function of $\mu_{x}$ and a decreasing function of $v_{x}$ for any dose distribution.
Proof. The median dose, $\mu_{50}$, corresponds to $\hat{P}=1 / 2$ which, in the limit of small infectivity, reduces to $f_{1}\left(\mu_{x}, v_{x}, \mu_{50}, v_{n}\right)=1 / 2$ (cf. Eq. 15). From this condition, the rate of variation of $\hat{P}$ at $\mu_{n}=\mu_{50}$ can be expressed as

$$
\left.\frac{\mathrm{d} \hat{P}}{\mathrm{~d} \mu_{n}}\right|_{\mu_{n}=\mu_{50}}=\frac{\mu_{x}}{2}\left(1+\frac{\mu_{x}}{2}\right)-\frac{v_{x}}{2}\left(\mu_{50}-\frac{1}{2}\right)
$$

This equation trivially proves the corollary for any reasonable median dose $\mu_{50}>1 / 2$.

query: Does a neutroelastic network transform with productivity shocks?
golden_answer: No, a neutroelastic network does not transform with productivity shocks.
source_title: The role of substitution elasticity in Domar aggregation
source_text:
# 2.3 Network transformation 

In this study, the monetary input-output coefficient matrix is reffered to as the production network. A sector's monetary input-output coefficient for the $i$ th factor is its cost-share of the $i$ th factor. By applying Shephard's lemma to CES unit cost function of the $j$ th sector, and together with zero profit condition, cost-share for the $i$ th factor, which we denote by $s_{i j}$, can be evaluated as follows:

$$
s_{i j}=\alpha_{i j}\left(\frac{p_{i}}{z_{j} p_{j}}\right)^{1-\sigma}=\alpha_{i j} \zeta_{j} \frac{\pi_{i}}{\pi_{j}}
$$

Here, $\pi_{i}=\left(p_{i}\right)^{1-\sigma}$ and $\pi_{j}=\left(p_{j}\right)^{1-\sigma}$ are solutions to the general equilibrium system of equations (7) that must only depend on the sectoral productivity levels $\boldsymbol{z}=\left(z_{1}, \cdots, z_{n}\right)$. We know, by virtue of (8), that $s_{i j}=\alpha_{i j}$ at the reference state, since it is $\mathbf{1}=\boldsymbol{z}=\boldsymbol{\zeta}$ and hence, $\boldsymbol{\pi}=\boldsymbol{p}=\mathbf{1}$. Conversely, productivity shocks, i.e., $\boldsymbol{z} \neq \mathbf{1}$ will transform the production network, i.e., $s_{i j} \neq \alpha_{i j}$, only if the elasticity of substitution is nonneutral, i.e., $\sigma \neq 1$. Note, if the elasticity of substitution is neutral, i.e., $\sigma=1$, it is always the case that $s_{i j}=\alpha_{i j}$, that is, the production network is invariable regardless of the productivity shocks and associated changes in prices.

For later convenience, let us call a production network subject to substitution elasticity less than unity $(\sigma<1)$, an inelastic network, and that subject to substitution elasticity greater than unity $(\sigma>1)$, an elastic network. A neutroelastic network $(\sigma=1)$ is otherwise called a Cobb-Douglas production network. Both inelastic and elastic networks are subject to transformation given sectoral productivity shocks, whereas neutroelastic network is not.
