query: How does quantum reservoir computing differ from recurrent neural networks (RNNs)?
golden_answer: Quantum reservoir computing differs from RNNs because the majority of the randomly initialized parameters of its reservoir are fixed from the start, reducing computational cost, although it typically requires more parameters to achieve comparable accuracy.
source_title: How quantum computing can enhance biomarker discovery
source_text:
# 3.2 Time series data 

The models used in predicting future values of a time series given a set of past values are fundamentally different to predicting labels or a quantity given a set of features. This is because the former is an extrapolation whereas (in most cases) the latter is an interpolation. Thus, common models (machine learning or otherwise) used in classification or regression problems usually do not perform well for time series prediction and forecasting, and time series data requires other approaches.

For many biomedical applications, analysis of time series data, also known as longitudinal data, presents a range of challenges for classical techniques, including machine learning models. Some of these challenges are algorithm selection, explainability, heterogeneous data, inconsistent labelling and annotations, missing data, and unbalanced data [123]. In addition, the many correlated variables typically found in biomarker data make it difficult to elucidate causal pathways [124]. Quantum computing techniques, particularly QML algorithms such as quantum reservoir methods [125], are actively researched in order to achieve enhanced time series processing [126].

There already exists a variety of techniques to tackle time series problems. For many examples, one can often get reasonable predictions by using relatively simple models such as auto-regressive moving average models and their many variants [127]. For time series data with additional challenges (such as the ones mentioned at the start of this section), the current state-of-the-art is arguably the long short-term memory (LSTM) ML model [128], which is able to capture some properties, such as seasonality and highly correlated variables, much better than the more traditional models. However, a recent QML technique that has also started to gain attention is quantum reservoir computing (QRC) [129]. Reservoir computing is a predecessor to recurrent neural networks (RNNs), where the hidden weights can be treated as a reservoir that projects the data into a higher-dimensional subspace, which can then be fed into a simple linear model; quantum analogues exist [130]. The reservoir (similar to the RNN) receives the time series data sequentially, and hence the dynamics of the reservoir are dependent on the previous time step. This reservoir can have many different forms, ranging from classical architectures like the echo state network [131] to physical implementations [132, 133]. The advantage of reservoir computing versus RNNs is that since the majority of the randomly initialized parameters of this reservoir is fixed from the

start, the computational cost of training them is much lower. On the other hand, this randomness typically requires reservoirs to have many more parameters to achieve a comparable accuracy. Still, the use of a quantum reservoir (for example, by generating a random quantum circuit) can decrease the number of parameters required for the model to perform well.

## D. Extension to an unknown number of sources

As evident from the preceding descriptions, our method requires prior knowledge of the number of sound sources. This necessity arises from the envelope estimation network's requirement. The envelope estimation network needs to predefine the number of sound sources to determine its number of output channels. The task of the envelope estimation network is essentially a coarse source separation - not separating source signals themselves, but rather separating the envelopes of source signals. Numerous existing methods have achieved source separation with an unknown number of sources, such as encoder-decoder attractor (EDA) [51], [52], recursion-based methods [53], and approaches constrained on the maximum number of sources [54]. Inspired by [54], We extend the envelope estimation network to handle an unknown number of sources under the premise of knowing the maximum number of sources $C_{\max }$. Both the network outputs and training labels have dimensions of $C_{\max } \times 1 \times T$. For cases where the actual source count $C<C_{\max }$, the training labels consist of $C$ ground-truth source envelopes concatenated with $C_{\max }-C$ all-zero tensor of dimension $1 \times T$. The network training loss for the $c$-th channel is defined as:

$$
\mathcal{L}_{e n v, c}= \begin{cases}\operatorname{NMSELoss}\left(\hat{\mathbf{E}}_{c}^{e s t}, \hat{\mathbf{E}}_{c}^{t r g}\right) & c<C \\ \mathcal{L}^{\text {inactive }}\left(\hat{\mathbf{E}}_{c}^{e s t}, \hat{\mathbf{E}}_{c}^{t r g}\right) & C \leq c \leq C_{\max }\end{cases}
$$

where $\mathcal{L}^{\text {inactive }}$ is defined as the loss function when $\hat{\mathbf{E}}_{c}^{\text {trg }}$ is an all-zero tensor:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathcal{L}^{\text {inactive }}\left(\hat{\mathbf{E}}_{c}^{e s t}, \hat{\mathbf{E}}_{c}^{t r g}\right)= & 10 \log _{10}\left(\sum_{t=0}^{T}\left(\hat{E}_{c}^{e s t}(t)-\hat{E}_{c}^{t r g}(t)\right)^{2}\right. \\
& \left.+\tau \sum_{t=0}^{T}\left(\hat{E}^{m i x}(t)\right)^{2}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

where $\hat{E}_{z}^{\text {trg }}(t) \equiv 0, \hat{\mathbf{E}}^{\text {mix }}$ denotes the groundtruth envelope of the zero-th order of the audio mixture and $\tau$ equals to 0.01 , which is the same as [54]. The uPIT is also utilized during training. During testing, if the maximum value of an output channel in the envelope estimation network falls below 0.25 , we consider the corresponding channel to contain no active sound source.

To validate the effectiveness of our method under an unknown number of sources, we conducted experiments under an unknown number of sources. The experimental setup mirrored the two-source scenario, except that the number of sources is randomly set to 2 or 3 and remained unknown to our method. The results demonstrate high estimation accuracy for both 2-source and 3-source scenarios. query: What condition characterizes when every ideal of a Prüfer domain is a co-Kasch module?
golden_answer: Every ideal of a Prüfer domain is characterized as being a co-Kasch module if and only if the Prüfer domain is Dedekind.
source_title: Co-Kasch Modules
source_text:
# 4. CO-KASCH MODULES OVER COMMUTATIVE RINGS 

In this section we study co-Kasch modules over commutative rings. We prove that, a Prüfer domain $R$ is Dedekind if and only if every ideal of $R$ is a co-Kasch module. We also characterize co-Kasch modules over the ring of integers.

Proposition 4.1. Let $R$ be a domain and $M$ be an $R$-module. If $M \neq T(M)$, then $M$ is a co-Kasch module if and only if $\operatorname{Hom}_{R}\left(M, \frac{R}{P}\right) \neq 0$ for each $P \in \Omega$.

Proof. Suppose that, $M$ is a co-Kasch module. Since $M \neq T(M)$, there is an $m \in M$ such that $m R \cong R$. Thus every simple module is a homomorphic image of $M$ by the coKasch module assumption. Then for each maximal ideal $P$ of $R$, there is an epimorphism $f_{P}: M \rightarrow \frac{R}{P}$. This follows the necessity. Sufficiency is clear.

Lemma 4.2. Let $R$ be a valuation domain. Every ideal of $R$ is a co-Kasch module if and only if $R$ is a DVR.

Proof. Sufficiency is clear. To prove the necessity, let $\mathbf{p}$ be the unique maximal ideal of $R$. By the hypothesis $\mathbf{p}$ is a co-Kasch module, and so $\mathbf{p}^{2} \neq \mathbf{p}$, otherwise $\mathbf{p}$ would have no simple factors. Let $p \in \mathbf{p}-\mathbf{p}^{2}$. Then $\mathbf{p}=R p$, because $R$ is a valuation domain. Now consider the ideal $I=\cap_{n \in \mathbb{Z}^{+} } R p^{n}$. Then by [2, Proposition 15] $I$ has no maximal submodules i.e. $\operatorname{Rad}(I)=I$. Thus, since $I$ is co-Kasch by the assumption, $I=0$, by Proposition 3.1(1). Therefore $R$ is a DVR by [4, page 99, Exercise 4].

Proposition 4.3. Let $R$ be a Prüfer domain. The following statements are equivalent.
(1) Every ideal of $R$ is a co-Kasch module.
(2) Every ideal of $R_{\mathbf{p}}$ is a co-Kasch module for every $\mathbf{p} \in \Omega$.
(3) $R_{\mathbf{p}}$ is a DVR for every $\mathbf{p} \in \Omega$.
(4) $R$ is Dedekind.

Proof. (1) $\Rightarrow$ (2) Let $\mathbf{p}$ be a maximal ideal of $R$, and $B$ be a nonzero proper ideal of $R_{\mathbf{p}}$. Then there is a proper ideal $A$ of $R$ such that $A_{\mathbf{p}}=B$. By the hypothesis, $A$ is a co-Kasch module. Thus there is a maximal submodule $C$ of $A$ such that $\frac{A}{C} \cong \frac{R}{\mathbf{p}}$. Localizing at $\mathbf{p}$ gives: $\left(\frac{A}{C}\right)_{\mathbf{p}} \cong\left(\frac{R}{\mathbf{p}}\right)_{\mathbf{p}}$, because localization preserves isomorphisms (see, [12, page 26: B)]) Then $\frac{A_{\mathbf{p}}}{C_{\mathbf{p}}} \cong \frac{R_{\mathbf{p}}}{P_{\mathbf{p}}}$ by [12, page 26: C)]. Since $R_{\mathbf{p}}$ is a local ring with the unique maximal ideal $\mathbf{p}_{\mathbf{p}}$ and $A_{\mathbf{p}}=B$, we get $\frac{B}{C_{\mathbf{p}}} \cong \frac{R_{\mathbf{p}}}{\mathbf{p}_{\mathbf{p}}}$ is simple. Thus $C_{\mathbf{p}}$ is a maximal ideal of $B$, and so $B$ is a co-Kasch module by Proposition 3.1(b).
(2) $\Rightarrow$ (3) Since $R$ is Prüfer, $R_{\mathbf{p}}$ is a valuation domain for each $\mathbf{p} \in \Omega$. Thus (3) follows by Lemma 4.2.
(3) $\Rightarrow$ (2) Every nonzero ideal of a DVR is isomorphic to $R$. Hence (2) follows.
(3) $\Longleftrightarrow(4)$ is clear.
(4) $\Rightarrow$ (1) Let $I$ be a nonzero ideal of $R$. Note that $I$ is finitely generated. Since $R$ embeds in $I, I$ has a subfactor isomorpic to every simple $R$-module. For the proof, we need to show that $\operatorname{Hom}\left(I, \frac{R}{J}\right) \neq 0$ for each maximal ideal $J$ of $R$. Assume that $\operatorname{Hom}\left(I, \frac{R}{J}\right)=0$ for some maximal ideal $J$ of $R$. Then $I=J \cdot I$. Localizing at the maximal ideal $J$, we obtain $I_{J}=J_{J} \cdot I_{J}$. Since $R_{J}$ is a local ring with the unique maximal ideal $J_{J}$, the fact that $I_{J}$ is finitely generated and $I_{J}=J_{J} \cdot I_{J}$ implies that $I_{J}=0$ by Nakayama's Lemma. As $R$ is a domain $I_{J}=0$ gives $I=0$. Contradiction. Therefore $I \neq J \cdot I$ for each maximal ideal $J$ of $R$, and so $\operatorname{Hom}\left(I, \frac{R}{J}\right) \neq 0$. Hence $I$ is a co-Kasch module, and this proves (1).

Now, we shall give a characterization of co-Kasch modules over the ring of integers. For a $\mathbb{Z}$-module $M, T(M)$ is the torsion submodule of $M$. If $p$ is a prime integer the submodule $T_{p}(M)=\left\{m \in M \mid p^{n} m=0\right.$ for some positive integer $\left.n\right\}$ is said to be the $p$-primary component of $M$. It is well known that $T(M)=\bigoplus_{p \in \mathcal{P}} T_{p}(M)$, where $\mathcal{P}$ is the set of prime integers.

Proposition 4.4. The following are hold.
(a) A nonzero torsion $\mathbb{Z}$-module $M$ is a co-Kasch module if and only if $p M \neq M$ for each prime $p$ with $T_{p}(M) \neq 0$.
(b) If $T(M) \neq M$, then $M$ is a co-Kasch module if and only if $p M \neq M$ for each prime $p$.

Proof. (a) Since $M$ is torsion, $M=\oplus_{p \in A} T_{p}(M)$, where $T_{p}(M)$ is the (nonzero) $p$-primary component of $M$. Suppose $M$ is an $H$-module. Let $p$ be a prime such that $T_{p}(M) \neq 0$. Then $S=\operatorname{Soc}\left(T_{p}(M)\right) \cong \frac{\mathbb{Z}}{p \mathbb{Z}}$ is a subfactor of $M$. Since $M$ is a co-Kasch module, $\frac{M}{L} \cong \frac{\mathbb{Z}}{p \mathbb{Z}}$. This implies that $p M \neq M$. This show the necessity. Conversely, let $\frac{X}{Y} \cong \frac{\mathbb{Z}}{p \mathbb{Z}}$ be a simple subfactor of $M$. We have $\frac{X}{Y} \subseteq \frac{M}{Y} \cong \oplus \frac{T_{p}(M)}{T_{p}(Y)}$. For a prime $q \neq p, \operatorname{Hom}\left(\frac{\mathbb{Z}}{p \mathbb{Z}}, \frac{T_{q}(M)}{T_{q}(Y)}\right)=0$. Therefore, $\operatorname{Hom}\left(\frac{\mathbb{Z}}{p \mathbb{Z}}, \frac{T_{p}(M)}{T_{p}(Y)}\right) \neq 0$. So that $T_{p}(M) \neq 0$. Now by the hypothesis $p M \neq M$, and so $M$ has a simple factor isomorphic to $\frac{\mathbb{Z}}{p \mathbb{Z}}$.
(b) Sufficiency is clear. For necessity suppose $T(M) \neq M$. Then $M$ has a submodule isomorphic to $\mathbb{Z}$. Thus, $M$ has a factor isomorphic to $\mathbb{Z}_{p}$ for each prime $p$, by the co-Kasch module assumption. Therefore $p M \neq M$ for each prime $p$.

query: What is the purpose of using surrogate deep trees in the analysis?
golden_answer: The purpose of using surrogate deep trees is to identify relevant predictors by approximating BART predictions with a flexible function of only a handful of covariates.
source_title:
Combining BART and Principal Stratification to estimate the effect of
  intermediate variables on primary outcomes with application to estimating the
  effect of family planning on employment in Nigeria and Senegal
source_text:
# 6. Summarizing BART results 

While BART is more flexible than logistic regression, it is also less easy to interpret. A general strategy to summarize complex "black box" models is to fit simpler, surrogate models (Molnar et al., 2020). We use variations of this strategy, termed surrogate deep and shallow tree, respectively, to: (i) identify relevant predictors of latent class membership and of outcome, conditional on class membership, (ii) identify combinations of predictors defining segments with relatively homogenous CATEs.

Surrogate "deep" trees to identify relevant predictors

[^0]
[^0]:    ${ }^{10}$ Based on the ratio of the posterior probabilities of the trees.

Carvalho et al. (2020) suggest the use of deep trees to identify relevant predictors. In this approach, the goal is to approximate BART predictions with a flexible function of only a handful of the covariates. At this point, there is no interest in learning or understanding the approximating function itself. Instead, we care about keeping it as flexible as possible, to reflect the fact that predictors may be relevant in different ways (e.g., by interacting with other predictors).

Let $\hat{y}$ denote the predicted values (the posterior mean or median) from BART for the response variable $y$ based on the entire set of covariates $X$ of dimension $p$. Consider a subset of $X$, of dimension $s<p$, say $Q$. We fit a single regression tree to $\hat{y}$ as a function of $Q$ using a standard algorithm (Breiman et al., 1984; Therneau \& Atkinson, 2022), but letting the tree grow without constraints. We obtain new fitted value say $\hat{y}$ based on this deep surrogate regression tree. These are predictions of the fitted values from BART (not predictions of the outcome itself, $y$ ) based on only a subset of the predictors. We assess how close is $\hat{y}$ to $\hat{y}$ using Person $R^{2}$.

Initially, we consider all possible subsets of size one and chose the subset with the larger $R^{2}$. Starting from that subset (i.e., the single best predictor), we use a stepwise forward algorithm to consider subsets of covariates of increasing size. The $R^{2}$ tends to increase fast initially and slows down as the number of predictors included grows larger. We stop when an additional predictor will not increase $R^{2}$ by more than $1 \%$.

The procedure is useful to identify a handful of relevant predictors without restricting the functional form of the relationship between these predictors and BART fitted values. No claim is made that the subset identified is the only possible subset of relevant predictors.

Surrogate "shallow" tree to identify relevant segments

To learn how the set of predictors identified maybe important, we rely on a second regression tree. The response variable is again $\hat{y}$, the fitted value from BART, which we regress on the set of relevant predictors identified in the previous step, say $Q^{*}$. Unlike the first step, we now constrain the tree to a maximum depth of 3 . This constraint reflects that the priority in this step is to understand the relationship, more than predict the fitted values with maximum accuracy. A similar procedure is used in Logan et al., (2019), to examine effect heterogeneity - other examples include J. Hill \& Su (2013); Hahn et al. (2020); and Chen et al. (2024).

query: What is geometric elimination of imaginaries in an $\mathcal{L}$-theory?
golden_answer: An $\mathcal{L}$-theory has geometric elimination of imaginaries if every imaginary is $\mathcal{L}$-interalgebraic with a real tuple.
source_title:
Stationarity and elimination of imaginaries in stable and simple
  theories
source_text:
# 4. IMagINARIES 

Recall that an $\mathcal{L}$-theory $T$ has geometric elimination of imaginaries if every imaginary $\alpha$ is $\mathcal{L}$-interalgebraic with a real tuple $\bar{a}$. The theory has weak elimination of imaginaries if additionally $\alpha$ is definable over $\bar{a}$. If $T$ has weak elimination of imaginaries, then $\operatorname{acl}_{\mathcal{L}}^{c g}(A)=\operatorname{dcl}_{\mathcal{L}}^{c g}\left(\operatorname{acl}_{\mathcal{L}}(A)\right)$ for every real set $A$, so types over real algebraically closed sets are stationary. By [8, Proposition 3.4], a stable theory has weak elimination of imaginaries if it has geometric elimination of imaginaries and types over real algebraically closed sets are stationary.

Delon showed in [11, p. 36] that the theory $S C F_{p}^{\infty}$ does not have elimination of imaginaries. Her proof easily generalizes to show that geometric elimination also fails. A similar proof was given by Messmer and Wood [19, Remark 4.3] to show that elimination of imaginaries fails in the theory $D C F_{p}$ of differentially closed fields of positive characteristic. Pillay and Vassiliev showed in [22, Lemma 3.3] with a different proof that whenever the stable nfcp theory $T_{0}$ has elimination of imaginaries, the theory $T=T_{0} P$ of beautiful pairs of $T_{0}$ has geometric elimination of imaginaries if and only if no infinite group is definable in $T_{0}$. In particular, the theory of proper pairs of algebraically closed fields does not have geometric elimination of imaginaries.

In this section, we present a criterion for a theory not to have geometric elimination of imaginaries that extracts the essences of Delon's proof as well as Messmers's and Wood's proof and which applies to all examples mentioned above.

We work in the setting of Lemma 3.9 in the previous Subsection 3.2: Let $T_{0}$ be a stable $\mathcal{L}_{0}$-theory (with elimination of imaginaries and quantifiers) and $\mathcal{M}_{0}$ a sufficiently saturated model. Consider a (simple) $\mathcal{L}$-theory $T$ such that $T_{0}^{\vee} \subset T$ and choose a sufficiently saturated model $\mathcal{M}$ of $T$ inside $\mathcal{M}_{0}$.

We again suppose that there are an $\mathcal{L}_{0}$-definable group $(G, \cdot)$ in $M_{0}$ as well as $\mathcal{L}$-definable subsets $H_{2} \subset H_{1}$ of $M$ such that $\left(H_{1}, \cdot\right)$ and $\left(H_{2}, \cdot\right)$ are groups in $\mathcal{M}$; all $G, H_{1}$ and $H_{2}$ being defined over a small elementary substructure $\mathcal{N}$ of $\mathcal{M}$.

The first lemma we present is somewhat technical but contains the common idea of the different applications.

Lemma 4.1. Suppose that in the setting just described the following conditions are satisfied:
(i) For tuples $\bar{a}$ and $\bar{b}$ from $M$ holds $\bar{a} \perp_{N}^{\mathcal{L}} \bar{b} \quad \Rightarrow \quad \bar{a} \perp_{N}^{0} \bar{b}$.
(ii) There exists an element $h$ of $H_{2}(M)$ that is $\mathcal{L}_{0}$-generic over $N$ in $\operatorname{dc}_{G}\left(H_{1}(N)\right)$.
(iii) There exists an element $g$ of $H_{1}(M)$ with $g \perp^{\mathcal{L}}{ }_{N} h$ such that $\operatorname{acl}_{\mathcal{L}}(g, N) \subset \operatorname{acl}_{0}(g, N)$ as well as $\operatorname{acl}_{\mathcal{L}}(g \cdot h, N) \subset \operatorname{acl}_{0}(g \cdot h, N)$.

If the canonical parameter of the coset $g \cdot H_{2}$ of $H_{2}$ in $H_{1}$ is $\mathcal{L}$-interalgebraic over $N$ with a real tuple, then the coset is $\mathcal{L}(N)$-definable. Moreover, we then have that the right-stabilizer $\operatorname{Stab}_{H_{1}}^{r}\left(\operatorname{tp}_{\mathcal{L}}(g / N)\right)$ is contained in $H_{2}$.

Note that if we further assume that $T$ is stable and $H_{2} \subset \operatorname{Stab}_{H_{1}}^{r}\left(\operatorname{tp}_{\mathcal{L}}(g / N)\right)$, the conclusion of Lemma 4.1 that $g \cdot H_{2}$ is $\mathcal{L}(N)$-definable yields $\operatorname{Stab}_{H_{1}}^{r}\left(\operatorname{tp}_{\mathcal{L}}(g / N)\right)=H_{2}$. By [21, Lemma 4.4] we then have that $H_{2}$ is connected and that $\operatorname{tp}_{\mathcal{L}}(g / N)$ is the generic type of $g \cdot H_{2}$.

Proof. Given $g$ and $h$ as in (ii) and (iii), let $\alpha$ be the canonical parameter of the coset $g \cdot H_{2}=g \cdot h \cdot H_{2}$. Suppose that $\alpha$ is $\mathcal{L}$-interalgebraic over $N$ with the real tuple $\bar{a}$.

By Condition (i), the $\mathcal{L}$-independence implies that $g \perp_{N}^{0} h$. Working now in $\mathcal{M}_{0}$, observe that $g$ and $h$ are both in $H_{1}(M) \subset \operatorname{dc}_{G}\left(H_{1}(M)\right)=\operatorname{dc}_{G}\left(H_{1}(N)\right)$ by Remark 3.7. Thus, genericity of $h$ in $\operatorname{dc}_{G}\left(H_{1}(N)\right)$ yields that

$$
g \cdot h \underset{N}{\perp_{N}^{0}} g
$$

Considering $\mathcal{M}$ again, note that $\alpha$ is $\mathcal{L}(N)$-definable over any element of the coset because $H_{2}$ is $\mathcal{L}(N)$-definable. Thus, the tuple $\bar{a}$ is $\mathcal{L}$-algebraic both over $N, g$ and $N, g \cdot h$.

Condition (iii) and the independence in $(\star)$ now yield that

$$
\bar{a} \in \operatorname{acl}_{0}(g, N) \cap \operatorname{acl}_{0}(g \cdot h, N) \cap M \subset \operatorname{acl}_{0}(N) \cap M=N
$$

Hence, the imaginary $\alpha$ lies in $\operatorname{acl}_{\mathcal{L}}^{e q}(N)=N^{e q}$ (since $N$ is a model of $T$ ). In particular, the coset $g \cdot H_{2}$ is $N$-definable.

For the moreover part note that it is enough to check that $\operatorname{St}_{H_{1}}^{r}\left(\operatorname{tp}_{\mathcal{L}}(g / N)\right) \subset H_{2}$ where $\operatorname{St}_{H_{1}}^{r}\left(\operatorname{tp}_{\mathcal{L}}(g / N)\right)=\left\{h^{\prime} \in H_{1} \mid \exists g^{\prime} \stackrel{\mathcal{L}}{=}_{N} g\right.$ with $\left.g^{\prime} \perp_{\mathcal{L}}^{\mathcal{L}} h^{\prime}\right.$ and $\left.g^{\prime} \cdot h^{\prime} \stackrel{\mathcal{L}}{=}_{N} g\right\}$. Let thus $h^{\prime}$ be in $\operatorname{St}_{H_{1}}^{r}\left(\operatorname{tp}_{\mathcal{L}}(g / N)\right)$, witnessed by $g^{\prime} \stackrel{\mathcal{L}}{=}_{N} g$. Since $g \cdot H_{2}$ is $\mathcal{L}(N)$-definable, we have that $g^{\prime} \cdot H_{2}=g \cdot H_{2}=g^{\prime} \cdot h^{\prime} \cdot H_{2}$. By left-cancellation this implies that $h^{\prime}$ is in $H_{2}$.

Remark 4.2. Some of the conditions in Lemma 4.1 have already appeared in a previous context in this paper:

- As a model of $T$, the set $N$ is $\mathcal{L}$-algebraically closed. Thus Property ( $\#$ ) introduced in Section 1 yields by Fact 1.5 that Condition (i) holds. The Property ( $\#$ ) will be satisfied in all our examples.
- Since $T$ is controlled by $T_{0}$, the second part of Condition (iii) is equivalent by Remark $1.1(4)$ to $\operatorname{acl}_{\mathcal{L}}(g, N)=\operatorname{acl}_{0}(g, N) \cap M$ and $\operatorname{acl}_{\mathcal{L}}(g \cdot h, N)=\operatorname{acl}_{0}(g \cdot h, N) \cap M$.

In order to show the failure of elimination of imaginaries, we first give a criterion for the case that $T$ is stable:
Proposition 4.3. Consider a stable $\mathcal{L}$-theory $T$ with $T_{0}^{\text {st }} \subset T$ for the stable $\mathcal{L}_{0}$-theory $T_{0}$ (see Section 1). Inside a sufficiently saturated model $\mathcal{M}_{0}$ of $T_{0}$ choose $\mathcal{M} \models T$ also sufficiently saturated.

Suppose that there is an $\mathcal{L}_{0}$-definable group $(G, \cdot)$ in $M_{0}$ and an $\mathcal{L}$-definable subset $H_{1}$ of $M$ such that $\left(H_{1}, \cdot\right)$ is a group in $\mathcal{M}$; both $G$ and $H_{1}$ being defined over a small elementary substructure $\mathcal{N}$ of $\mathcal{M}$. Assume further that:
(1) For tuples $\bar{a}$ and $\bar{b}$ from $M$ holds $\bar{a} \perp_{\mathcal{N}}^{\mathcal{L}} \bar{b} \quad \Rightarrow \quad \bar{a} \perp_{\mathcal{N}}^{0} \bar{b}$.
(2) There exists a type $p$ over $N$ of an element of $H_{1}$ such that for every realization $g$ of $p$ holds $\operatorname{acl}_{\mathcal{L}}(g, N) \subset \operatorname{acl}_{0}(g, N)$.
(3) The right stabilizer $\operatorname{Stab}_{H_{1}}^{r}(p)$ contains a proper (infinite) $\mathcal{L}(N)$-definable subgroup $H_{2}$ such that the definable hull $\operatorname{dc}_{G}\left(H_{2}(N)\right)$ is principal in the definable hull $\operatorname{dc}_{G}\left(H_{1}(N)\right)$ (c.f. Definition 3.4), that is $\operatorname{dc}_{G}\left(H_{2}(N)\right)^{0}=\operatorname{dc}_{G}\left(H_{1}(N)\right)^{0}$.

Then, the theory $T$ does not have geometric elimination of imaginaries, even after adding constants for the model $\mathcal{N}$ to the language.

Proof. By Lemma 3.9, the second part of Condition (3) yields an element $h$ of $H_{2}(M)$ that is $\mathcal{L}_{0}$-generic over $N$ in $\operatorname{dc}_{G}\left(H_{1}(N)\right)$. Let $g$ in $H_{1}$ be a realization of $p$ with $g \perp_{N}^{\mathcal{L}} h$. Since $T$ is stable and $H_{2} \subset \operatorname{Stab}_{H_{1}}^{r}(p)$, it follows that $g \cdot h$ is a realization of $p$ and in particular that $\operatorname{acl}_{\mathcal{L}}(g \cdot h, N) \subset \operatorname{acl}_{0}(g \cdot h, N)$. Hence, all conditions of Lemma 4.1 are satisfied.

Suppose for a contradiction that the canonical parameter of the coset $g \cdot H_{2}$ is interalgebraic over $N$ with a real tuple. Lemma 4.1 then yields that $\operatorname{Stab}_{H_{1}}^{r}(g / N)=\operatorname{Stab}_{H_{1}}^{r}(p)$ is contained in $H_{2}$, which contradicts Condition (3).

If the group $H_{1}$ in Proposition 4.3 is connected and $p$ a generic type of $H_{1}$, the subgroup $H_{2}$ in Condition (3) is simply an infinite index subgroup of $H_{1}$. This observation yields the following criterion for simple theories.

Proposition 4.4. Consider a simple $\mathcal{L}$-theory $T$ with $T_{0}^{\forall} \subset T$ for the stable $\mathcal{L}_{0}$-theory $T_{0}$ (see Section 1). Inside a sufficiently saturated model $\mathcal{M}_{0}$ of $T_{0}$ choose $\mathcal{M} \models T$ also sufficiently saturated.

Suppose that there is an $\mathcal{L}_{0}$-definable group $(G, \cdot)$ in $M_{0}$ and an $\mathcal{L}$-definable subset $H_{1}$ of $M$ such that $\left(H_{1}, \cdot\right)$ is a group in $\mathcal{M}$; both $G$ and $H_{1}$ being defined over a small elementary substructure $\mathcal{N}$ of $\mathcal{M}$. Assume further that:
(1) For tuples $\bar{a}$ and $\bar{b}$ from $M$ holds $\bar{a} \perp_{\mathcal{N}}^{\mathcal{L}} \bar{b} \quad \Rightarrow \quad \bar{a} \perp_{\mathcal{N}}^{0} \bar{b}$.
(2') For every $\mathcal{L}$-generic $g$ in $G(M)$ over $N$ we have that $\operatorname{acl}_{\mathcal{L}}(g, N) \subset \operatorname{acl}_{0}(g, N)$.
(3') There is an infinite $\mathcal{L}(N)$-definable subgroup $H_{2}$ of $H_{1}$ of infinite index such that the definable hull $\operatorname{dc}_{G}\left(H_{2}(N)\right)$ is principal in the definable hull $\operatorname{dc}_{G}\left(H_{1}(N)\right)$ (c.f. Definition 3.4), that is $\operatorname{dc}_{G}\left(H_{2}(N)\right)^{0}=\operatorname{dc}_{G}\left(H_{1}(N)\right)^{0}$.

Then, the theory $T$ does not have geometric elimination of imaginaries, even after adding constants for the model $\mathcal{N}$ to the language.

Proof. By Lemma 3.9 there exists an element $h$ of $H_{2}(M)$ that is $\mathcal{L}_{0}$-generic over $N$ in $\operatorname{dc}_{G}\left(H_{1}(N)\right)$. Work in $\mathcal{M}$ and choose an element $g$ of $H_{1}$ that is $\mathcal{L}$-generic over $N h$. In particular, $g \perp_{\mathcal{N}}^{\mathcal{L}} h$ and thus $g \cdot h$ is also generic in $H_{1}$ over $N$. Condition (2') yields that $\operatorname{acl}_{\mathcal{L}}(g, N) \subset \operatorname{acl}_{0}(g, N)$ as well as $\operatorname{acl}_{\mathcal{L}}(g \cdot h, N) \subset \operatorname{acl}_{0}(g \cdot h, N)$

We will again show that the canonical parameter of the coset $g \cdot H_{2}$ in $H_{1}$ cannot be geometrically eliminated: Otherwise, by Lemma 4.1, we have that $\operatorname{Stab}_{H_{1}}^{r}(g / N) \subset H_{2}$. As

$g$ is $\mathcal{L}$-generic in $H_{1}$, this stabilizer equals the connected component $H_{1}^{0}$ which contradicts that $H_{2}$ has infinite index in $H_{1}$.
Remark 4.5. Most parts of the proofs of the two previous criteria were carried out in the stable theory $T_{0}$. The stability or simplicity of $T$ was mainly used to choose an appropriate element $g$. Indeed, suppose that $T$ is an arbitrary $\mathcal{L}$-theory controlled by $T_{0}$ such that Condition (3') of Proposition 4.4 holds. Assuming moreover that $\operatorname{acl}_{\mathcal{L}}(g, N) \subset \operatorname{acl}_{0}(g, N)$ for every $g$ in $H_{1}$ and that there exists an independence relation $\perp^{*}$ in $T$ satisfying full existence with $\perp^{*} \Rightarrow \perp^{0}$ over $N$ (instead of (1)), the proof of Lemma 4.1 yields that all cosets of $H_{2}$ are $N$-definable which is a contradiction by a straightforward compactness argument.

In particular, the criterion applies to some non-simple theories; for example d'Elbée's $N S O P_{1}$-theory $A C F G_{p}$ presented in [10, p.16], the model companion of the theory of algebraically closed fields in positive characteristic with a predicate for an additive subgroup.

In the proofs of Proposition 4.3 and 4.4 we only used that $\operatorname{dc}_{G}\left(H_{2}(N)\right)^{0}=\operatorname{dc}_{G}\left(H_{1}(N)\right)^{0}$ to find an element $h$ in $H_{2}$ such that for $g$ in $H_{1}$ (generic or realizing the type $p$ ) with $g \perp^{\mathcal{L}}{ }_{N} h$ holds $g \perp^{0}{ }_{N} g \cdot h$. We will now see that in the case of $g$ being generic in $H_{1}$ and $T$ stable, the above gives an equivalent condition. In order to do so, we need to recall a result of Ziegler, originally stated for abelian groups in [33]. For the purpose of this note, we will use a generalized reformulation given by Blossier, Martin-Pizarro and Wagner in $[5]$.
Fact 4.6. (c.f. [5, Lemme 1.2]) Let $(G, \cdot)$ be a type-definable group in a stable theory and suppose there are elements $g$ and $h$ of $G$ such that $g, h$ and $g \cdot h$ are pairwise independent over a set $A$. Then $h$ is generic in the coset $\operatorname{Stab}_{G}(\operatorname{stp}(h / A)) \cdot h$ and moreover $g \cdot \operatorname{Stab}_{G}(\operatorname{stp}(h / A)) \cdot g^{-1}=\operatorname{Stab}_{G}(\operatorname{stp}(g / A))$.
Lemma 4.7. Suppose that $T, T_{0},(G, \cdot)$ and $\left(H_{1}, \cdot\right)$ are as in Proposition 4.3 and let $\left(H_{2}, \cdot\right)$ be an $\mathcal{L}(N)$-definable subgroup of $H_{1}$. Moreover suppose that Property ( $\left.\approx^{\star}\right)$ (c.f. Section 1) holds. The following are equivalent:
(i) The definable hull $\operatorname{dc}_{G}\left(H_{2}(N)\right)$ is principal in the definable hull $\operatorname{dc}_{G}\left(H_{1}(N)\right)$ (see Condition (3') of Proposition 4.3).
(ii) There exist elements $h$ in $H_{2}$ and $g$ in $H_{1}$ such that $g$ is $\mathcal{L}$-generic in $H_{1}$ over $N$ with $g \perp^{\mathcal{L}}{ }_{N} h$ and $g \perp^{0}{ }_{N} g \cdot h$.
Proof. First note that Property ( $\left.\approx^{\star}\right)$ yields Condition (1) of Proposition 4.3 (by Fact 1.5). The proof of Lemma 4.1 (using Lemma 3.9) then shows that (i) implies (ii).

On the other hand suppose that (ii) holds. Let $h$ in $H_{2}$ and $g$ in $H_{1}$ generic over $N, h$ be as in the assumption. Since $g \perp^{\mathcal{L}}{ }_{N} h$, we obtain $g \cdot h \perp^{\mathcal{L}}{ }_{N} h$ by genericity of $g$. As Condition (1) holds, the $\mathcal{L}$-independences imply that

$$
g \perp_{N}^{0} h \quad \text { and } \quad g \cdot h \perp_{N}^{0} h
$$

From our assumption, it follows that $g, h$ and $g \cdot h$ are pairwise $\mathcal{L}_{0}$-independent elements of $\operatorname{dc}_{G}\left(H_{1}(M)\right)=: \tilde{G}$ (for simplicity of notation).

Recall that all $\mathcal{L}_{0}$-types are stationary over $N$ by Fact 1.3. By Fact 4.6, the type $\operatorname{tp}_{0}(h / N)$ is hence generic in a coset of its stabilizer and the latter is a conjugate of $\operatorname{Stab}_{\tilde{G}}\left(\operatorname{tp}_{0}(g / N)\right)$. By Remark 3.8, the element $g$ is $\mathcal{L}_{0}$-generic over $N$ in $\tilde{G}$ and thus $\operatorname{Stab}_{\tilde{G}}\left(\operatorname{tp}_{0}(g / N)\right)=\tilde{G}^{0}$. Since the connected component is a normal subgroup of $\tilde{G}$, we have $\operatorname{Stab}_{\tilde{G}}\left(\operatorname{tp}_{0}(h / N)\right)=\tilde{G}^{0}$.

In particular, the element $h$ of $H_{2}(M)$ is $\mathcal{L}_{0}$-generic over $N$ in $\tilde{G}=\operatorname{dc}_{G}\left(H_{1}(M)\right)$. By Lemma 3.9 this is equivalent to (i) (using that $\operatorname{dc}_{G}\left(H_{1}(M)\right)=\operatorname{dc}_{G}\left(H_{1}(N)\right)$ by Remark 3.7).
4.1. Examples. Since Lemma 4.1 was inspired by Delon's proof for separably closed fields of infinite degree of imperfection, the criterion in Proposition 4.3 or 4.4 can easily be applied to this theory. Moreover, these propositions yield a new proof of non-elimination for beautiful pairs of theories with a definable groups.

Corollary 4.8. The following theories do not have geometric elimination of imaginaries even after adding constants for a small submodel to the language:
a) The theory $S C F_{p}^{\infty}$ of separably closed fields of infinite degree of imperfection.
b) The theory $T_{0} P$ of beautiful pairs of a stable $\mathcal{L}_{0}$-theory $T_{0}$ (with elimination of quantifiers and imaginaries) where $T_{0}$ does not have the finite cover property and an infinite group is definable in $T_{0}$.

In particular the theories $A C F_{p} P, D C F_{0} P$ and $S C F_{p}^{e} P$ of beautiful pairs of algebraically closed fields, differential closed fields in characteristic 0 resp. separably closed fields of finite degree of imperfection do not have geometric elimination of imaginaries; yet types over real algebraically closed sets are stationary.

Proof. The desired statement follows from Proposition 4.4 after checking that all conditions hold. (We could also use Proposition 4.3, but since our group $H_{1}$ is connected in both cases, this amounts to checking the same conditions.)
a) As in Section 2, we consider $T=S C F_{p}^{\infty}$ in the language $\mathcal{L}=\left\{0,1,+,-,-,^{-1}\right\}$ and $T_{0}=A C F_{p}$ with $\mathcal{L}_{0}=\mathcal{L}$. Given models $\mathcal{M}_{0} \models T_{0}$ and $\mathcal{M} \models T$ as in Proposition 4.4, we put $G=\left(M_{0},+\right)$ the additive group of the algebraically closed field, and $H_{1}=(M,+)$ the additive group of $M$ itself.
(1): This follows immediately from the characterization of independence given by Srour in [26] (see Section 2).
(2'): Note that an element of $M$ is additively generic over $N$ if it does not lie in the field $M^{p} \cdot N$. In particular, the extension $M / N(g)$ of fields is separable which by the characterization of algebraic closure in separably closed fields yields Condition (2').
(3'): Set $H_{2}=M^{P}$ the subfield of $p$-powers which is by definition a subgroup of infinite index. Since $A C F_{p}$ is strongly minimal and $H_{2}(N)$ and $H_{1}(N)$ are infinite subgroups of $\left(M_{0},+\right)$, it follows that $\operatorname{dc}_{G}\left(H_{2}(N)\right)=\left(M_{0},+\right)=\operatorname{dc}_{G}\left(H_{1}(N)\right)$.
b) Let $T_{0}$ be a stable nfcp theory and consider the theory $T=T_{0} P$ of beautiful pairs of $T_{0}$ as in Section 2 in the language $\mathcal{L}=\mathcal{L}_{0} \cup\{P\}$. Choose $\mathcal{M} \models T$ sufficiently saturated, then by definition $\mathcal{M} \models T_{0}$ (so we can put $\mathcal{M}_{0}=\mathcal{M}$ ). By assumption, there exist an $\mathcal{L}_{0}$-definable group $(G, \cdot)$ in $T_{0}$ which we may assume to be defined over $P(M)$ by

saturation of the predicate. We choose a small elementary substructure $\mathcal{N}$ containing the necessary parameters and will now show that $T$ does not eliminate imaginaries in $\mathcal{L}(N)$. For simplicity we assume again that $G=M_{0}$. Put $H_{1}=G$ (since $M_{0}=M$ ).
(1): This is immediate from the characterization of independence in [1] (see Section 2).
(2'): By the characterization of independence, the element $g$ of $H_{1}$ is generic in $T=T_{0} P$ over $N$ if and only if it is generic in $T_{0}$ over $N, P(M)$. In particular, for $g$ generic in $H_{1}$ over $N$ holds

$$
g \underset{P(N)}{\perp^{0}} N, P(M)
$$

which implies that the substructure $\langle g, N\rangle_{\mathcal{L}}$ is $P$-independent. This yields Condition (2') by the characterization of the algebraic closure in [22, Lemma 2.6].
(3'): Let $H_{2}=G(M) \cap P(M)$ be the $\mathcal{L}(N)$-definable subgroup of $P$-points of $G$. Note that the index is infinite by saturation. Moreover, since $H_{1}(M)=G$, we immediately have $\operatorname{dc}_{G}\left(H_{1}(N)\right)=\operatorname{dc}_{G}\left(H_{1}(M)\right)=G$ by Remark 3.7.

Similarly $\operatorname{dc}_{G}(H_{2}(N))=\operatorname{dc}_{G}\left(H_{2}(M)\right)$. Now, the subgroup $H_{2}(M)$ is a subset of $P(M)$. By Fact 3.3 (1), we have that $\operatorname{dc}_{G}\left(H_{2}(M)\right)$ is given by the $M$-points of $\operatorname{dc}_{G(P(M))}\left(H_{2}(M)\right)$ and hence equals $G$ as $H_{2}(M)=G(P(M))$. Thus Condition (3') holds.

Note that the result for $S C F_{p}^{\infty}$ answers negatively Yoneda's question in [32, Question 3.1 (4)] whether $S C F_{p}^{\infty}$ has geometric elimination of imaginaries in the language of fields.

We will now present an application of Proposition 4.3 with a non-generic type $p$ in Condition (2): A straightforward adaption of the proof of Messmer and Wood [19, Remark 4.3] yields the failure of non-elimination in a broader class of differential fields.

A differential field $K$ of positive characteristic $p$ is separably differentially closed if $K$ is existentially closed in all separable differential extensions. The differential degree of imperfection is the cardinality of a $p$-basis of $C_{K}$ over $K^{p}$. Ino and León Sanchez introduced the theory $S D C F_{p, e}$ of separably differentially closed fields of fixed differential degree of imperfection $e$ in $\mathbb{N} \cup\{\infty\}$ in [17] and showed completeness and stability. The case $e=0$ yields the theory $D C F_{p}$ which was already studied by Wood in [29, 30, 31] and Shelah in [25] as the characteristic $p$ analogue of $D C F_{0}$.

We consider $T=S D C F_{p, e}$ in the language $\mathcal{L}=\{0,1,+,-, \cdot,^{-1}, D\}$ where $D$ is a unary function symbol interpreted as the derivation. Note that for every $e$, the theory $T$ contains the universal part of the theory $T_{0}=A C F_{p}$ in the language $\mathcal{L}_{0}$ of fields.

Fact 4.9. Let $K \models T$ and let $k_{0}$ be a differential subfield such that the extension of fields $K / k_{0}$ is separable, then $\operatorname{acl}_{\mathcal{L}}\left(k_{0}\right)=\operatorname{acl}_{0}\left(k_{0}\right) \cap K$.

For $e=\infty$ this follows directly from [17, Lemma 4.8] (using [17, Lemma 3.8]). The same works for $e$ finite since $T$ can be viewed by the quantifier elimination result in [14, Section 6.1] as the model completion of an almost derivation-like theory (c.f. [17, Remark 3.10]).

Lemma 4.10. For every $e$ in $\mathbb{N} \cup\{\infty\}$, the theory $S D C F_{p, e}$ does not have geometric elimination of imaginaries even after adding constants for a small submodel to the language.

Proof. As above let $T$ be the theory $S D C F_{p, e}$ and $T_{0}=A C F_{p}$. Given models $\mathcal{M}_{0} \models T_{0}$ and $\mathcal{M} \models T$ as in Proposition 4.3, we put $G=\left(M_{0} \backslash\{0\}, \cdot\right)$ the multiplicative group of the algebraically closed field and $H_{1}=(M \backslash\{0\}, \cdot)$ the multiplicative group of $M$. We are done by Proposition 4.3 after checking that the conditions hold.
(1): This condition follows from Fact 1.5 since Property ( $\#$ ) is satisfied in every theory of fields (see Remark 1.2).
(2): Let $p$ be the type of an element $g$ with $D(g)=g$ and such that $g$ does not lie in the field $C_{M} \cdot N$ (i.e. $g$ is $p$-independent over $N$ ). Note that these conditions define a complete type by the quantifier elimination results of Ino and León Sánchez [14, Theorem 6.3 and 6.6]. For any realization $g$ of $p$, the field $N(g)$ is by definition a differential subfield of $M$ with $M / N(g)$ separable. We hence obtain Condition (2) from Fact 4.9 .
(3): An easy computation shows that $\operatorname{Stab}_{H_{1}}^{r}(p)=C_{M} \backslash\{0\}$. We thus put $H_{2}=M^{p^{2}} \backslash\{0\}$ which is for all $e$ a proper subgroup (since $M^{p} \subset C_{M}$ ). As in Corollary 4.8 we have $\operatorname{dc}_{G}\left(H_{2}(N)\right)=\left(M_{0} \backslash\{0\}, \cdot\right)=\operatorname{dc}_{G}\left(H_{1}(N)\right)$ by strongly minimality of $A C F_{p}$.
For the case $e=\infty$ we could have alternatively done the same proof as for $S C F_{p}^{\infty}$ (but with $H_{1}=C_{M}$ instead of $M$ ).
Remark 4.11. In fact, our proof of stationarity over real algebraically closed sets from Theorem 1.10 also applies to $S D C F_{p, \infty}$. Similar to the case of $S C F_{p}^{\infty}$, an $\mathcal{L}$-substructure $A$ of $\mathcal{M}$ is strong if the field extension $M / A$ is separable. Using the characterization of independence given by León Sánchez and Mohamed in [17] with respect to independence in $S C F_{p}^{\infty}$, the other properties also follow.

Actually, an inspection of the proof of [17, Theorem 2.14] shows that stationarity transfers from $S C F_{p}^{\infty}$ to $S D C F_{p, \infty}$ over arbitrary $\mathcal{L}$-algebraically closed sets (and not just models). Hence, types over real algebraically closed sets in $S D C F_{p, \infty}$ are stationary.

query: Is $x_{\min}$ a minimum transaction amount in the Pareto model for transactions?
golden_answer: Yes, $x_{\min}$ is the minimum transaction amount such that $T_{i, l} \geq x_{\min}$.
source_title: On-Chain Credit Risk Score in Decentralized Finance
source_text:
# On-Chain Credit Risk Score in Decentralized Finance 

The Pareto distribution is a suitable model for transaction data, as it captures the presence of infrequent, high-value transactions within a large number of smaller transactions. We model the transaction amount $T_{i, l}$ for the $i$-th wallet's $l$-th transaction as:

$$
T_{i, l} \sim \operatorname{Pareto}\left(\alpha, x_{\min }\right)
$$

where:

- $\alpha>1$ is the shape parameter, controlling the "heaviness" of the distribution tail,
- $x_{\min }$ is the minimum transaction amount, such that $T_{i, l} \geq x_{\min }$.

This distribution choice allows for tractable calculations of expectation and variance while realistically modeling the likelihood of large transaction values, which are essential for assessing risk.

query: Is it possible for an agent to have zero swap regret using a contextual no-swap-regret algorithm?
golden_answer: No, but a contextual no-swap-regret algorithm guarantees that the agent is at most \(\frac{\operatorname{CSReg}(T)}{T}\) worse compared to using an optimal strategy.

source_text:
# 3.3 Agent's No-Swap-Regret Learning: Upper Bound on Principal's Utility 

As we mentioned in Section 2.2, the fact that the principal moves after the learning agent in each round gives the principal a possibility to exploit the agent to do better than $U^{*}$. However, exploiting the agent in a single round may cause the agent to learn a bad strategy for the principal in later rounds. It turns out that, if the agent's learning algorithm satisfies the contextual no-swap-regret property, then the principal cannot exploit the agent in the long run. Formally:
Theorem 3.4. Against a contextual no-swap-regret learning agent, the principal cannot obtain utility more than $\frac{1}{T} \mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{t=1}^{T} u\left(x^{t}, a^{t}\right)\right] \leq \overline{\mathrm{OBJ}}{ }^{\mathcal{R}}\left(\frac{\mathrm{CSReg}(T)}{T}\right)$, even if the principal knows the agent's learning algorithm and chooses $\pi^{t}$ based on $\rho^{t}$.

Before presenting the full proof of this theorem, we give the high level idea of the proof. The key idea is to think of the signal $s^{t} \sim \pi^{t}$ from the principal and the action $a^{t} \sim \rho^{t}\left(s^{t}\right)$ recommended by the agent's learning algorithm together as a joint signal $\left(s^{t}, a^{t}\right)$ from some hypothetical signaling scheme $\pi^{\prime}$. In response to $\pi^{\prime}$, the agent takes the action $a^{t}$ recommended by the algorithm, namely using the mapping $\left(s^{t}, a^{t}\right) \mapsto a^{t}$ as his strategy. A contextual no-swap-regret algorithm guarantees that the agent is at most $\frac{\operatorname{CSReg}(T)}{T}$ worse compared to using the strategy $d^{*}: S \times A \rightarrow A$ that best responds to $\pi^{\prime}$. So, the agent's overall strategy is a $\frac{\operatorname{CSReg}(T)}{T}$-approximate best response to $\pi^{\prime}$. This limits the principal's overall utility to be at most $\overline{\mathrm{OBJ}}{ }^{\mathcal{R}}\left(\frac{\operatorname{CSReg}(T)}{T}\right)$. See details below:
Proof. Let $p_{s}^{t}=\operatorname{Pr}\left[s^{t}=s\right]=\mathbb{E}\left[\mathbb{1}\left[s^{t}=s\right]\right]=\mathbb{E}\left[\pi_{s}^{t}\right]$ be the (unconditional) probability that signal $s \in S$ is sent in round $t$. Let $p_{a \mid s}^{t}=\operatorname{Pr}\left[a^{t}=a \mid s^{t}=s\right]$ be the probability that the agent's algorithm takes action $a$ conditioning on signal $s^{t}=s$ being sent in round $t$. Let $d: S \times A \rightarrow A$ be any deviation function for the agent. The agent's utility gain by deviation is upper bounded by the contextual swap-regret:

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \frac{\operatorname{CSReg}(T)}{T} \geq \frac{1}{T} \mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{t=1}^{T}\left(v\left(x^{t}, d\left(s^{t}, a^{t}\right)\right)-v\left(x^{t}, a^{t}\right)\right)\right] \\
& =\frac{1}{T} \sum_{t=1}^{T} \sum_{s \in S} p_{s}^{t} \sum_{a \in A} p_{a \mid s}^{t} \mathbb{E}_{x_{s}^{t} \mid s^{t}=s}\left[v\left(x_{s}^{t}, d(s, a)\right)-v\left(x_{s}^{t}, a\right)\right] \\
& =\frac{1}{T} \sum_{t=1}^{T} \sum_{s \in S} p_{s}^{t} \sum_{a \in A} p_{a \mid s}^{t}\left(v\left(\mathbb{E}\left[x_{s}^{t} \mid s^{t}=s\right], d(s, a)\right)-v\left(\mathbb{E}\left[x_{s}^{t} \mid s^{t}=s\right], a\right)\right) \quad \text { by linearity of } v(\cdot, a) \\
& =\sum_{s \in S} \sum_{a \in A} \frac{\sum_{j=1}^{T} p_{s}^{t} p_{a \mid s}^{j}}{T} \frac{1}{\sum_{j=1}^{T} p_{s}^{t} p_{a \mid s}^{j}} \sum_{t=1}^{T} p_{s}^{t} p_{a \mid s}^{j}\left(v\left(\mathbb{E}\left[x_{s}^{t} \mid s^{t}=s\right], d(s, a)\right)-v\left(\mathbb{E}\left[x_{s}^{t} \mid s^{t}=s\right], a\right)\right) \\
& =\sum_{s \in S} \sum_{a \in A} \frac{\sum_{j=1}^{T} p_{s}^{t} p_{a \mid s}^{j}}{T}\left[v\left(\frac{\sum_{t=1}^{T} p_{s}^{t} p_{a \mid s}^{t} \mathbb{E}\left[x_{s}^{t} \mid s^{t}=s\right]}{\sum_{j=1}^{T} p_{s}^{t} p_{a \mid s}^{j}}, d(s, a)\right)-v\left(\frac{\sum_{t=1}^{T} p_{s}^{t} p_{a \mid s}^{t} \mathbb{E}\left[x_{s}^{t} \mid s^{t}=s\right]}{\sum_{j=1}^{T} p_{s}^{t} p_{a \mid s}^{j}}, a\right)\right]
\end{aligned}
$$

Define $q_{s, a}=\frac{\sum_{j=1}^{T} p_{s}^{j} p_{a \mid s}^{j}}{T}$ and $y_{s, a}=\frac{\sum_{t=1}^{T} p_{s}^{t} p_{a \mid s}^{t} \mathbb{E}\left[x_{s}^{t} \mid s^{t}=s\right]}{\sum_{j=1}^{T} p_{s}^{j} p_{a \mid s}^{j}}$ $\in \mathcal{X}$. Then the above is equal to

$$
=\sum_{s \in S} \sum_{a \in A} q_{s, a}\left[v\left(y_{s, a}, d(s, a)\right)-v\left(y_{s, a}, a\right)\right]
$$

We note that $\sum_{s \in S} \sum_{a \in A} q_{s, a}=\frac{\sum_{j=1}^{T} \sum_{s \in S} \sum_{a \in A} p_{s}^{j} p_{a \mid s}^{j}}{T}=1$, so $q$ is a probability distribution over $S \times A$. And note that

$$
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{s, a \in S \times A} q_{s, a} y_{s, a} & =\sum_{s, a \in S \times A} \frac{1}{T} \sum_{t=1}^{T} p_{s}^{t} p_{a \mid s}^{t} \mathbb{E}\left[x_{s}^{t} \mid s^{t}=s\right]=\frac{1}{T} \sum_{t=1}^{T} \sum_{s \in S} p_{s}^{t} \mathbb{E}\left[x_{s}^{t} \mid s^{t}=s\right] \\
& =\frac{1}{T} \sum_{t=1}^{T} \sum_{s \in S} \mathbb{E}\left[\mathbb{1}\left[s^{t}=s \mid x_{s}^{t}\right]=\frac{1}{T} \sum_{t=1}^{T} \mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{s \in S} \mathbb{1}\left[s^{t}=s\right] x_{s}^{t}\right]=\frac{1}{T} \sum_{t=1}^{T} \mathbb{E}\left[x^{t}\right]\right. \\
& =\frac{1}{T} \sum_{t=1}^{T} \mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{s \in S} \pi_{s}^{t} x_{s}^{t}\right] \in \mathcal{C} \quad \text { because } \sum_{s \in S} \pi_{s}^{t} x_{s}^{t} \in \mathcal{C}
\end{aligned}
$$

This means that $\pi^{\prime}=\left\{\left(q_{s, a}, y_{s, a}\right)\right\}_{(s, a) \in S \times A}$ defines a valid principal strategy with the larger signal space $S \times A .{ }^{3}$ Then, we note that (10) is the difference between the agent's expected utility under principal strategy $\pi^{\prime}$ when responding using strategy $d: S \times A \rightarrow A$ and using the strategy that maps signal $(s, a)$ to action $a$. And (10) is upper bounded by $\frac{\operatorname{CSReg}(T)}{T}$ by (9):

$$
(10)=V\left(\pi^{\prime}, d\right)-V\left(\pi^{\prime},(s, a) \mapsto a\right) \leq \frac{\operatorname{CSReg}(T)}{T}, \quad \forall d: S \times A \rightarrow A
$$

In particular, this holds when $d$ is the agent's best-responding strategy. This means that the agent strategy $(s, a) \mapsto a$ is a $\left(\frac{\operatorname{CSReg}(T)}{T}\right)$-best-response to $\pi^{\prime}$. So, the principal's expected utility is upper bounded by the utility in the approximate-best-response model:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{1}{T} \mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{t=1}^{T} u\left(x^{t}, a^{t}\right)\right] & =\frac{1}{T} \sum_{t=1}^{T} \sum_{s \in S} p_{s}^{t} \sum_{a \in A} p_{a \mid s}^{t} v\left(\mathbb{E}\left[x_{s}^{t} \mid s^{t}=s\right], a\right) \\
& =\sum_{s \in S} \sum_{a \in A} q_{s, a} u\left(y_{s, a}, a\right)=U\left(\pi^{\prime},(s, a) \rightarrow a\right) \leq \overline{\operatorname{OBJ}}^{\mathcal{R}}\left(\frac{\operatorname{CSReg}(T)}{T}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

query: What is the purpose of using jackknife samples in halo profile estimation?
golden_answer: Jackknife samples are used to evaluate the estimation error in halo profile estimation.
source_title:
FAST drift scan survey for HI intensity mapping: simulation on hunting
  HI filament with pairwise stacking
source_text:
## A.1. Jackknife error for halo profile estimation

To assess the accuracy of the halo profile estimation, we use jackknife samples (see e.g. McIntosh (2016)) to evaluate the estimation error. As described in Section 3, the full galaxy pair sample is divided into 153 sub-samples and construct the 2DPSM, individually. These 153 2D-PSMs are then averaged to form the final 2D-PSM, which is used for the rest analysis, including the halo profile estimation. The error in the halo profile estimation is evaluated as,

$$
\sigma_{\mathrm{JK}}=\sqrt{\frac{n-1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n}\left[\hat{\theta}_{(i)}-\hat{\theta}_{(\cdot)}\right]^{2}}
$$

where $n=153$ is the number of jackknife samples, $\hat{\theta}_{(i)}$ is the halo profile estimated without the $i$-th sample, and $\hat{\theta}_{(\cdot)}$ is the empirical average of these halo profile estimations,

$$
\hat{\theta}_{(\cdot)}=\frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \hat{\theta}_{(i)}
$$

The estimation error evaluated using the filament-only Hi sky map is shown in Figure 19, where the left panel shows the errors of each 2D-PSM pixel and the right panel shows the histogram distribution of pixel errors. The errors are significantly amplified near the halo center and the edges, since few pixels are included for halo-profile estimation. We use the mean of the errors, i.e. $\left\langle\sigma_{\mathrm{JK}}\right\rangle=0.01 \mu \mathrm{~K}$, as the reference for the estimation uncertainty.
The jackknife error represents the variance raised from the scattering of individual halo profile and it is negligible compared to the absolute filament brightness temperature $T_{\mathrm{f}}=0.29 \pm 0.09 \mu \mathrm{~K}$ (as listed in Table 2).

query: What theorem allows thinking of a randomized allocation as a bistochastic matrix?
golden_answer: The Birkhoff-von Neumann Theorem.
source_title: Unambiguous Efficiency of Random Allocations
source_text:
# 2 The Model 

Let $\boldsymbol{A}$ be a set of at least three objects and $\boldsymbol{N}$ be a set of exactly as many agents. When there are fewer than three objects the issues discussed in this paper become trivial so we omit that case. Let $\boldsymbol{\Delta}(\boldsymbol{A})$ be the set of lotteries over $A$. As it does not cause confusion, we identify degenerate lotteries in $\Delta(A)$ with $A$ itself. So, for each $a \in A$, we denote the lottery that places probability one on $a$ by $a$. We denote a generic lottery that agent $i$ might consume by $\pi_{i} \in \Delta(A)$ and its support by $\operatorname{supp}\left(\pi_{i}\right)$. Each agent has preferences over the lottery that they receive.

Assumption 1. Agents' preferences are represented by utility functions, with $u_{i}: \Delta(A) \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ representing agent i's preferences.

We denote by $\mathcal{U}$ the universe of possible utility functions for an agent. Fixing the set of agents and the objects to assign to them, an economy is described by a profile of agents' preferences $u \in \mathcal{U}^{N}$.

We are interested in settings where agents are mapped to objects so that each agent consumes a unique object and each object is consumed by a single agent. We consider the possibility of randomizing over such bijections. By the Birkhoff-von Neumann Theorem, we can think of a (randomized) allocation as a bistochastic matrix (Birkhoff, 1946; von Neumann, 1953). That is, an allocation $\pi$ specifies a lottery over $A$ for each agent $i \in N$ such that for each $a \in A, \sum_{i \in N} \pi_{i a}=1$. Denote by $\Pi$ the set of all such allocations.

Given that an economy describes each agent's complete preferences over allocations, the definition of efficiency is straightforward. An allocation $\pi \in \Pi$ is efficient at $\boldsymbol{u}$ if there is no alternative allocation $\pi^{\prime} \in \Pi$ that makes at least one agent better off without making any other agent worse off. Formally, there is no $\pi^{\prime} \in \Pi$ such that for some $i \in N$, $u_{i}\left(\pi_{i}^{\prime}\right)>u_{i}\left(\pi_{i}\right)$ and for no $i \in N, u_{i}\left(\pi_{i}^{\prime}\right)<u_{i}\left(\pi_{i}\right)$.

query: Can Kohn's theorem be bypassed to couple LLL to a constant electric field, and if so, how?
golden_answer: Yes, it can be bypassed via an external potential for electrons such as a confining potential or disorder.
source_title:
Theory of fractional quantum Hall liquids coupled to quantum light and
  emergent graviton-polaritons
source_text:
## E. Role of gradients

In a clean system, gradients are fundamental to couple the cavity field to electrons within the LLL. This is a consequence of the celebrated Kohn's theorem [46], whose corollary is that a uniform field can only couple to the cyclotron mode [27], generating transitions among different Landau levels. In view of that we now consider a further simplified cavity mode by considering a linear expansion $f_{c}(x)=C_{0}+C_{1} x$ and leave the discussion of more complicated modes for Sec. VI. For this particular shape of the mode function, the LLL matrix elements are:

$$
\chi_{k}=\frac{e E_{c}}{\omega_{c}}\left(\frac{l_{B}^{2}}{4} C_{1}+C_{0}\left(k l_{B}^{2}-x_{0}\right)+\frac{1}{2} C_{1}\left(k l_{B}^{2}-x_{0}\right)^{2}\right)
$$

with $x_{0}$ the origin for the integration in Eq. (12). In the Coulomb gauge $\hat{\tilde{H}}^{\text {coul }}$, the matrix elements of the coupling can be readily understood by the dressing of
$\hat{H}_{\text {int }}$ and $\hat{H}_{0}$. For the interaction term $\hat{H}_{\text {int }}$, we have that the four-body terms $\hat{c}_{k_{1}}^{\dagger} \hat{c}_{k_{2}}^{\dagger} \hat{c}_{k_{3}} \hat{c}_{k_{4}}$ get dressed with the following phase factor:

$$
\exp \left[i\left(\hat{a}+\hat{a}^{\dagger}\right)\left(\chi_{k_{1}}+\chi_{k_{2}}-\chi_{k_{3}}-\chi_{k_{4}}\right)\right]
$$

However, from momentum conservation along $y$, we have that $k_{1}+k_{2}=k_{3}+k_{4}$, and for the explicit expression of $\chi_{k}$ the dressing phase can be written as:

$$
\exp \left[i \frac{e E_{c} C_{1} l_{B}^{4}}{\omega_{c}}\left(\hat{a}+\hat{a}^{\dagger}\right)\left(k_{1}-k_{4}\right)\left(k_{4}-k_{2}\right)\right]
$$

The other important cavity-induced effect is the presence of a vacuum-induced Stark shift $\mu_{k}$ which, in the case of a simple gradient and up to overall constants, reads:

$$
\mu_{k}=\frac{1}{\omega_{c}}\left[e l_{B} E_{c}\left(C_{0}+C_{1} k l_{B}^{2}\right)\right]^{2}
$$

At this point, we highlight two important properties:

- First, as anticipated from the Kohn's theorem [46], the constant part of the electric field $\left(C_{0}\right)$ is decoupled;
- Second, an uniform gradient of the electric field generates a uniform light-matter coupling plus a non-uniform single particle potential.

The latter follows by the fact that in Eq. (43) only differences in momenta, hence relative distance on $x$, appear. Alternatively, when sticking to the dipole gauge formulation, one can see that, single-particle potentials aside, the constant part of the field $\left(C_{0}\right)$ only couples to conserved quantities, such as the number of electrons and momentum along $y$. In contrast, the gradient $\left(C_{1}\right)$ couples to the $x x$-component of the quadrupole moment operator, $\hat{Q}^{x x} \propto \sum_{k k^{\prime}} \int \mathrm{d}^{2} r x^{2} \psi_{k}^{*}(\boldsymbol{r}) \psi_{k^{\prime}}(\boldsymbol{r}) \hat{c}_{k^{\prime}}^{\dagger} \hat{c}_{k^{\prime}}$, associated to electrons in the LLL [48].

Another way to avoid Kohn's restriction and actually couple the LLL to a constant electric field is via the presence of an external potential for the electrons. Either a confining potential [79] or disorder will do the job, realizing however quite different scenarios. A confining potential on $x$ will have a dominant effect at the edges where its variation are stronger while disorder will contribute to bulk properties [80]. These effects can be important in actual experimental realization but go beyond the scope of this work.

query: Is interpretability an advantage of using the geometric mean in path planning algorithm evaluation?
golden_answer: Yes.
source_title:
LLM-A*: Large Language Model Enhanced Incremental Heuristic Search on
  Path Planning
source_text:
## D. 3 Advantages

Using the geometric mean of ratios offers several benefits in the context of evaluating path planning algorithms:

1. Sensitivity to Relative Changes: The geometric mean is sensitive to the relative differences between performance measures, making it suitable for comparing ratios.
2. Mitigation of Outliers: Unlike the arithmetic mean, the geometric mean minimizes the impact of extreme values or outliers, providing a more stable and representative metric.
3. Interpretability: The geometric mean allows for easy interpretation of performance improvements or deteriorations. A geometric mean greater than 1 indicates that, on average, the proposed algorithm performs better than the baseline, while a value less than 1 suggests poorer performance.
4. Scalability: The geometric mean naturally scales with multiplicative factors, making it appropriate for comparing algorithms across different scales or units of measurement.

golden_answer: Yes, the disk temperature profile largely overestimates the flux longward of $4 \mu \mathrm{m}$.

Unveiling two deeply embedded young protostars in the S68N Class 0
  protostellar core with JWST/NIRSpec
source_text:
### 5.1. Modeling setup

We model the NC's source spectrum in two separate steps. Firstly, we model the observed flux between 1.9 and $2.45 \mu \mathrm{~m}$ with the following model (adopted from Greene et al. (2018)):

$$
\begin{aligned}
& F_{\lambda}=\left[F_{\star, \lambda}\left(T_{\star, \text { eff }}, \log g,[\mathrm{Fe} / \mathrm{H}]\right) \Omega_{\star}+\right. \\
& \left.\int_{R_{\mathrm{t}, \text { disk }}}^{R_{\max }} B_{\lambda}\left(T_{\mathrm{t}, \text { disk }} \sqrt{\frac{R_{\mathrm{t}, \text { disk }}}{r}}\right) d \Omega_{\text {disk }}(r)\right] \times 10^{-0.4 A_{K}\left(\frac{\lambda}{A_{K}}\right)^{-\alpha}}
\end{aligned}
$$

where $F_{\star, \lambda}\left(T_{\star, \text { eff }}, \log g,[\mathrm{Fe} / \mathrm{H}]\right)$ is the flux from the protostellar photosphere of effective temperature $T_{\star, \text { eff }}$ surface gravity $\log g$ and metallicity $[\mathrm{Fe} / \mathrm{H}]$ (that we restrict to the solar value), $\Omega_{\star}$ is the surface solid angle of the photosphere,
$B_{\lambda}\left(T_{\text {disk }}(r)\right) d \Omega_{\text {disk }}(r)$ is the disk temperature profile modeling the $K$-band continuum emission with $\Omega_{\text {disk }}(r)$ for the disk solid angle at the radius $r$ and $T_{\text {disk }}(r)=T_{\mathrm{t}, \text { disk }} \sqrt{R_{\mathrm{t}, \text { disk }} / r}$ the temperature profile as a function of radius, $A_{K}$ is the effective $K$-band extinction with wavelength dependence $\left(\lambda / \lambda_{K}\right)^{\alpha}$ (where $\lambda_{K}$ is $2.2 \mu \mathrm{~m}$, the $K$-band effective wavelength). We fix $\alpha$ to 1.54 to match the extinction law from Pontoppidan et al. (2024) used throughout this paper. We fix $R_{\max }$ to 10 AU , but this parameter does not influence much the fitting. Greene et al. (2018) performed a first model of this object, using however relative flux-calibrated Keck NIRSPEC data of spectral resolution $\simeq 1000$. Our JWST NIRSpec data are flux calibrated, more sensitive, and of higher spectral resolution, which allows us to derive more physical parameters. We turn the star and disk solid angles into actual emitting radii, using the distance adopted for the core of 445 pc (assuming an emission of $R$ in radius at a distance $d$, we have $\Omega=\pi R^{2} / d^{2}$ ).
We restrain this model exploration to the $1.9-2.45 \mu \mathrm{~m}$ spectral region in order to minimize any wavelength depen-

dence in the extinction due to the scattering off grains in the cavity walls. This range also contains spectral features needed to determine the photospheric properties, i.e., the different absorption features ( $\mathrm{Na}, \mathrm{Ca}, \mathrm{CO}$, for the deepest ones). The photospheric spectral features longward of 2.5 $\mu \mathrm{m}$ becomes sub-dominant with respect to the disk contribution, and contains several ice absorption features. Expanding the range would dilute their contributions and increase the uncertainty of the photospheric fit. Within this spectral region, we remove the $\mathrm{H}_{2}$ emission lines from the spectra using the emission line fitting procedure outlined in Section 3.3 to avoid biasing the covariance estimation. $\mathrm{H}_{2} 1 \rightarrow 0 \mathrm{~S}(3)$, $\mathrm{H}_{2} 1 \rightarrow 0 \mathrm{~S}(2), \mathrm{H}_{2} 1 \rightarrow 0 \mathrm{~S}(1), \mathrm{H}_{2} 1 \rightarrow 0 \mathrm{~S}(0), \mathrm{H}_{2} 2 \rightarrow 1 \mathrm{~S}(1)$, $\mathrm{H}_{2} 2 \rightarrow 1 \mathrm{~S}(3), \mathrm{H}_{2} 2 \rightarrow 1 \mathrm{~S}(2)$, are considered detected and their fit is subtracted from the spectra before performing the fitting.

We use the Starfish modeling framework from Czekala et al. (2015) and Gully-Santiago et al. (2017) and fit the parameters described in Equation 3 via a Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) model exploration. A radial velocity (RV) parameter was also used to allow for shifting the wavelength array. We detail the Starfish fitting and the MCMC processes in Appendix A.

Secondly, we model the full $1.9-5.3 \mu \mathrm{~m}$ continuum to improve our characterization of the disk thermal emission. The disk temperature profile we use in the first step described above largely overestimates the flux longward of $4 \mu \mathrm{~m}$, as the $1.9-2.4 \mu \mathrm{~m}$ region we focused on is only sensitive to the hot dust. The $1.9-2.4 \mu \mathrm{~m}$ slope of this disk component is also steeper compared to what is expected from a heated disk (e.g., see the modeling of (Chiang \& Goldreich 1997)), which is probably related to the role of scattered light and the unknown subsequent extinction law of the NC source. Therefore, in order to better account for the hot dusty disk contribution, we construct a simple model for the full $1.9-5.3 \mu \mathrm{~m}$ continuum using both the photospheric parameters we just constrained (i.e., $T_{\star, \text { eff }}, \log g$, and $R_{\star}$ ), and a geometrically flat, optically thick disk with a temperature profile following $T_{\text {disk }}(r)=$ $T_{\text {disk,i }} \times\left(R_{\text {disk,i }} / r\right)^{\beta}$, between an inner and outer disk radius $R_{\min }$ and $R_{\max }$. No inclination effects are taken into account since they are directly correlated with the flux-loss problem induced by the dominance of scattered light (see Section 5.3). The fit only broadly reproduces the full spectra, but while this approach corresponds to a total flux density (integration of $\lambda F_{\lambda}$ on $1.9-5.3 \mu \mathrm{~m}$ ) which agrees within $10 \%$ with the observed $1.9-5.3 \mu \mathrm{~m}$ integrated flux density, the $K$-band only modeling overestimates it by a factor of $\sim 3$. The posterior and adopted prior distributions for the photosphere ( $T_{\star, \text { eff }}$, and $\log g$ ) and circumstellar disk parameters ( $T_{\text {disk }}(1 A U)$, $\left.R_{\min }, R_{\max }, \beta\right)$ are listed in Table 3. We do not report on the stellar radius in this Table because its value is most likely an underestimate, since scattered light is likely the major contributor to the NIR light.

query: What distance metric is used to demonstrate the identifiability of features?
golden_answer: The standardized MSE distance, denoted as \(D_{\text{std}}\), is used to demonstrate the identifiability of features.
source_title:
Alleviating Non-identifiability: a High-fidelity Calibration Objective
  for Financial Market Simulation with Multivariate Time Series Data
source_text:
## D. Proof of Selecting Linearly Independent Features

Proof 4: We demonstrate that if two features are correlated by an affine transformation, there exists a distance metric for which their non-identifiable sets are identical. Therefore, features should be chosen to be linearly independent.

Let $\mathbf{X}_{T}^{k}$ and $\overline{\mathbf{X}}_{T}^{k}$ (for $k=1,2$ ) represent generated and target time series features related by:

$$
\left\{\begin{array}{l}
\overline{\mathbf{X}}_{T}^{1}=a \overline{\mathbf{X}}_{T}^{2}+b \\
\mathbf{X}_{T}^{1}=a \mathbf{X}_{T}^{2}+b
\end{array}, \quad a \neq 0, b \in \mathbb{R}\right.
$$

The non-identifiable sets are:

$$
S^{D, k, \epsilon}=\left\{\omega \mid D\left(\overline{\mathbf{X}}_{T}^{k}(\omega), \mathbf{X}_{T}^{k}\right) \leq \epsilon\right\}
$$

Choose $D$ as the standardized MSE distance, denoted as $D_{\text {std }}(X, Y)$,

$$
D_{\text {std }}\left(\mathbf{X}_{T}^{k}, \mathbf{Y}_{T}^{k}\right) \triangleq \frac{1}{T} \sum_{t=t_{x}}^{t_{c}}\left(\frac{X_{t}-\mu_{\mathbf{X}_{T}^{k}}}{\sigma_{\mathbf{X}_{T}^{k}}}-\frac{Y_{t}-\mu_{\mathbf{Y}_{T}^{k}}}{\sigma_{\mathbf{Y}_{T}^{k}}}\right)^{2}
$$

and the mean and standard deviation can be computed as $\mu_{\mathbf{X}_{T}^{k}} \triangleq \frac{1}{T} \sum_{t=t_{x}}^{t_{c}} X_{t}$, and $\sigma_{\mathbf{X}_{T}^{k}} \triangleq \sqrt{\frac{1}{T} \sum_{t=t_{x}}^{t_{c}}\left(X_{t}-\mu_{\mathbf{X}}\right)^{2}}$.
For affine-related features $\frac{\overline{\mathbf{X}}_{T}^{1}-\mu_{\mathbf{X}_{T}^{1}}}{\sigma_{\mathbf{X}_{T}^{1}}}=\operatorname{sign}(a) \frac{\mathbf{X}_{T}^{2}-\mu_{\mathbf{X}_{T}^{2}}}{\sigma_{\mathbf{X}_{T}^{2}}}$, the relationship for $\mathbf{X}_{T}^{k}$ and $\overline{\mathbf{X}}_{T}^{k}$ is analogous, which yields $D_{\text {std }}\left(\overline{\mathbf{X}}_{T}^{1}, \mathbf{X}_{T}^{1}\right)=D_{\text {std }}\left(\overline{\mathbf{X}}_{T}^{2}, \mathbf{X}_{T}^{2}\right)$.

Consequently, the non-identifiable sets are identical, i.e., $S^{D_{\text {std }}, 1, \epsilon}=S^{D_{\text {std }}, 2, \epsilon}$.

Under the max-aggregation $F$, we obtain $S^{F, \epsilon}=S^{D_{\text {std }}, 1, \epsilon} \cap$ $S^{D_{\text {std }}, 2, \epsilon}=S^{D_{\text {std }}, k, \epsilon} \quad \forall k$.

Thus, the measure remains unchanged:

$$
\mu\left(S^{F, \epsilon}\right)=\mu\left(S^{D_{\text {std }}, k, \epsilon}\right) \quad \forall k
$$

query: Does the boosted process provide a valid sequential test for the composite null hypothesis?
golden_answer: Yes.
source_title:
Improving Wald's (approximate) sequential probability ratio test by
  avoiding overshoot
source_text:
# 3.3 Handling composite nulls in one-sided testing problems 

An even more common testing setup in practice is

$$
H_{0}: \theta^{*} \leqslant \theta_{0} \quad \text { vs. } \quad H_{1}: \theta^{*}>\theta_{0} \quad\left(\theta_{0} \in \Theta\right)
$$

meaning we have a composite null hypothesis and a composite alternative. Throughout this section, we assume that for all $\theta_{1} \in \Theta$ with $\theta_{1} \geqslant \theta_{0}$,

$$
\lambda(x)=\frac{p_{\theta_{1}}(x)}{p_{\theta_{0}}(x)} \text { is nondecreasing in } x
$$

Robbins and Siegmund [22] showed that under this assumption the process $\left(\Lambda_{t}^{\text {plugin }}\right)$ defined in Equation (18) also provides a valid sequential test for the composite null hypothesis above. In the following, we show that the same holds for our boosted process.

Proposition 3.1. Consider the one-sided testing problem (20) under the monotone likelihood ratio property (21) and let $\lambda_{t}\left(X_{t}\right)=\frac{p_{\theta_{t}}\left(X_{t}\right)}{p_{\theta_{0}}\left(X_{t}\right)}$ for some predictable parameter $\theta_{t} \geqslant \theta_{0}$. Then,

$$
\mathbb{E}_{\theta_{0}}\left[T_{\alpha}\left(b_{t} \lambda_{t}\left(X_{t}\right) ; M\right) \mid \Lambda_{t-1}^{\text {boost }}\right] \leqslant 1 \Longrightarrow \mathbb{E}_{\theta}\left[T_{\alpha}\left(b_{t} \lambda_{t}\left(X_{t}\right) ; M\right) \mid \Lambda_{t-1}^{\text {boost }}\right] \leqslant 1 \quad\left(\theta \leqslant \theta_{0}\right)
$$

To summarize, for the composite testing problem above and under the monotone likelihood ratio property, we can do exactly the same as described in Section 3.2 for the simple null hypothesis without inflating type I error.

Remark 3. An important class satisfying property (21) is the one-parameter exponential family, where each density is given by $p_{\theta}(x)=h(x) \exp (T(x) \eta(\theta)-A(\theta))$ with $h, T, \eta$ and $A$ being known functions. It is easy to see that (21) is fulfilled for the sufficient statistic $T(x)$, if $\eta(\theta)$ is nondecreasing in $\theta$.

query: How are trades validated in a constant function market maker (CFMM)?
golden_answer: Trades are valid if they do not decrease the CFMM's utility and do not require more assets than the AMM holds, i.e., $u(\Pi) \leq u(\Pi+\delta)$ and $\Pi+\delta \in \mathbb{R}_{+}^{n}$.

source_text:
### 2.1 Background on Automated Market Maker

An AMM is, in brief, a pool of assets against which any individual trader can transact. The key innovation of these types of asset pools within decentralized finance is that they permit investors to add their own assets to the AMM in exchange for a fraction of the fees collected by the AMM. The most common AMM construction is that of the constant function market maker (CFMM) which is defined by a multivariate utility function $u: \mathbb{R}_{+}^{n} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}_{+}$and the size of the asset pool $\Pi \in \mathbb{R}_{+}^{n}$ (such that $u(\Pi)>0$ ). As summarized in, e.g., [4], the CFMM then permits trades $\delta \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ that do not decrease the CFMM's utility nor does it require more assets than the AMM holds, i.e., $\delta$ is a valid trade if:

$$
u(\Pi) \leq u(\Pi+\delta) \quad \text { and } \quad \Pi+\delta \in \mathbb{R}_{+}^{n}
$$

These AMMs are called constant function market makers because, under mild assumptions (see, e.g., [6]), the utility before and after a transaction are equal $(u(\Pi)=u(\Pi+\delta))$.

Based on the constant function construction, the marginal price of asset $i$ in terms of the numéraire asset $j$ can be determined via the relation $P_{i}^{j}(\Pi)=\frac{\partial}{\partial \Pi_{i}} u(\Pi) / \frac{\partial}{\partial \Pi_{j}} u(\Pi)$. This mapping is often called the pricing oracle. As is clear from the construction, $P_{i}^{j}(\Pi)=P_{j}^{i}(\Pi)^{-1}$ for any $\Pi \in \mathbb{R}_{+}^{n}$; this makes clear that there do not exist fees within this construction. In practice, fees are charged on a fraction of the assets being sold to the AMM, i.e., $\gamma \in(0,1)$ of the incoming assets (asset $i$ such that $\delta_{i}>0$ ) are taken to compensate the market maker for its service as a counterparty. Mathematically this modifies the CFMM construction so that $u(\Pi)=u\left(\Pi+\left[I-\gamma \operatorname{diag}\left(\mathbb{I}_{\{\delta>0\}}\right)\right] \delta\right)$.

Finally, investors are able to deposit their assets into the AMM in exchange for a fraction of

the fees collected; these depositors are often referred to as liquidity providers (LPs). This is done following the constant pricing oracle construction so that the prices before and after the liquidity provision remain equal, i.e., $\delta \in \mathbb{R}_{+}^{n}$ is deposited if $P_{i}^{j}(\Pi)=P_{i}^{j}(\Pi+\delta)$ for any pair of assets $(i, j)$; in practice, and as presented explicitly in the preceding equation, no fees are charged on these deposits. Similarly, LPs can later withdraw their assets at any time taking from the AMM the same fraction of the asset pool that they initially deposited. The fraction of fees collected by any individual LP is equal to the fraction of the assets that they hold at the AMM. Throughout this work, and as implemented within Uniswap v3 [1], the fees are distributed immediately upon collection to the liquidity providers.

Assumption 2.1. For the remainder of this work, we will consider the constant product market maker (CPMM) in the $n=2$ asset setting as is utilized by Uniswap and Sushiswap pools (i.e., $u(x, y):=x y)$. In addition, throughout, we take the second asset as the numéraire (i.e., $P(x, y):=$ $\left.P_{1}^{2}(x, y)\right)$.

In practice, AMMs exist as smart contracts that operate in a decentralized manner directly on a blockchain. This means that transactions are only processed at the block-writing times. By construction of the blockchain, this occurs at discrete times. For the Bitcoin blockchain, which utilizes a proof-of-work construction, each block is processed in approximately 10 minute intervals. However, more modern blockchains - using, e.g., proof-of-stake consensus - have nearly constant inter-block times $\Delta t>0$. For the Ethereum blockchain, the inter-block time is $\Delta t=12$ seconds; for the Polygon blockchain, the inter-block time is $\Delta t=2$ seconds.

Assumption 2.2. For the remainder of this work, we will assume that the inter-block time is fixed at $\Delta t>0$. Therefore the realized price process is $P_{i \Delta t}$ for $i \in \mathbb{N}$.

query: What is the stable length of a loxodromic element $g$ in a $\delta$-hyperbolic space?
golden_answer: The stable length of $g$, denoted as $\tau(g)$, is defined as $\lim _{n} \frac{d\left(g^{n} o, o\right)}{n}$.
