source_title:
Electric-Field Control of Magnetic Skyrmion Chirality in a
  Centrosymmetric 2D van der Waals Magnet
source_text:
#### Abstract

Two-dimensional van der Waals magnets hosting topological magnetic textures, such as skyrmions, show promise for spintronics and quantum computing. Electrical control of these topological spin textures is crucial for enhancing operational performance and functionality. Here, using electron microscopy combined with in situ electric and magnetic biasing, we show that the skyrmion helicity, whether left-handed or right-handed, in insulating $\mathrm{Cr}_{2} \mathrm{Ge}_{2} \mathrm{Te}_{6}$, can be controlled by the direction of external electric field applied during the magnetic field cooling process. The electric field-tuned helicity remains stable, even amid variations in magnetic and electric fields. Our theoretical investigation reveals that nonzero Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interactions between nearest neighbors, induced by the electric field, change their sign upon reversing the electric field direction, thereby facilitating helicity selection. The electrical control of magnetic helicity demonstrated in this study can be extended to other centrosymmetric skyrmion-hosting magnets, paving the way for future device designs in topological spintronics and quantum computing.


Keywords: skyrmion helicity, electric field control, van der Waals magnets, DzyaloshinskiiMoriya interaction

Magnetic skyrmions and topologically nontrivial spin structures in two-dimensional (2D) van der Waals (vdW) materials have been studied extensively due to their relevance fundamental spin physics in low dimensions and their potential spintronic applications. ${ }^{1-3}$ These topologically protected spin structures exhibit particle-like stability, making them promising information carriers in spintronic devices ${ }^{4}$. In 2D vdW materials, the integration of skyrmions with other 2D vdW layers featuring diverse and tunable physical properties offers exciting opportunities for designing novel states with emergent properties and behaviors. ${ }^{5-7}$ Experimentally, topological spin structures have been reported in various 2D vdW ferromagnetic materials, including skyrmionic bubbles in $\mathrm{Cr}_{2} \mathrm{Ge}_{2} \mathrm{Te}_{6}(\mathrm{CGT})^{8}$ with perpendicular uniaxial anisotropy, and Néel-type skyrmions in oxidized $\mathrm{Fe}_{3} \mathrm{GeTe}_{2}{ }^{9}$ and $\mathrm{WTe}_{2} / \mathrm{Fe}_{3} \mathrm{GeTe}_{2} .{ }^{10}$ There are two primary types of skyrmions in ferromagnetic 2D vdW magnets, based on their stabilization mechanisms: one with Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction (DMI) and the other without DMI. Analogous to bulk chiral magnets, ${ }^{11}$ DMI in non-centrosymmetric crystal structures stabilizes chiral spin arrangements. ${ }^{12}$ The chirality of DMI-stabilized skyrmions is determined by the crystal chirality. Conversely, in centrosymmetric crystals with uniaxial anisotropy, such as CGT, ${ }^{8}$ dipolar interactions stabilize Bloch-type skyrmionic bubbles, which are topologically equivalent to Bloch-type skyrmions in chiral magnets. However, due to the absence of DMIs, the helicity of skyrmionic bubbles in centrosymmetric magnets is random. Here, the helicity represents the in-plane rotation sense, either clockwise (CW) or counterclockwise (CCW).

The ability to control the helicity of skyrmionic spin structures by electric means is crucial for advancing spintronic applications and designing novel states in 2D heterostructures ${ }^{13-15}$ and quantum computing applications. ${ }^{16}$ In particular, deterministic control of skyrmion helicity can

provide a viable method to realize skyrmion-based quantum qubit where electric field control of skyrmion helicity is required ${ }^{16}$.

We note that electric fields can polarize insulating ferromagnetic 2D vdW materials. In a polarized state, nonzero DMIs may arise as the centrosymmetry is broken. Theoretical studies have predicted that out-of-plane electric fields can induce skyrmionic spin structures in insulating 2D $\mathrm{vdW} \mathrm{CrI}_{3}\left(\sim 1 \mathrm{eV}\right.$ bandgap $\left.{ }^{17}\right)$ monolayer ${ }^{18-19}$ and CGT $\left(\sim 0.4 \mathrm{eV}\right.$ bandgap $\left.{ }^{20}\right)$ heterostructures. ${ }^{21}$ As the sign of electric-field-induced DMIs is switchable by reversing the direction of the electric field, the magnetic helicity in skyrmionic spin structures can be controlled in insulating or semiconducting 2D ferromagnets. ${ }^{22}$ Additionally, the magnetic properties of CGT can be manipulated with electric stimuli. For instance, electrogating experiments performed on CGT layers with an ionic gel showed not only a dramatic increase in $T_{C}$ (from 60 K to 200 K ), but also an easy axis rotation from out-of-plane to in-plane direction, significantly altering magnetic spin structures. ${ }^{23}$ A recent study demonstrated that the spin helicity in a metallic helimagnet MnP can be controlled by spin-transfer torque when the current direction is parallel to the external magnetic field applied. ${ }^{24}$ Notably, two studies have demonstrated the electric field control of Néel-type skyrmion chiralities in multilayered magnetic films. ${ }^{25-26}$ Nevertheless, there has been no experimental work on the control of topological magnetic spin structures by external electric fields in insulating or semiconducting 2D vdW magnets.

In this letter, we integrate in situ electric and magnetic fields with cryogenic Lorentz transmission electron microscopy (LTEM) to experimentally demonstrate the tunable helicity of skyrmionic bubbles in CGT flakes. Our data reveal that the helicity (the direction of in-plane spin rotation) of Bloch-type skyrmionic bubbles can be reversed by changing the electric field direction, without altering the polarity (the core spin direction), thus favoring one of the two possible

helicities by an external electric field. Our density functional theory (DFT) calculations support these experimental observations, attributing the helicity selection in skyrmionic bubbles to the electric-field-induced DMIs between nearest neighbors. Achieving helicity control via an electric field, as demonstrated in this study, opens up promising avenues for designing novel spintronic devices and quantum qubits based on topological spin structures in the 2D vdW heterostructures.

Figure 1a shows a few-layer graphene (FLG)/CGT/FLG heterostructure fabricated over an electron-beam imaging window (vacuum), patterned in a custom designed silicon nitride membrane chip with two pre-patterned electrodes (Norcada Inc., Fig. S1 in the Supplementary Information). Due to the bandgap of CGT ( $\sim 0.4 \mathrm{eV}$ ), no significant current is expected to flow through the heterostructure, especially at low temperatures where thermally excited carriers are quenched. To ensure low leakage current and avoid Joule heating, we also fabricated heterostructures with an additional insulator layer, composed of FLG/hexagonal boron nitride (hBN)/CGT/FLG (Fig. S2). The resistance measured during cooling under a constant voltage of 1 V (Fig. 1c) from the FLG/CGT/FLG sample shows an increase in the resistance with decreasing temperature, characteristic of an insulator. As shown in the inset of Fig. 1c, a local minimum in the resistance gradient at $T \sim 55 \mathrm{~K}$ occurs close to the $T_{C}$, indicating a correlation between magnetic spin structures and electrical transport properties.

Figure 1d shows an over-focused LTEM image taken after 50 mT magnetic field cooling in the absence of an electric field. Hexagonally-close-packed skyrmionic bubbles with $\sim 150 \mathrm{~nm}$ diameter were observed. When the exfoliated flakes are imaged along the $c$-axis, the bubble core (magnetization direction up) and peripheral (magnetization direction down) spin components do not generate any contrast in the LTEM imaging as they align with the imaging direction. Instead, the visible LTEM contrast arises from the Bloch walls, where the magnetic spins are perpendicular

to the direction of imaging electrons, consistent with previous LTEM studies. ${ }^{8,27}$ Based on the magnetic contrast in Fig. 1d, two distinguishable skyrmionic bubbles can be identified, as marked with the blue and red boxes. In an over-focus imaging condition, a CCW skyrmionic bubble displays a dark-to-bright contrast from the perimeter to the core due to the Lorentz-force-induced converging electron beams. Conversely, for a CW skyrmionic bubble, the contrast is reversed to bright-to-dark due to the diverging electron beams. Since the LTEM contrast also reverses when transitioning from underfocus to overfocus (Fig. S3), we used over-focus imaging to determine the chirality of skyrmionic bubbles. Here, all skyrmionic bubbles have their core spin direction antiparallel to the applied magnetic field, hence the polarity ( P , the core spin orientation) of skyrmionic bubbles is always positive (+P), as schematically shown in Fig. 1e. Helicity is defined as the in-plane rotation sense, either CW or CCW, within the Bloch walls that separate the core domain from the peripheral domain (Fig. 1e). Note that the polarity in skyrmionic bubbles is fixed in our experiment. This was confirmed by micromagnetic simulations and LTEM contrast simulations, as shown in Fig. 1e. In our micromagnetic simulations, right-handed and left-handed skyrmionic bubbles are induced by negative and positive bulk DMIs ( $\pm 1.25 \times 10^{-4} \mathrm{~J} / \mathrm{m}^{2}$ ), respectively. It should be noted that nonzero bulk DMI values are used to ensure controlled formation of CW and CCW bubbles for comparison with experimental LTEM contrast.

To study the effects of electric fields on skyrmionic bubble helicity, electric fields of different magnitude were applied during separate cooling processes from $T>80 \mathrm{~K}$ to 12 K through $T_{C}$ under a constant magnetic field of 50 mT . After the cooling process, the magnetic field was reduced to a residual value of approximately $\sim 11 \mathrm{mT}$ inside our electron microscope. ${ }^{8}$ It should be noted that the directions of the electric and magnetic fields are parallel to the crystallographic $c$-axis and the imaging direction in the electron microscope (see Fig. 1b). We define the positive electric field

direction as parallel to the imaging direction, and negative direction as antiparallel. Figure 2a-b show LTEM images of the FLG/CGT/FLG heterostructure taken at $\mathrm{T}=14 \mathrm{~K}$ after cooling with a 50 mT magnetic field and simultaneous application of positive and negative $18 \mathrm{mV} / \mathrm{nm}$ electric fields, respectively. Based on the LTEM image contrast of each bubble, which exhibited either bright-to-dark or dark-to-bright transitions from the perimeter to the core, we found that the negative electric field induced CCW skyrmionic bubbles (Fig. 2a), while the positive electric field induced CW bubbles. This demonstrates that the helicity of skyrmionic bubbles has been selectively controlled by an external electric field throughout the field cooling process. As shown in Fig. 2c, attempts to reverse the helicity of the CW skyrmionic bubbles (Fig. 2b) by applying a negative electric field up to $36 \mathrm{mV} / \mathrm{nm}$ at 16 K , far below $T_{C}$, resulted in sample damage. The application of such a high electric field caused Joule heating, leading to a significant alteration in the magnetic domain structure characterized by coexisting stripe domains and skyrmionic bubbles (Fig. 2c), suggesting that the sample was heated above $T_{C}$. Importantly, the helicity of skyrmionic bubbles could be reversed from CW to CCW (see Fig. 2c) if the sample was heated and then cooled under an applied positive electric field ( $36 \mathrm{mV} / \mathrm{nm}$ ) and 11 mT magnetic field. This underscores that the presence of nonzero DMIs is required during formation of skyrmionic bubbles for helicity selection.

To reduce current through the sample under high external electric fields, we fabricated a FLG/hBN/CGT/FLG heterostructure and performed LTEM imaging in situ during the field cooling processes (Supplementary Videos S1-S2 and Figs. S4-S5). Figs. 2d-h show LTEM images obtained after different field cooling processes, with electric fields ranging from $-43 \mathrm{mV} / \mathrm{nm}$ to $+36 \mathrm{mV} / \mathrm{nm}$. The presence of the hBN layer allows the application of a broader range of electric fields without heating or damaging from leakage current with the voltage drop still mainly being

across the CGT layer (see Supplementary Information for electric field calculation). A FLG/hBN/CGT/hBN/FLG heterostructure with an extra hBN may enable the application of a larger electric field before the sample breaks down. A substantial negative electric field of -43 $\mathrm{mV} / \mathrm{nm}$ (Fig. 2d) predominantly induced CCW skyrmionic bubbles. Conversely, when a positive electric field of $+36 \mathrm{mV} / \mathrm{nm}$ was applied, only CW skyrmionic bubbles were observed (Fig. 2h), confirming the helicity dependence on the electric field direction. With intermediate electric fields, both CCW and CW skyrmionic bubbles coexist after field cooling. In Fig. 2i, we quantify the percentage of CCW skyrmionic bubbles in a wide field of view (Fig. S6) as a function of electric field, finding almost a linear dependence on the electric field. We observe nearly random helicity ( $50 \%$ CCW and $50 \%$ CW) under an electric field of $-18 \mathrm{mV} / \mathrm{nm}$. This electric field offset may be attributed to an electron-beam-induced charging in the sample. In TEM, electron-transparent samples, especially if insulating, are often positively charged by secondary and/or Auger electron emission. ${ }^{28}$ Thus, the 500 nm thick silicon nitride substrate is likely positively charged under electron beam illumination, resulting in a net positive electric field. This electron beam induced charging explains our previous study, which reported the observation of skyrmionic bubbles with single helicity observed in CGT flakes on silicon nitride membranes. ${ }^{8}$

The electric field-induced helicity of skyrmionic bubbles remained stable even after the electric field was fully turned off and magnetic field was reduced to 11 mT . Figures 2 j -k show two LTEM images obtained before and after increasing the magnetic field from 11 mT to 113 mT , following a field cooling with a $-18 \mathrm{mV} / \mathrm{nm}$ electric field and 50 mT magnetic field. Although the increased magnetic field caused the skyrmionic bubbles to shrink, their LTEM contrast remained unchanged. This indicates that the helicity and polarity were preserved despite variations in magnetic field.

To understand the microscopic origin of helicity selection, we conducted DFT calculations using SIESTA-TB2J ${ }^{29}$, focusing on DMIs in CGT under external electric fields. The magnetic $\mathrm{Cr}^{3+}$ ions in the edge-shared Te octahedra are arranged in a honeycomb lattice. Considering the honeycomb lattice as two interdigitated triangular lattices, there are two distinguishable Cr sites. In our DFT study, we identified two primary DMIs: nearest neighbor (NN) and next nearest neighbor (NNN). In the absence of an electric field, the NN interactions involving two $\mathrm{Te}^{2-}$ anions do not exhibit a net DMI due to the centrosymmetric interaction pathway, as schematically shown in Fig. 3a. When an electric field is applied, the insulating CGT crystal becomes polarized by ionic displacements and/or electronic polarization. In a simple ionic charge screening scenario, the $\mathrm{Cr}^{3+}$ cations move along the electric field direction while the $\mathrm{Te}^{2-}$ anions shift in the opposite direction, resulting in the shortening of two $\mathrm{Cr}-\mathrm{Te}$ bonds and the stretching of the other two. In Fig. 3a-c, the stretched Cr-Te bond lengths are indicated with gray lines. These ionic displacements break the inversion symmetry in the NN interaction pathway, resulting in nonzero DMIs. The primary components of electric-field-induced NN DMIs are in-plane and perpendicular to the nearest Cr Cr bonds (see Table S1 in the Supplementary Information). In Figs. 3b and 3c, we show the calculated NN DMIs induced by negative and positive electric fields ( $\pm 2 \times 10^{4} \mathrm{mV} / \mathrm{nm}$ ) for two Cr sites in the honeycomb lattice. Similar electric-field-induced DMI vector patterns have been calculated for $\mathrm{CrI}_{3}$ crystals, which also have a honeycomb lattice of Cr in edge-shared I octahedra. ${ }^{17}$ A structural distinction between CGT and $\mathrm{CrI}_{3}$ lies in the presence of the Ge dimer at the center of the Cr honeycomb lattice, which does not significantly influence exchange interactions. We found that the vector sums of in-plane components of NN DMIs are relatively small while the vector sum of out-of-plane components remains finite: +0.0737 meV and -0.0730 meV (Table S1) for negative and positive electric fields, respectively. Note that the resultant out-

of-plane components of NN DMIs align with the applied electric field direction and consequently change their sign when the electric field direction is reversed, as shown in Fig. 3d. This vector sum of out-of-plane components of NN DMIs dictates the rotation sense of in-plane magnetic spins within the Bloch domain walls. Considering the DMI energy term $-D_{i j} \cdot\left(S_{i} \times S_{j}\right)$, CCW and CW spin arrangements are energetically favored for negative and positive electric fields, respectively, consistent with our experimental observations and micromagnetic simulations (Fig. 1e). According to our DFT calculations, the magnitude of the total NN DMIs scales linearly with the magnitude of electric field (see Fig. S7b). Consequently, the helicity response is linear with the magnitude of the external electric field, as demonstrated in Fig. 2i. The magnitude of electric fields applied in our DFT calculations exceeds those employed in the experiments by two orders of magnitude (Fig. 2). In experiments, not only is there a limitation in the maximum external voltage applied due to dielectric breakdown or leakage currents, but the external voltage applied may also not be entirely across the CGT layer due to air gaps, contact resistances, and other imperfections within the heterostructure. It also suggests that the resultant electric field-induced DMIs in experiments are not strong enough to alter the helicity of pre-existing skyrmionic bubbles, as observed in Figs. 2bc. However, they may be potent enough to influence helicity selection at the onset of skyrmionic bubble formation during the field cooling process, as shown in Figs. 2d-h. Thus, although there is a discrepancy in electric field magnitude between theory and experiments, our study qualitatively demonstrates electric-field effects on helicity selection in skyrmionic bubbles. We rule out the effects of NNN DMIs on skyrmion helicity, as all NNN DMI vectors cancel each other regardless of the electric field direction (see Figs. 3b - c and Table S1).

Finally, we study skyrmionic bubble formation while field cooling the CGT across the $T_{\mathrm{C}}$ with an applied electric field. In Fig. 4, we present LTEM images showing the skyrmionic bubble

formation process during electric and magnetic field cooling. At 54 K , slightly below $T_{C}$, smalldiameter skyrmionic bubbles are prominent, as depicted in Fig. 4e (see also Supplementary Videos 1-2 and Figs. S4-S5). These small skyrmionic bubbles undergo dynamic formation and annihilation processes down to 35 K . For example, we observed CCW and CW skyrmionic bubbles merging into a CW bubble, as shown in Figs. 4b-c. The average radius gradually increases from 67 nm to $\sim 77 \mathrm{~nm}$ as the temperature decreases. The external magnetic field of 50 mT applied during the cooling process likely suppresses the formation of bubbles with large sizes, resulting in a narrow size distribution. Upon further cooling, we observed continuous fluctuations in the distance between neighboring skyrmionic bubbles down to 15 K , as shown in Fig. 4f. Overall, in situ LTEM imaging provides direct observation of the formation and evolution of topologically nontrivial skyrmionic bubbles during magnetic phase transitions.

In conclusion, we studied the effect of electric fields on the helicity of skyrmionic bubbles in 2D vdW CGT. Using electron microscopy imaging of skyrmionic bubble formation across the phase transition, we demonstrated that the helicity of these bubbles can be controlled by the direction of the electric field during magnetic field cooling. The resultant skyrmionic bubbles and their helicity remained stable at low temperatures, even with variations in applied magnetic and electric fields. The proportion of skyrmionic bubbles in CW versus CCW configurations exhibited almost a linear scaling with the electric field magnitude, facilitated by the insertion of a currentblocking hBN layer. According to our DFT calculations, the collective vector sum of NN DMIs aligns in the out-of-plane direction and reverses polarity when the direction of the electric field is altered, playing a pivotal role in chirality selection. Our study demonstrates that external electric fields, applied along the out-of-plane direction, can effectively control the in-plane spin helicity of nonmetallic 2D vdW magnets. This capability for electric field control of skyrmionic bubble

chirality paves the way for developing advanced topological spintronic and quantum computing devices that utilize topological spin textures in 2D vdW magnets.

query: What is a dominant strategy for candidate 1 when combining a large valence advantage with policy motivation?
golden_answer: It is a dominant strategy for candidate 1 to choose $p_{1}=\omega$, and this policy indeed wins the election.
source_title: Motivated Reasoning and the Political Economy of Climate Change Inaction
source_text:
# 4.2 Valence Differences 

Next, consider valence differences as in Ansolabehere and Snyder (2000), Groseclose (2001), Aragones and Palfrey (2002), and more recently Denter (2021). Specifically, assume that voters evaluate candidates not only by the policies they offer but by $v_{i}+u\left(p_{i}, \omega\right)$, where $v_{i} \in \mathbb{R}$ is the valence utility the voter gets from candidate $i$ in the office and $u(p, \omega)$ is policy utility and defined as before in (1). Let $v_{1}>v_{2}$, implying that candidate 1 has a valence advantage. How does introducing valence alter the model's conclusions? On the one hand, it has no effect on $\tilde{\mu}^{*}(s)$, which remains as described in Lemma 1, because valence is independent of the state $\omega$. However, valence does affect a voter's choice at the ballot box for a given belief $\pi(s, \mathbf{p}, \tilde{\mu})$. If both candidates choose the same policy, candidate 1 always wins because $v_{1}>v_{2}$. Equilibrium in the extended game resembles equilibrium in Ansolabehere and Snyder (2000). If the valence advantage is not too large, candidate 1 will always choose $p_{1}=0$, while candidate 2 may choose any $p_{2} \in\{0,1\}$ without having a chance to win. If the valence advantage is large enough, candidate 1 may choose any $p_{1} \in\{0,1\}$ and still win with certainty. Thus, it is possible that a candidate with a large valence advantage might use this advantage to propose an optimal policy. In fact, if we combine a large valence advantage with policy motivation as described in Section 4.1, then it is a dominant strategy for candidate 1 to choose $p_{1}=\omega$, and this policy indeed wins the election.

query: What is a loose Legendrian?
golden_answer: A loose Legendrian is a type of Legendrian submanifold that has a loose chart around a point, allowing for certain flexibility in its structure.
source_title: Non-orderability and the contact Hofer norm
source_text:
# 3.9. Proof of Theorem 1.16. 

Lemma 3.4. Let $L$ be a loose Legendrian with loose chart $V$ around a point $p \in$ $L \cap V$. Furthermore, let $U \subset V$ be an open neighbourhood of $p$ and $W$ a Darboux ball with $\bar{V} \subset W$. Then there exists a contactomorphism $\varphi \in \mathcal{G}$ compactly supported in $W$ such that $\varphi(V) \subset U$ and $\varphi(L) \subset L \cup U$. In particular $\varphi(L)$ is a loose Legendrian with loose chart $\varphi(V)$.

Proof. Without restriction, we can assume that $L \subset \mathbb{R}^{2 n+1}$ equipped with the contact form $\alpha:=d z-y d x$. Note that for simplicity, we omit the indices of the coordinates $\left(x_{i}, y_{i}\right)$, where $1 \leq i \leq n$. Assume further that $p=0$ and that $U, W$ are balls of radius $R_{1}<R_{2}$, respectively. By the definition of a loose chart, we can further assume that outside of $V$ the Legendrian $L$ coincides with the set $\{z=y=0\}$.

Look at the contact Hamiltonian $h=f(x, y, z)(-2 z+x y)$, where $f=1$ on $V$ and $f=0$ outside of $W$. It generates a contact vector field of the form

$$
X_{h}=\left(h+y g_{1}(x, y, z)\right) \partial_{z}+g_{1}(x, y, z) \partial_{x}+g_{2}(x, y, z) \partial_{y}
$$

Since $d \alpha(X, \cdot)+d h=\partial_{z} h \alpha$, a simple computation shows that

$$
g_{2}=\partial_{x} h+y \partial_{z} h=\partial_{x} f(-2 z+x y)+f y+y \partial_{z} h
$$

In particular it follows that $g_{2}=0=h+y g_{1}(x, y, z)$ on $\{y=z=0\}$, i.e., the flow of $X_{h}$ preserves $L$ outside of $V$. On $V$ the flow of $X$ coincides with the scaling map $t \mapsto\left(e^{-t} x, e^{-t} y, e^{-2 t} z\right)$ and squeezes $V$ into $U$ for $t$ large enough.

Write $f_{t}=\varphi_{t}^{\alpha}$ for $t \geq 0$ and $\mathbb{L}^{\prime}$ for the image of $L^{n-1}$ under the Reeb flow. We start by suitably adjusting the open book to $f_{t}$ as follows.

Lemma 3.5. Let $(K, \theta)$ be the open book from Theorem 1.16 and let $f_{t}$ be as above. Let $L$ be the skeleton of one of the pages of the open book (it is a loose isotropic complex). There exists an equivalent open book decomposition $(\tilde{K}, \tilde{\theta})$ with skeleton $\tilde{L}$ of a page such that $\tilde{L}^{n-1}=L^{n-1}$, and each connected component $\tilde{L}_{i}^{\text {crit }}$ admits a loose chart $V_{i}$ with $V_{i} \cap \tilde{\mathbb{L}}^{\prime}=\emptyset$. In particular, the image of $\tilde{L}^{n-1}$ under the Reeb flow of $\alpha$ is still $\tilde{\mathbb{L}}^{\prime}=\mathbb{L}^{\prime}$. Moreover, one can assume that $V_{i} \cap V_{j}=\emptyset$ for $i \neq j$.

Proof. Since the Reeb flow is periodic near $L^{n-1}$, [23, Proposition 3.11] implies that the intersection of $\mathbb{L}^{\prime}$ with $L$ does not contain any sets that are open in $L$. Therefore, for each connected component $L_{i}^{\text {crit }}, i \in\{1, \cdots, k\}$ of the critical locus $L^{\text {crit }}$ of $L$, we can find a loose chart $U_{i}$ and a point $p_{i} \in U_{i} \cap L_{i}^{\text {crit }}$ such that an open ball $U_{i}^{\prime}$ around $p_{i}$ with closure contained in $U_{i}$ does not intersect $\mathbb{L}^{\prime}$. Moreover, we can assume that $U_{i} \cap U_{j}^{\prime}=\emptyset$ for all $i \neq j$. For each $i$, Lemma 3.4 provides us with a contactomorphism $\varphi_{i} \in \mathcal{G}$ of $M$ compactly supported in an arbitrarily small neighbourhood of $U_{i}$ inside the complement of $L^{n-1}$ such that $V_{i}:=\varphi_{i}\left(U_{i}\right) \subset U_{i}^{\prime}$ and $\varphi_{i}\left(L_{i}^{\text {crit }}\right) \cap L_{j}^{\text {crit }}=\emptyset$ for all $j \neq i$. Note that one can assume that $\varphi_{i}$ is supported away from $L_{j}^{\text {crit }}$ for $j \neq i$. Consider $\varphi:=\varphi_{1} \cdots \varphi_{k}$. Then $\varphi(L)$ is a loose isotropic complex with disjoint loose charts $V_{i}$ and $(\varphi(L))^{n-1}=L^{n-1}$. In particular, the charts $V_{i}$ are disjoint from $\mathbb{L}^{\prime}$. Set $(\tilde{K}, \tilde{\theta})=\left(\varphi(K), \theta \circ \varphi^{-1}\right)$.

By Lemma 3.5 we can assume that the open book has pages $W_{ \pm}$with skeletons $L_{ \pm}$ such that $\mathbb{L}_{-}^{\prime}$ does not intersect the loose charts $V_{i}$ of the connected components $L_{-, i}^{\text {crit }}$. Set $V=\bigcup_{i} V_{i}$ and define the size of $V$ to be $C(V)=\max _{i} C\left(V_{i}\right)$, where $C\left(V_{i}\right)=\sup |\tilde{\theta}|_{\alpha}$ over all $\widetilde{\theta} \in \widetilde{\mathcal{G}}\left(V_{i}\right)$.
Now, following the arguments from Sections 3.3 and 3.8, there exists a neighbourhood $U$ around $\mathbb{L}^{\prime}$, disjoint from $V$, and a Hofer-small perturbation $f_{t}^{\prime}=g_{t} f_{t}$ of $f_{t}$ with $\left|\tilde{g}_{t}\right|_{\alpha}<\delta$ and $\operatorname{supp}\left(g_{t}\right) \subset U$ such that $f_{t}^{\prime}\left(L_{-}^{n-1}\right) \cap L_{+}=\emptyset$ for all $t$. Hence, we may write $f_{t}^{\prime}$ for all $t$ as

$$
f_{t}^{\prime}=f_{t}^{-} f_{t}^{+}
$$

where $\operatorname{supp}\left(f_{t}^{+}\right) \subset\left(M \backslash L_{+}\right) \cap U$ and $\operatorname{supp}\left(f_{t}^{-}\right) \subset M \backslash L_{-}^{n-1}$ for all $t$. In particular, as $U \cap V=\emptyset$, we have that on $V, f_{t}=f_{t}^{\prime}=f_{t}^{-}$, which in particular is strict there and

$$
d_{\alpha}\left(\tilde{f}_{t}, \tilde{f}_{t}^{-}\right)<\delta+C_{+}
$$

where $C_{ \pm}=\sup |\tilde{\theta}|_{\alpha}<\infty$ over all $\widetilde{\theta} \in \widetilde{\mathcal{G}}\left(M \backslash L_{ \pm}\right)$. Furthermore, $f_{t}^{-}=$id on a neighbourhood $U^{\prime} \subset U$ of $L_{-}^{n-1}$. Set $\varphi_{t}=f_{t}^{-}$.

Applying the argument of [45], which readily extends to the relative case, we see that for every $\delta>0$ there exists an isotopy $\psi_{t}$ with $\psi_{t}=\mathrm{id}$ on $U^{\prime}, \psi_{1}(L)=\varphi_{1}(L)$, $\psi_{t}(L)$ is $\delta$ close in the $C^{0}$-metric to $\varphi_{t}(L)$, and finally

$$
\left|\tilde{\psi}_{1}\right|_{\alpha}<C(V)+C\left(\varphi_{1}(V)\right)+\delta=2 C(V)+\delta
$$

Here we used the fact that $\varphi_{1}$ is strict on $V$.

Finally, for $\delta$ sufficiently small, $\varphi_{t}^{-1} \psi_{t}\left(L_{-}\right) \cap L_{+}=\emptyset$ for all $t$, whence

$$
d_{\alpha}\left(\tilde{\varphi}_{1}, \tilde{\psi}_{1}\right)=\left|\tilde{\varphi}_{1}^{-1} \tilde{\psi}_{1}\right|_{\alpha} \leq C_{+}+C_{-}
$$

In total we estimate

$$
\left|\tilde{f}_{t}\right|_{\alpha} \leq\left|\tilde{\varphi}_{1}\right|_{\alpha}+\delta+C_{+} \leq\left|\tilde{\psi}_{1}\right|_{\alpha}+\delta+2 C_{+}+C_{-} \leq 3 \delta+C(V)+2 C_{+}+C_{-}
$$

a bound independent of $t$. Therefore the contact Hofer norm on $\tilde{\mathcal{G}}$ is bounded along the one-parameter subgroup given by the Reeb flow of $\alpha$. In particular $(M, \xi)$ is not orderable.
3.10. Proof of Theorem 1.5. The skeleton $L$ of a Weinstein domain $W$ is an exact Lagrangian complex. We consider it as part of the page $W$ of the standard open book on $M=\partial_{\infty}(W \times \mathbb{C})$. As such, it is a Legendrian complex. Furthermore, as the monodromy of this open book is trivial, it follows immediately from e.g. [54, Section 2.11] that there is a contact form $\alpha$ on $M$ that is periodic near $L$. Furthermore, as $W$ is obtained by attachment of $N$ critical Weinstein $n$-handles to the subcritical subdomain $W^{\prime}$ of $W$, the co-cores of the handles provide disjoint Lagrangian disks $D_{i}, 1 \leq i \leq N$, each one of which intersects transversely $L$ at precisely one point. Moreover the cores of the handles correspond to the components $L_{i}^{n}, 1 \leq i \leq N$, of $L^{n}=L \backslash L^{n-1}$, and $D_{i} \cap L_{i}^{n}=D_{i} \cap L$. It follows from [15, Proposition 2.9] that $L$ is a loose Legendrian complex in $M$. Finally, by Theorem 1.16, we obtain that $M$ is not orderable.

query: What role does information about other agents play in mechanism design?
golden_answer: In mechanism design, the information that agents have about other agents' preferences can significantly impact the outcomes of a game. The study explores how additional information about other agents can influence the implementability of social choice functions (SCFs), particularly in achieving desirable equilibrium outcomes.
source_title: Information About Other Players in Mechanism Design
source_text:
## 1 Introduction

The goal of a social planner in any mechanism design problem is to design a game under which a desirable outcome emerges in equilibrium. In implementation theory, agents have private information consisting of their own preferences over a set of outcomes as well as information about the preferences of other agents. Naturally, the set of equilibrium outcomes that can emerge from a mechanism is sensitive to the details of the information available to agents. A considerable body of mechanism design literature focuses on the effects of changing information structures on achieving desirable outcomes. Most of this work focuses on how much agents know about variables that directly affect their own payoffs - for example, the information a bidder knows about her own valuation for an object (Bergemann et al. (2022)) - rather than information about other agents' preferences.

In this paper, we examine how the planner can have an interest in agents possessing additional information about the preferences of other agents, revisiting the Bayesian implementation problem as studied by Jackson (1991), as well as Postlewaite and Schmeidler (1986) and Palfrey and Srivastava (1989). In this setting, agents fully understand their own preferences over a set of outcomes but do not know the preferences of other agents. Agents' beliefs about the preferences of other agents are drawn from a common prior, which will be

[^0]
[^0]:    *This article subsumes my undergraduate thesis at Harvard University. I am indebted to my thesis advisor Eric Maskin for constant and invaluable guidance and Stephen Morris for generous discussions, as well as Michal Kowalik, Shengwu Li, Matthew Rabin, Madison Shirazi, and Charlie Yang for helpful comments.

assumed to have full support. This paper additionally supposes that agents can receive a full-support signal regarding the preferences of other agents. The model, which is explained in section 2, considers how the implementability of a social choice function (SCF) changes as the information structure varies. The question is whether and when there exist SCFs that are not implementable when agents have no information about the types of other agents but are implementable when one or more agents receive additional information about other agents.

This question can be asked with respect to either partial or full implementation. Partial implementation requires only that the planner's desired outcome is achieved by some equilibrium of the game, while full implementation demands that every equilibrium of the game yields a desirable outcome. It is well-known that the partial implementability of an SCF depends only on whether it satisfies incentive compatibility, which requires that it is a best response for an agent to behave truthfully if all other agents are behaving truthfully. In section 3, we show that any SCF which satisfies incentive compatibility when agents receive informative signals about the types of other agents also satisfies incentive compatibility when agents do not have this additional information. This implies that a planner concerned only with partial implementation will never prefer an agent to have additional information about other agents. The reason is when an agent has access to an informative signal about the preferences of other agents, the planner must ensure that the agent is incentivized to report truthfully in each signal realization. However, a weighted average of these constraints across signal realizations yields the incentive constraint needed for the agent if she did not have access to additional information, making this latter constraint easier to satisfy.

The remainder of the paper shows how additional information about the types of other agents can help an agent signal to the planner that an undesirable equilibrium is being played, which is relevant if the planner is concerned with full implementation. In section 4 we present the main example of the paper: an SCF that is not fully implementable when agents do not have access to informative signals about the preferences of other agents but is fully implementable when agents have access to a sufficiently accurate signal about other agents. The condition that rules out undesired equilibria in Bayesian implementation settings is Bayesian monotonicity, which guarantees that agents have sufficient incentives to signal to the planner that an undesirable equilibrium strategy is being played. Much of this paper examines how Bayesian monotonicity varies with the information agents have about other agents. Section 5 presents a sufficient condition under which an SCF that is not fully implementable when agents have no information about the types of other agents becomes fully implementable under a more informative information structure.

An obvious concern with endowing an agent with additional information about the pref-

erences of other agents is that it can affect their own incentive to report truthfully to the mechanism. Indeed, the conclusion of section 3 is that incentive compatibility becomes harder to satisfy as agents receive additional information about other agents. To simplify the analysis, this paper focuses on the effects of modifying the beliefs of agents with dominant strategies. In both the main example and the general results, informative signals about other agents are only accessed by agents for which truth-telling is already a dominant strategy. This prevents the elimination of the planner's desired equilibrium outcome after the agents receive informative signals about the types of other agents and focuses the analysis on how additional information can allow an agent to signal undesirable deviations to the planner.

The signal we construct - in order to incentivize an agent $i$ to report to the planner that a specific untruthful equilibrium is being played - relies on a partition of the set of types of agents other than $i$ into two groups and informs agent $i$, with a sufficiently high degree of accuracy, whether the realized types of other agents belong to one group or the other. The intuition of this partition construction is the following: Each group should contain a type profile of other agents such that if the agent $i$ knew this type profile realized, she would prefer all other agents report truthfully rather than misreport according to the untruthful equilibrium, regardless of her own type. If agent $i$ is confident enough that the realized type profile is in one of these groups, she can propose an alternate SCF that swaps the outcomes implemented under the truthful strategy versus the untruthful strategy. By construction, this alternate SCF can only give agent $i$ a weakly lower payoff relative to the original if all other agents report truthfully, so agent $i$ would only propose it if an untruthful strategy profile is being played. Agent $i$ will have an incentive to propose this alternate SCF whenever the signal is sufficiently accurate.

Though a planner may want, for the goal of full implementation, agents to have access to informative signals about the types of other agents compared to no information, a key point of the analysis is that the planner does not always prefer a more informative signal structure. In particular, the signals constructed do not accurately inform any agent of the exact type profiles of other agents. One can imagine many reason why such a signal structure would be ineffective. For example, if there is a type profile of other agents such that all types of an agent $i$ would prefer play an untruthful equilibrium strategy as opposed to a truthful one, there will be no way to incentivize agent $i$ to report the untruthful equilibrium to the planner if she is sufficiently confident that this undesirable type profile has been realized. The conclusion that a designer may prefer information structures that are more informative, but not too much more informative, is consistent with the rapidly growing literature on information design spurred by Rayo and Segal (2010) and Kamenica and Gentzkow (2011). Thorough reviews of recent advancements in information design can be found in Bergemann and Morris (2019)

and Kamenica (2019).

Related Literature This paper most directly contributes to the literature on full Bayesian implementation, which began with Postlewaite and Schmeidler (1986), Palfrey and Srivastava (1989), and Jackson (1991). This paper also adds to the extensive literature on the effect of changing information structures in mechanism design settings pioneered by Bergemann and Välimäki (2002). It relates especially to the literature on information disclosure in mechanism design. In auction settings, Ganuza (2004) studies the optimal way for a seller to disclose a costly public signal about a good's characteristic in a second-price auction, which is a component of bidders' private valuations, while Bergemann and Pesendorfer (2007) investigate the joint design problem in which the seller controls the information bidders have about their own valuations and the auction rules. Other papers that have investigated the effects of information disclosure in auction settings include Esô and Szentes (2007), and Bergemann et al. (2022). Similar questions have also been investigated in screening settings by Li and Shi (2017) and Roesler and Szentes (2017). As previously stated, much of the current literature focuses on how much agents know about their own preferences. This thesis focuses on a mechanism designer's interest in agents knowing about other agents. Additionally, unlike the auction papers that portray the auctioneer as having the ability to provide information to agents, this thesis remains agnostic on where the information about other agents comes from. The emphasis is on how changing information structures can affect the planner's implementation goals. Finally, while our paper asks whether a planner can be interested in agents' information about other agents, one can also ask about an agent's incentives to acquire such information, as done in Gleyze and Pernoud (2023), who show that most economically meaningfully mechanisms cannot prevent an agent who has the option of acquiring information about her own type as well as types of other agents from choosing to acquire information about other agents.

query: What types of point spread functions are used in simulation-based methods for generating density maps?
golden_answer: Gaussian, triangular, or hard-sphere point spread functions are used.
source_title:
Struc2mapGAN: improving synthetic cryo-EM density maps with generative
  adversarial networks
source_text:
# 2 Related work
### 2.1 Existing simulation-based methods

Simulation-based methods for generating density maps from their associated PDB structures are based on the convolution of atom points with resolution-lowering point spread functions such as Gaussian, triangular, or hard-sphere [17, 18]. Given a PDB structure containing $M$ atoms, a general Gaussian simulation formula for producing a density value $\rho$ at a grid point $\mathbf{x}$ is expressed as:

$$
\rho(\mathbf{x})=\sum_{i=1}^{M} \theta Z_{i} e^{-k\left|\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{r}_{i}\right|^{2}}
$$

where $Z_{i}$ represents the atomic number and $\mathbf{r}_{i}$ is the position vector of the i-th heavy atom, $\theta$ is a scaling factor and $k$ is defined in terms of the resolution [9, 5]. Such methods including $e 2 p d b 2 m r c$ in EMAN2 [11] (originally called $p d b 2 m r c$ in EMAN1 [8]), molmap in UCSF ChimeraX [12], StructureBlurrer in TEMPy2 [13], and $p d b 2 v o l$ in Situs [14], generate 3D density maps using a Gaussian point spread function, where the real-space dimension corresponds to the desired resolution, which varies based on the specific resolution convention of each package.

query: What does WROBV stand for in high-frequency trading?
golden_answer: WROBV stands for Windowed Relative On-Balance Volume.
source_title:
Risk-Adjusted Performance of Random Forest Models in High-Frequency
  Trading
source_text:
### 3.3.10 Windowed Relative OBV (WROBV)

The windowed relative OBV (WROBV) is a modified version of the OBV. It is the weighted sum of the values, for a rolling window of size $N$, of the cumulative OBV. This smooths out the indicator:

$$
\mathrm{WROBV}_{t}=\frac{\sum_{i=0}^{N-1} \mathrm{OBV}_{t-i}}{\sum_{i=0}^{N-1} V_{t-i}}
$$

This rolling normalization prevents the OBV from becoming excessively large, and focuses on recent price-volume dynamics.

query: What does DANP stand for?
golden_answer: DANP stands for Decorrelated Activity-based Node Perturbation.
source_title: Noise-based Local Learning using Stochastic Magnetic Tunnel Junctions
source_text:
# Input decorrelation 

For single-layer networks, we can show that ANP is robust, highly performant, and trains extremely well. However, although ANP is more aligned with the true gradient, still performance lags significantly behind that of gradient descent in multi-layer networks. It was shown in Ref. [20] that this performance gap can be overcome by ensuring that the inputs to each network layer are decorrelated. That is, using a decorrelating transform $\bar{x}_{l}=R_{l} x_{l}$, we replace $x_{l}$ in the preceding by its decorrelated representation $\bar{x}_{l}$ for multi-layer networks. It was shown in [30] that the decorrelation matrix $R_{l}$ can be learned in an iterative manner using the update rule

$$
R_{l} \leftarrow R_{l}-\epsilon\left\langle\bar{x}_{l} \bar{x}_{l}^{\top}-\operatorname{diag}\left(\bar{x}_{l}^{2}\right)\right\rangle R_{l}
$$

where $\epsilon$ is a small constant learning rate and $R_{l}$ is initialised as the identity matrix. Integrating this into the preceding leads to decorrelated activity-based node perturbation (DANP), which has been shown to approach the performance of stochastic gradient descent in multilayer networks $[20]$.

query: How does outer Lipschitz geometry relate to complex surface germs?
golden_answer: Outer Lipschitz geometry provides a way to characterize and differentiate between various types of complex surface germs. It is determined by specific functions associated with m-primary ideals, which reflect geometric properties like singularities.
source_title:
Lipschitz geometry of complex surface germs via inner rates of primary
  ideals
source_text:
#### Abstract

Let $(X, 0)$ be a normal complex surface germ embedded in $\left(\mathbb{C}^{n}, 0\right)$, and denote by m the maximal ideal of the local ring $\mathcal{O}_{X, 0}$. In this paper, we associate to each m-primary ideal $I$ of $\mathcal{O}_{X, 0}$ a continuous function $\mathcal{I}_{I}$ defined on the set of positive (suitably normalized) semivaluations of $\mathcal{O}_{X, 0}$. We prove that the function $\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{m}}$ is determined by the outer Lipschitz geometry of the surface $(X, 0)$. We further demonstrate that for each m -primary ideal $I$, there exists a complex surface germ $\left(X_{I}, 0\right)$ with an isolated singularity whose normalization is isomorphic to $(X, 0)$ and $\mathcal{I}_{I}=\mathcal{I}_{\mathrm{m}_{I}}$, where $\mathrm{m}_{I}$ is the maximal ideal of $\mathcal{O}_{X_{I}, 0}$. Subsequently, we construct an infinite family of complex surface germs with isolated singularities, whose normalizations are isomorphic to $(X, 0)$ (in particular, they are homeomorphic to $(X, 0)$ ) but have distinct outer Lipschitz types.

query: What equilibrium concept is used to analyze the dynamic voting game?
golden_answer: The equilibrium concept used is Subgame Perfect Nash Equilibrium (SPNE) with the refinement of stage-undomination.
source_title: Voting with Random Proposers: Two Rounds Suffice
source_text:
# Equilibrium concept 

To analyze the dynamic voting game, we use the equilibrium concept of Subgame Perfect Nash Equilibrium (SPNE), with the refinement of stage-undomination (Baron \& Kalai, 1993), i.e. given future play prescribed by the strategy profile, no player ever plays a weakly dominated action in any voting subgame. Stage-undomination allows also to pin down the voting behavior of individuals who are not critical, which is not constrained by subgame perfection. Under stage-undomination, individuals always vote for the alternative that maximizes their continuation utility, as if they were critical. Henceforth, we call an SPNE satisfying the refinement of stage-undominated strategies simply an equilibrium.

query: Why is it significant that containers preserve least and greatest fixed points?
golden_answer: The preservation of least and greatest fixed points by containers is significant because it ensures that these structures can be consistently applied within different mathematical frameworks, such as intensional type theory, thereby broadening their applicability.
source_title: Formalising Inductive and Coinductive Containers
source_text:
#### Abstract

Containers capture the concept of strictly positive data types in programming. The original development of containers is done in the internal language of locally cartesian closed categories (LCCCs) with disjoint coproducts and W-types, and uniqueness of identity proofs (UIP) is implicitly assumed throughout. Although it is claimed that these developments can also be interpreted in extensional Martin-Löf type theory, this interpretation is not made explicit. In this paper, we present a formalisation of the results that 'containers preserve least and greatest fixed points' in Cubical Agda, thereby giving a formulation in intensional type theory. Our proofs do not make use of UIP and thereby generalise the original results from talking about container functors on Set to container functors on the wild category of types. Our main incentive for using Cubical Agda is that its path type restores the equivalence between bisimulation and coinductive equality. Thus, besides developing container theory in a more general setting, we also demonstrate the usefulness of Cubical Agda's path type to coinductive proofs.

query: What method is used to weigh points when computing the center of an ROI as an alternative to calculating geometric centers?
golden_answer: Local uncertainties and softmax probabilities are used to weigh points when computing the center of an ROI.
source_title:
LUDO: Low-Latency Understanding of Deformable Objects using Point Cloud
  Occupancy Functions
source_text:
## C. Target Position Prediction

To obtain the structural information of the deformable phantom, we first acquire a point cloud of its surface using our depth camera. The phantom surface is segmented from the background by color. From the input surface point cloud, the ON then infers a dense output point cloud that includes both the external shape and internal structures of the deformable phantom. We then transform the dense output point cloud into the robot coordinate system for trajectory planning. The goal position for puncturing is defined as the center of each ROI. The straightforward way of determining the ROI centers is calculating the geometric center of points in the point cloud that are labeled as belonging to the ROI. As an alternative, we further investigate the use of local uncertainties and softmaxprobabilities to weigh the influence of each point when computing the center.

Uncertainty Weighted Centroid (UWC) is the centroid of a set of points, using the prediction uncertainty of each point as a weight. Given a set of points $\left\{\left(x_{i}, y_{i}, z_{i}, u_{i}\right)\right\}_{i}$ where $\left(x_{i}, y_{i}, z_{i}\right)$ are the coordinates of the $i$-th point and $u_{i}$ is the uncertainty of the predicted label, the UWC is a weighted arithmetic mean of the coordinates. To compute the UWC, we

1) normalize the uncertainties

$$
u_{i}^{\prime}=\frac{u_{i}}{\sum_{j} u_{j}}
$$

2) convert uncertainties to certainties

$$
c_{i}=1-u_{i}^{\prime}
$$

3) normalize certainties

$$
c_{i}^{\prime}=\frac{c_{i}}{\sum_{j} c_{j}}, \text { and }
$$

4) compute the UWC

$$
\mathrm{UWC}=\left(\sum_{i} c_{i}^{\prime} x_{i}, \sum_{i} c_{i}^{\prime} y_{i}, \sum_{i} c_{i}^{\prime} z_{i}\right)
$$

Finally, we consider the Softmax Probability Weighted Centroid (SPWC). The SPWC is the centroid of a set of points, using the softmax probabilities of each point as a weight. For this we consider the per-point softmax probability of the predicted label as a weight, see Equation (11). Similar to the UWC, these weights are normalized over all points with the same label.

R\right\}$ ) ensures that generated orders are realistic and aligned with both the user-defined scenario and the underlying market structure.
